whyWrongByChoice.A: Nodal spread is captured by the N component of TNM, not by the stage letter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The letter only stratifies within a numbered stage; it does not override the higher stage number.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The letter is part of staging, not grading; grade is a separate histologic assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stage 3A (14%) and stage 2B (31%) have clearly different 5-year survival rates.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with newly diagnosed colon cancer has a staging summary that includes the designation N3. Which of the following does this designation most likely indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cancer has metastasized to three distant organs

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cancer has spread to many nearby lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The primary tumor is 3 cm in greatest dimension

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor invades to the third layer of the bowel wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is grade 3 with marked nuclear atypia

explanation.summary: The N component of TNM is quantified from 0 to 3; N0 means no lymph node spread and N3 means spread to many lymph nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Node describes whether the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes. It is quantified from 0-3, with 0 meaning no spread to lymph nodes and 3 referring to spread to many lymph nodes. After metastasis, it is the second most important of the three TNM prognostic factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spread to other organs is the M component, quantified only as 0 or 1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Size of the primary tumor is described by the T component, quantified 1-4, not by N.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Depth of invasion is part of the T component, not the N component.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Grade describes histologic appearance and mitoses and is not part of the TNM designation.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man's pathology report for a newly diagnosed carcinoma lists the tumor as T4 N0 M0. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A grade 4 anaplastic tumor confined to the organ of origin

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large or deeply invasive primary tumor without nodal or distant spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: A primary tumor of any size with metastasis to four distant sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: A small primary tumor with spread to four regional lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Four separate primary tumors without lymph node involvement

explanation.summary: T describes the size or depth of invasion of the original tumor on a 1-4 scale, with 4 the largest; N0 and M0 mean no nodal and no distant spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor refers to the size (or depth of invasion) of the original tumor and is quantified from 1-4, with 1 the smallest and 4 the largest. N0 means no spread to lymph nodes, and M0 means no metastasis, so T4 N0 M0 is a large or deeply invasive primary tumor that has not spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grade is a separate histologic assessment; the T category is not a grade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M is quantified only as 0 or 1, and M0 means there is no metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The number of involved lymph nodes is captured by N, and N0 here means no nodal spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T4 describes the size or invasion depth of one primary tumor, not a count of tumors.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: Two patients have the same type of cancer. Patient 1 has a stage 1 tumor that is grade 3 (poorly differentiated). Patient 2 has a stage 3B tumor that is grade 1 (well differentiated). Which of the following best compares their prognoses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patient 1 has the better prognosis because stage outweighs grade

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient 1 has the worse prognosis because poorly differentiated tumors are more aggressive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient 2 has the better prognosis because grade is the most important factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their prognoses are equivalent because stage and grade offset each other

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their prognoses cannot be compared without tumor marker levels

explanation.summary: Staging is generally the most important prognostic factor; grading contributes but is not as important as staging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stage is generally the most important factor for determining prognosis. Although grading is an important prognostic factor, with higher grade conferring a worse prognosis, it is not as important as staging. A stage 1 tumor therefore carries a better prognosis than a stage 3B tumor of the same type even when its grade is higher.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Poorly differentiated tumors are usually more aggressive, but this grade effect does not outweigh the large difference in stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Grade is not the most important factor; stage is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stage and grade do not carry equal weight; stage dominates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor markers help track response and recurrence but are not required to compare prognoses that differ by stage.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: Which of the following patient characteristics is associated with a worse prognosis for a given type and stage of cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A strong initial response to treatment

explanation.summary: A patient's age and general health affect prognosis; elderly and immunosuppressed patients tend to do worse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond stage and grade, a patient's age and general health are prognostic factors. Elderly patients and immunosuppressed patients, such as those with HIV or diabetes, tend to have a worse prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Responding very well to initial treatment might improve prognosis; lack of response worsens it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers carry a better prognosis than receptor-negative ones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HER2/Neu-negative breast cancers carry a better prognosis than HER2/Neu-positive ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is elderly patients, not younger ones, who tend to have a worse prognosis.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with lung cancer returns for a follow-up visit. Which of the following new findings would most likely indicate a worsening of his prognosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decrease in his tumor marker level

choices.label: B
choices.text: A marked response to his initial treatment

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tumor marker level that remains at his post-treatment baseline

explanation.summary: Patients who become hypercalcemic because of their cancer, whether from a paraneoplastic syndrome or bone metastasis, usually carry a worse prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The severity of certain signs and symptoms affects prognosis. Patients who become hypercalcemic because of their cancer usually carry a worse prognosis, whether the hypercalcemia results from a paraneoplastic syndrome or from bone metastasis. Cachexia carries a similarly poor implication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A decrease in a tumor marker usually signifies a positive response to treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A very good response to initial treatment might improve prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A stable post-treatment baseline is reassuring; it is an increase above baseline that suggests recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Well-differentiated histology is low grade and is associated with a better, not worse, prognosis.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman with advanced gastric cancer has lost substantial muscle mass over 3 months even though her food intake has been maintained. Her physician recognizes a hypercatabolic state that cannot be explained by diminished intake. Approximately what proportion of patients with cancer develop this state?

explanation.summary: Cancer cachexia occurs in about 50% of cancer patients and accounts for about 30% of cancer deaths.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer cachexia is a hypercatabolic state defined by a loss of muscle mass (with or without loss of fat) that cannot be explained by diminished food intake. It occurs in about 50% of cancer patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5% greatly underestimates the prevalence of cachexia among cancer patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 10% greatly underestimates the prevalence of cachexia among cancer patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 30% is the proportion of cancer deaths attributed to cachexia, not the proportion of patients who develop it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 90% overstates the prevalence; about half of cancer patients are affected.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman treated for breast cancer has been in complete remission for 2 years, with no evidence of cancer on physical examination, blood work, or imaging. She asks why she must continue follow-up visits for years. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her tumor grade may increase over time without treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her tumor will be restaged with the TNM system at each visit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial remission must be confirmed before treatment ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor markers are the primary tool for diagnosing new cancers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Undetected cancer cells may remain and cause the cancer to grow back

explanation.summary: Even in complete remission, undetected cancer cells may remain and cause regrowth, which is why patients are monitored for years after being declared cancer free.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete remission means all evidence, signs, and symptoms of cancer have disappeared, yet some undetected cancer cells may remain and might cause the cancer to grow back. This is why the word cure is seldom used and why patients must still be monitored for years after they are declared cancer free.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grade is a histologic feature of the tumor; follow-up is driven by the possibility of recurrence, not a rising grade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TNM staging describes the extent of a cancer at diagnosis; ongoing follow-up is about detecting recurrence, not routine restaging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She is already in complete remission, which is beyond partial remission; confirming partial remission is not the reason for follow-up.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor markers should not be used as a primary tool for diagnosing or screening for cancer.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man completed treatment for colorectal cancer and has had no signs or symptoms of cancer since. Some oncologists would consider his cancer cured once he has remained free of signs and symptoms for at least which of the following periods after finishing treatment?

explanation.summary: Some oncologists consider cancer cured if a patient has no signs or symptoms of cancer for at least 5 years after finishing treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although cure is seldom declared because undetectable cells may remain, some oncologists consider cancer to be cured if patients have no signs or symptoms of cancer for at least 5 years after finishing treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One year is too short; the threshold some oncologists use is 5 years.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two years is too short; the threshold some oncologists use is 5 years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three years is too short; the threshold some oncologists use is 5 years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ten years exceeds the 5-year threshold that some oncologists use.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with newly diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer sees the summary "T2b, N0, M0" in his online health record and asks what it means. Which of the following is the most accurate explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tumor has spread to distant sites but not to lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tumor is 2 cm with spread to two nearby lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tumor is 4 to 5 cm with no spread to lymph nodes or distant sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tumor is grade 2 with no mitotic activity or metastasis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is less than 2 cm with no lymph node involvement

explanation.summary: TNM reports tumor size (T), lymph node spread (N), and distant metastasis (M); T2b N0 M0 non-small cell lung cancer is a 4-5 cm tumor with no nodal or distant spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: The abbreviation reports the staging of the lung cancer: the size of the tumor (T), whether it has spread to lymph nodes (N), and whether there is distant spread or metastases (M). T2b describes a tumor between 4 and 5 cm in size, and N0 M0 means no spread to either the lymph nodes or distant sites. This corresponds to a 5-year survival of 31%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M0 means there is no distant metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: N0 means no lymph node spread, and T2b refers to a 4-5 cm tumor, not a 2-cm tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The T, N, and M categories describe extent of disease, not histologic grade or mitotic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T2b indicates a tumor between 4 and 5 cm, not one less than 2 cm.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with breast cancer is found to have a tumor that is HER2/Neu positive. Beyond its effect on her prognosis, which of the following best describes another way this molecular characteristic can matter clinically?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can make the tumor a target for a specific treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: It determines the T category assigned in staging

choices.label: C
choices.text: It establishes the tumor's lymph node status

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the need for histologic grading

choices.label: E
choices.text: It serves as a screening test in unaffected relatives

explanation.summary: Some molecular characteristics of a cancer can make it a target for a specific treatment, which in turn can affect prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancers can have specific molecular characteristics such as particular gene mutations or cell surface receptors. Beyond conferring a better or worse prognosis, some molecular characteristics can make the cancer a target for a specific treatment, which can in turn affect prognosis. HER2/Neu receptor status in breast cancer is one such example.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The T category reflects tumor size or depth of invasion, not receptor status.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph node status is the N component of staging and is not determined by receptor status.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grade is a separate histologic assessment that molecular testing does not replace.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HER2/Neu status is a characteristic of the tumor itself, not a screening test for relatives.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A medical student notices that a 3-cm colon tumor and a 3-cm lung tumor were assigned different T categories on their staging reports. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One of the tumors was misstaged and the report should be revised

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stage criteria are cancer-specific and set by expert committees

choices.label: C
choices.text: T category depends on the number of involved lymph nodes rather than size

choices.label: D
choices.text: T category is assigned by histologic grade rather than tumor size

choices.label: E
choices.text: T category reflects serum tumor marker levels at diagnosis

explanation.summary: The exact anatomic and molecular criteria that determine stage differ greatly from one cancer to another and are established by committees of experts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The exact anatomical and molecular parameters that determine the specific stage of a cancer can be complex and differ greatly from one cancer to the other. A committee of experts establishes the exact criteria for each cancer, so the same tumor size can fall into different T categories in different organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Different T categories for the same size in different organs are expected, not an error.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph node involvement is captured by the N component, not the T component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T refers to size or depth of invasion; grade is a separate histologic assessment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor markers are not part of the TNM staging categories.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman undergoes biopsy of a breast mass showing infiltrating ductal carcinoma. The pathologist notes that tubule formation is still present, but the cells are larger and more pleomorphic than normal, with increased mitoses. Which grade best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Grade 2 infiltrating ductal carcinoma is the middle ground: tubules are still formed, but cells are larger and more pleomorphic with increased mitoses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In infiltrating ductal carcinoma, grade 1 tumors form glands with uniform nuclei and virtually no mitotic activity, whereas grade 3 tumors show nests of cells with no gland formation, marked nuclear atypia, and substantial mitotic activity. Grade 2 is best thought of as the middle ground: tubule formation persists but with larger, more pleomorphic cells and increased mitoses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaplastic describes the highest grade with a complete lack of differentiation, not a tumor that still forms tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grade 1 tumors have uniform nuclei and virtually no evidence of mitotic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grade 3 tumors show no evidence of gland or tubule formation, unlike this specimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stage describes size and spread, not histologic appearance.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a tumor marker?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A compound measurable in serum or urine that is elevated in the presence of cancer

choices.label: B
choices.text: A gene mutation that makes a tumor susceptible to a targeted therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: A histologic feature that indicates the degree of cellular differentiation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A numeric category describing spread to regional lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: An imaging measurement of the primary tumor's greatest dimension

explanation.summary: A tumor marker is a compound measured in serum or urine that is elevated in the presence of cancer, usually because the tumor produces it.
explanation.whyCorrect: A tumor marker is a compound that can be measured in the serum or urine and is elevated in the presence of cancer. These markers are usually substances produced by the tumors, resulting in levels higher than is otherwise normal. Examples include CA19-9, CEA, AFP, chromogranin, PSA, and CA-125.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene mutations and receptors are molecular characteristics of the tumor, distinct from measurable serum or urine markers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Degree of differentiation is the basis of tumor grade, not a tumor marker.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymph node spread is the N component of staging, not a tumor marker.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor size is the T component of staging, not a tumor marker.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: Which of the following cancers has the greatest mortality across both men and women?

explanation.summary: Lung cancer is the most common cancer killer in both men and women.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer in both men and women, and it is the most common cancer killer in both. Stated another way, lung cancer has the greatest mortality across both men and women.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women (greatest morbidity), not the greatest killer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colorectal cancer has a 5-year overall survival of 65% and is not the leading cancer killer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hodgkin lymphoma has an 86% 5-year overall survival and is not the leading cancer killer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men (greatest morbidity), not the greatest killer.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about cancer incidence and mortality is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women and the leading cancer killer in women

choices.label: B
choices.text: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, but lung cancer is the leading cancer killer in women

choices.label: C
choices.text: Colorectal cancer is the second most common cancer in both men and women

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lung cancer is the most common cancer in men, and prostate cancer is the leading cancer killer in men

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prostate cancer has the greatest mortality in men, and breast cancer has the greatest mortality in women

explanation.summary: Breast cancer has the greatest morbidity in women and prostate cancer the greatest morbidity in men, but lung cancer has the greatest mortality in both.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men and breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, but lung cancer is the second most common cancer in both and the most common cancer killer in both. Thus breast cancer has the greatest morbidity for women while lung cancer has the greatest mortality.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, but lung cancer, not breast cancer, is the leading cancer killer in women.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lung cancer, not colorectal cancer, is the second most common cancer in both men and women.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostate cancer, not lung cancer, is the most common cancer in men, and lung cancer is the leading killer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate and breast cancer have the greatest morbidity in men and women respectively; lung cancer has the greatest mortality in both.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 68-year-old asymptomatic man asks his physician to order a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test to determine whether he has prostate cancer. Which of the following best explains why PSA is not a reliable primary tool for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PSA becomes detectable in serum only after treatment has begun

choices.label: B
choices.text: PSA can be measured only in urine, so serum levels are uninformative

choices.label: C
choices.text: PSA is elevated primarily in colorectal carcinoma rather than prostate cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: PSA is produced only by prostate tumors that have already metastasized

choices.label: E
choices.text: PSA thresholds vary with age, so its sensitivity and specificity are low

explanation.summary: Tumor markers should not be used as a primary diagnostic or screening tool; PSA levels change with age, so it has low sensitivity and specificity for detecting prostate cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor marker levels vary from patient to patient and are affected by specific patient characteristics, so they are not a reliable tool for diagnosis or screening. PSA levels change as men age, so the threshold for an elevated PSA differs for men of different ages; therefore PSA has low sensitivity and specificity for detecting prostate cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The usefulness of PSA after diagnosis lies in tracking changes from a baseline, not in becoming detectable only with treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tumor markers, including PSA, can be measured in serum or urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PSA is a marker for prostate cancer; CEA is the nonspecific marker associated with colorectal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSA is a marker for prostate cancer generally; its limitation is variability, not restriction to metastatic disease.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with ovarian cancer has a markedly elevated serum CA-125 level measured before starting chemotherapy. After three cycles of treatment, the level has fallen by more than 80%. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cancer is responding to treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cancer is showing minimal response

choices.label: E
choices.text: The change is uninterpretable because marker levels vary between patients

explanation.summary: After a diagnosis is established, a decrease in a tumor marker from baseline usually signifies a positive response to treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once a cancer diagnosis is established, a physician can measure the baseline level of a tumor marker and track changes over time. A decrease usually signifies a positive response to treatment, while an increase suggests minimal response. CA-125 is the marker associated with ovarian cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cure means no trace of cancer that will never return; a falling marker during treatment does not establish this.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recurrence is suggested by a rising marker after a post-treatment baseline, not by a falling level during treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Minimal response is suggested by an increasing marker, not a decreasing one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Between-patient variability limits markers for diagnosis, but tracking changes within one patient from her own baseline is exactly how markers are useful.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is being evaluated for a suspected neuroendocrine tumor. Elevation of which of the following tumor markers would be most consistent with this diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Chromogranin is the tumor marker associated with neuroendocrine tumors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromogranin is the tumor marker for neuroendocrine tumors. Each of the other listed markers is associated with a different malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a marker for hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CA-125 is a marker for ovarian cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CA19-9 is a marker for colon cancer and pancreatic cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a nonspecific serum biomarker for colorectal carcinoma, among others.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: In an animal model, a renal artery is clamped briefly and then released. A biopsy taken during the clamp shows tubular epithelial cells that are swollen with pale, watery cytoplasm; the nuclei appear intact, and the swelling resolves after blood flow is restored. Which of the following best explains the reversible swelling of these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of homogeneous pink hyaline protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of lysosomal DNases digesting the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the plasma membrane with loss of cellular contents

explanation.summary: Cellular swelling is the classic morphologic change of reversible injury and stems from ATP depletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: When hypoxia depletes ATP, the Na+/K+ pumps that maintain osmotic balance can no longer be powered, so ions and water accumulate and the cell swells. Because this is early and the stimulus is transient, restoring ATP returns the cell to normal osmotic balance, making swelling the hallmark of reversible injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyaline change is an intracellular protein accumulation, not the mechanism of acute swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyorrhexis is a nuclear change of cell death, not the cause of reversible swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leakage of lysosomal enzymes reflects membrane damage in irreversible injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma membrane rupture is a hallmark of irreversible injury, not a reversible change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A cardiac myocyte is subjected to prolonged, severe hypoxia. Which of the following morphologic findings would most reliably indicate that the injury has become irreversible?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restoration of normal osmotic balance after reoxygenation

explanation.summary: Membrane rupture is a defining feature of irreversible cellular injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that a major defining feature of irreversible injury is membrane rupture, which allows leakage of cellular contents and, when lysosomal membranes fail, releases destructive enzymes. Once the membrane is breached the cell cannot recover.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic swelling is the classic change of reversible injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mild, reversible mitochondrial swelling does not by itself signal irreversibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recovery of osmotic balance after reoxygenation indicates the injury was reversible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A transient volume increase is a reversible osmotic change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 20-month-old infant is found to have a retinoblastoma driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB tumor-suppressor gene. When the pathologist identifies this loss-of-function mutation as the event that initiated the disease, which core aspect of pathologic inquiry is being described?

explanation.summary: Etiology is the initiating cause of a disease, which is typically genetic or environmental.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines etiology as the initiation of disease, often a genetic event such as an inherited or acquired mutation. Biallelic RB inactivation is the genetic event that starts the tumor, making it the etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical manifestations are the observed results, such as leukocoria on examination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Morphologic changes are the microscopic findings such as poorly differentiated cells and rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pathogenesis is the mechanism by which the unchecked cell cycle leads to tumor growth, not the initiating cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prognosis refers to the expected disease course, such as the favorable survival rate.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A firefighter is pulled unconscious from a burning building. Cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation is suspected. Cyanide injures cells primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating lysosomal proteases at the plasma membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generating free radicals through ionizing radiation

explanation.summary: Cyanide blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, halting aerobic ATP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that cyanide, a product of incomplete combustion, inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase and thereby inhibits oxidative phosphorylation, decreasing ATP production through aerobic respiration. This energy failure is what damages cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyanide's target is the mitochondrial electron transport chain, not lysosomal proteases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Injury tends to raise cytosolic calcium; cyanide does not primarily deplete calcium stores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyanide does not act by directly cross-linking DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ionizing radiation, not cyanide, generates free radicals that cause oxidative stress.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A patient's occluded coronary artery is successfully reopened. Paradoxically, myocardial tissue damage worsens after blood flow is restored. Which of the following best explains this ischemia-reperfusion injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sudden fall in systemic calcium levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued complete absence of oxygen delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Returning blood delivers oxygen and inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversal of anaerobic glycolysis to aerobic respiration

explanation.summary: Reperfusion can worsen injury because restored blood brings oxygen and inflammatory cells that generate ROS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that restoring blood flow not only brings nutrients but also an influx of oxygen and inflammation that lead to ROS-mediated injury of the already stressed tissue. This is the mechanism of ischemia-reperfusion injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ischemia-reperfusion injury is driven by ROS, not by a drop in systemic calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reperfusion restores, rather than continues to withhold, oxygen delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen depletion is not the described mechanism of reperfusion injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A return to aerobic respiration is beneficial and does not explain the added damage.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Aerobic cells continuously produce superoxide, a reactive oxygen species. Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the first step of neutralizing superoxide by converting it into hydrogen peroxide?

explanation.summary: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, the first step in radical scavenging.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase, and that hydrogen peroxide is then further converted to water by glutathione peroxidase and catalase. Superoxide dismutase performs the initial conversion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase acts downstream, converting hydrogen peroxide to water, not superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome oxidase is a mitochondrial electron-transport enzyme, not a radical scavenger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione peroxidase also acts on hydrogen peroxide, a later step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactate dehydrogenase functions in anaerobic glycolysis, not radical detoxification.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has had a blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg for several years without treatment. Which of the following cellular adaptations is most likely present in his myocardium?

explanation.summary: Chronic pressure overload causes cardiac myocytes to enlarge (hypertrophy).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that hypertrophy is an increase in cell size from increased protein production in response to functional demand, such as cardiac muscle facing an increased workload. Because muscle cells cannot replicate, the heart adapts to sustained hypertension by enlarging its existing myocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophy is a response to decreased demand, the opposite of the increased workload here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperplasia requires cell division, but cardiac muscle cells cannot replicate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is a change of one cell type to another and does not occur in the heart in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sustained hypertension produces a definite adaptive change over time.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman on unopposed estrogen therapy presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. An endometrial biopsy shows an increased number of endometrial glands compared with normal tissue. Which cellular adaptation does this represent?

explanation.summary: Excess estrogen stimulation increases endometrial cell number, producing hyperplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, and that pathologic hyperplasia from excess estrogen stimulation causes endometrial hyperplasia, which can present clinically as abnormal uterine bleeding. The increased number of glands reflects added cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size or number, the opposite of what is seen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dystrophic calcification is calcium deposition in damaged tissue, unrelated to glandular proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, not cell number.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is replacement of one cell type by another, not an increase in glands.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A long-term smoker undergoes bronchial biopsy, which shows the normal ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium replaced by tougher stratified squamous epithelium. This change is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Replacement of one differentiated epithelium by another is metaplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that metaplasia is a reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another, using the example of tobacco smoke inducing metaplasia of ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium into more resistant squamous cells. Removing the stimulus can reverse the change.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracosis is accumulation of black carbon pigment, not a change in epithelial type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size or number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, not a switch in cell type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: At autopsy of an elderly patient, hard, chalky deposits are found within a heavily damaged, atherosclerotic aortic valve. Review of records shows the patient's serum calcium and phosphate were normal. This calcification is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Calcification of damaged tissue with normal serum calcium is dystrophic calcification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines dystrophic calcification as deposition occurring in damaged tissues under normal systemic calcium homeostasis, using the example of a damaged, atherosclerotic aortic valve. Normal serum calcium plus locally damaged tissue fits this definition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin is an iron-rich blood-breakdown pigment, not calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaline change is a pink, glassy protein accumulation, not a calcium deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipofuscin is a brown wear-and-tear pigment of aging, not a calcium deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastatic calcification deposits in otherwise normal tissue due to hypercalcemia, such as excess parathyroid hormone; serum calcium here is normal.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A pathologist examines the heart of an elderly patient and notes a brown, granular pigment accumulating within cardiomyocytes. The pigment is composed of oxidized proteins and lipids, builds up with age particularly in non-dividing cells, and is not harmful to the cell. Which pigment is this?

explanation.summary: Lipofuscin is the brown wear-and-tear pigment of aging, seen in non-dividing cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes lipofuscin as a brown wear-and-tear pigment of proteins and lipids that accumulates with aging, particularly in non-dividing cells such as skeletal muscle, neurons, and cardiomyocytes, and notes it is not harmful to cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracotic pigment is inhaled black carbon that accumulates in the lung and lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilirubin is a yellow-brown bile pigment from abnormal bile excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemosiderin is a yellow-brown iron pigment from blood breakdown, not an aging pigment of oxidized lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanin is a brown-black pigment produced by melanocytes.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: To estimate how rapidly a lymphoma is proliferating, a pathologist orders a stain in which antibodies target a cell-cycle antigen, turning positive nuclei brown. Which of the following techniques is being used?

explanation.summary: Ki-67 immunohistochemistry uses antibodies against a cell-cycle antigen to estimate proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that immunohistochemistry deploys antibodies against a protein of interest, staining it brown or red, and that Ki-67 is an immunostain targeting an antigen involved in the cell cycle used to estimate cellular proliferation. Brown nuclear positivity in a lymphoma is a classic Ki-67 result.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin stains proteins in the cytoplasm pink and is not a proliferation marker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematoxylin stains nucleic acids blue-purple but does not measure cell-cycle activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H&E shows general morphology but does not specifically quantify proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PAS-D highlights substances such as glycogen or alpha-1 antitrypsin globules, not proliferation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A research group studies a neurodegenerative disorder by mapping the step-by-step sequence in which misfolded proteins aggregate, overwhelm degradation systems, and ultimately damage neurons. Which core aspect of pathologic inquiry does this investigation represent?

explanation.summary: Pathogenesis is the mechanism, the inner workings, by which a disease develops.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines pathogenesis as the molecular and cellular mechanisms leading to disease, the machinery and inner-workings of the disease. It gives the specific example that investigating how misfolded proteins lead to cellular damage is an inquiry of pathogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical manifestations are the observable end results of disease, such as a rash or the outcome of a heart attack.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Etiology is the initiating cause of disease, such as a mutation or an infectious agent, not the downstream mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Morphologic changes are the structural alterations a pathologist sees in cells and tissues, such as mitotic figures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prognosis is the expected disease course, to which pathologists contribute through diagnosis and risk factors.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews an H&E-stained section of a pediatric brain tumor and points out several dark purple mitotic figures composed of dividing chromosomes. Which component of the stain is responsible for the dark purple color of these structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A brown chromogen bound to antibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Periodic acid Schiff reacting with glycogen

explanation.summary: Hematoxylin stains nucleic acids and nuclear structures blue to purple.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that hematoxylin appears blue or purple and is useful for highlighting nucleic acids and related structures such as the nucleus. Mitotic figures, made of dividing chromosomes, therefore stain dark purple on H&E.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A brown or red chromogen bound to antibodies describes immunohistochemistry, not H&E.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosin stains proteins pink, which is why cytoplasm is usually pink, not why chromosomes are dark purple.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipofuscin is a brown wear-and-tear pigment, not a feature of dividing chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PAS is a special stain that highlights substances such as glycogen or protein globules red; it is not part of a routine H&E.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: At autopsy, the heart of a man with a long history of untreated systemic hypertension shows a markedly thickened left ventricular wall, whereas the right ventricular wall is of normal thickness. Which of the following best explains why the right ventricle was spared?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypertension causes atrophy of the right ventricle from disuse

choices.label: B
choices.text: Right ventricular myocytes are able to replicate rather than enlarge

choices.label: C
choices.text: The right ventricle pumps into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right ventricle receives less coronary blood flow than the left

choices.label: E
choices.text: The right ventricle undergoes metaplasia instead of hypertrophy

explanation.summary: Only the ventricle working against elevated systemic pressure hypertrophies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure of hypertensive heart disease notes that the right ventricle is of normal size because it delivers blood to the low-pressure lungs and is not directly working against the increased systemic blood pressure. Hypertrophy is a response to increased workload, so the chamber facing the increased load enlarges.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypertension does not reduce the right ventricle's workload, so disuse atrophy is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Muscle cells cannot replicate; this limits their adaptive response to hypertrophy regardless of chamber.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes the difference to workload, not to differences in blood supply.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is a change of one cell type to another and does not occur in the heart in this setting.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with decades of chronic gastritis is found to have gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following environmental etiologies is most closely associated with this cancer?

explanation.summary: Chronic H. pylori infection of the stomach is an infectious environmental etiology of gastric adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick classifies etiology as genetic or environmental, with infectious agents among the environmental causes, and pairs gastric cancer with H. pylori bacteria. Chronic damage from H. pylori infection of the stomach can lead to gastric adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Excess lipids predispose to atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease, not gastric cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ionizing radiation is the etiology paired with papillary thyroid carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tobacco smoke is the well-documented etiology of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UV light damages DNA in the skin and is the etiology paired with cutaneous melanoma.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Two patients are pulled from the water on the same day. A competitive swimmer receives bystander CPR within a minute of losing consciousness and recovers fully. A shipwrecked castaway is rescued hours after drowning and is declared brain dead. Both suffered the same type of insult to their neurons. Which factor best accounts for the different outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Differences in lysosomal enzyme content between patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: The chemical nature of the injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duration of the injurious stimulus

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of reperfusion injury in the swimmer

choices.label: E
choices.text: The type of cell that was injured

explanation.summary: Whether injury is reversible depends on cell type, nature of the damage, and duration; here duration is the variable.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that reversibility depends on the cell type, the nature of the damage, and the duration of the damage, and illustrates this with exactly these cases: prompt CPR for an unconscious swimmer may save life and tissue with few lasting effects, whereas a castaway rescued hours after drowning may suffer brain death. Both patients had the same cell type and the same nature of insult, so the difference is the duration of oxygen deprivation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe interindividual differences in lysosomal enzymes as a determinant of reversibility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both experienced the same nature of injury, oxygen deprivation from drowning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reperfusion injury would worsen, not explain, the good outcome in the swimmer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both patients sustained injury to the same cell type (neurons), so cell type does not distinguish them.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A biochemist studies cultured hepatocytes in which superoxide is being converted normally, yet hydrogen peroxide accumulates to toxic levels within the cells. A defect in which of the following enzymes best explains this finding?

explanation.summary: Hydrogen peroxide is converted to water by glutathione peroxidase and catalase; failure of this step lets peroxide build up.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick recalls that superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase, and that hydrogen peroxide can be further converted to water by glutathione peroxidase and catalase. Since superoxide conversion is intact, the block must be in the downstream peroxide-removal step, which glutathione peroxidase performs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endonucleases degrade nucleic acids during injury and play no role in peroxide removal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Superoxide dismutase generates hydrogen peroxide from superoxide; a defect would lower, not raise, peroxide production, and the stem says superoxide conversion is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phospholipases are calcium-activated enzymes that degrade membrane phospholipids, not radical scavengers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome oxidase is a mitochondrial electron-transport enzyme inhibited by cyanide; it does not scavenge peroxide.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman develops an embolus that lodges in the superior mesenteric artery, sharply reducing blood flow to a segment of small bowel. Which of the following terms most precisely describes the reduction of blood flow itself?

explanation.summary: Ischemia is reduction of blood flow; hypoxia is the resulting oxygen deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines ischemia as reduction of blood flow, which may result in decreased oxygen availability, and hypoxia as the deficiency of oxygen. An arterial embolus reducing flow is ischemia; hypoxia is a consequence rather than the flow reduction itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaerobic glycolysis is the metabolic response to decreased aerobic respiration, not the vascular event.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypoxia is the deficiency of oxygen that may follow reduced blood flow, not the reduction of flow itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidative stress is damage from excess reactive oxygen species, not a description of blood flow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reperfusion injury occurs when blood flow is restored, not when it is reduced.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: An infant with progressive muscle weakness and marked cardiomegaly dies of heart failure. At autopsy, cardiac muscle fibers contain abundant clear spaces on H&E. The disease is caused by an inherited enzyme defect. Which of the following best describes the underlying abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of wear-and-tear pigment with aging

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of misfolded protein as hyaline globules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired lipid metabolism causing fatty change of myocytes

explanation.summary: Pompe disease is a genetic cause of injury in which glycogen accumulates from impaired lysosomal storage.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick presents Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) as a genetic cause of cell injury resulting from impaired lysosomal storage of glycogen, leading to cardiomegaly and heart disease. It notes that excess glycogen is seen as clear spaces on histology compared with normal heart, aiding diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipofuscin is a brown pigment of aging, not an inherited cause of infantile cardiomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcification appears as hard, chalky deposits, not clear intracellular spaces.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaline globules of misfolded protein describe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fatty change reflects impaired lipid metabolism, as in alcoholic hepatic steatosis, not a lysosomal glycogen defect in an infant's heart.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: During prolonged ischemia, a cardiac myocyte shifts from aerobic respiration to anaerobic glycolysis. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this metabolic shift on the cell's internal environment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lactic acid accumulation with a fall in pH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of basophilic staining of the nucleus

explanation.summary: Anaerobic glycolysis raises lactic acid, lowering intracellular pH and affecting enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in response to decreased aerobic respiration, anaerobic glycolysis results in increased lactic acid, lowering the pH of the cell and affecting various enzymes. This acidification is the direct consequence of the metabolic switch.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Injury from ischemia raises cytosolic calcium through release from mitochondria and the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome oxidase belongs to the aerobic electron transport chain, which is impaired, not enhanced, during ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fading of the basophilic nucleus (karyolysis) is a nuclear change of cell death, not the direct product of glycolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Damage to mitochondria and lack of oxygen decrease ATP; anaerobic glycolysis does not restore ATP to a higher level.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: In an experiment, hepatocytes exposed to a toxin show increased mitochondrial membrane permeability and release of a specific mitochondrial protein into the cytosol, after which the cells undergo programmed cell death. Which of the following mitochondrial products is responsible for initiating this pathway?

explanation.summary: Mitochondria trigger apoptosis by releasing cytochrome c under injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that mitochondria are important to the apoptotic pathway, programmed cell death, through the release of cytochrome c under injury. Increased mitochondrial permeability allowing cytochrome c into the cytosol is the initiating event described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acid hydrolases are lysosomal, not mitochondrial, enzymes released when lysosomal membranes are damaged.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ATP is the energy currency whose depletion impairs pumps and causes swelling, not the apoptosis trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactic acid is produced by anaerobic glycolysis in the cytosol and lowers pH; it does not initiate apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase is a ROS scavenger that converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Free radicals generated during ischemia-reperfusion attack the plasma membrane of endothelial cells. Which of the following best describes how a single radical can cause extensive membrane damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It directly cleaves the cytoskeletal anchors that tether the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: It fuses lysosomes with the plasma membrane, spilling acid hydrolases

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits the Na+/K+ pump by binding irreversibly to its ATP site

choices.label: D
choices.text: It initiates lipid peroxidation that propagates as a chain reaction

choices.label: E
choices.text: It shortens telomeres, halting the repair of the damaged membrane

explanation.summary: Free radicals injure membranes by lipid peroxidation, which propagates in a chain reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that free radicals injure membranes through lipid peroxidation, which can propagate in a chain reaction that leads to more lipid and protein damage. This self-propagating property is why a limited radical burst can cause widespread membrane injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoskeletal stress and detachment follow membrane abnormalities; the radical's primary attack is on membrane lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomal membrane damage releases enzymes into the cell; radicals do not cause lysosome-plasma membrane fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Na+/K+ pump failure in injury is due to ATP depletion, not radical binding of the pump.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Telomere shortening is a mechanism of cellular aging, unrelated to acute membrane injury.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A severely injured cell shows fragmentation of its DNA and RNA and digestion of its structural proteins, accompanied by a drop in cytoplasmic pH. Damage to which of the following structures most directly accounts for this combination of findings?

explanation.summary: Lysosomal membrane damage releases acid hydrolases, proteases, and nucleases into the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that damage to lysosomal membranes introduces destructive enzymes into the cell, leading to decreases of pH through activation of acid hydrolase activity and degradation of proteins (proteases) and nucleic acids (endonucleases, RNases, and DNases). The triad of nucleic acid and protein digestion with acidification points to lysosomal leakage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ER releases calcium under injury; it is not the source of proteases and nucleases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial membrane damage releases cytochrome c and calcium and lowers ATP, but does not release the digestive enzymes described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear envelope damage would not explain cytoplasmic acidification or protein digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma membrane damage causes impaired transport and leakage of cellular contents outward, not internal enzymatic digestion.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy from a patient with acute tubular injury shows tubular epithelial cells whose cytoplasm is more intensely pink than that of adjacent healthy cells on H&E. Which of the following best explains this increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of glycogen within the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of hemosiderin from blood breakdown

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of basophilic RNA from enzymatic degradation

explanation.summary: Degradation of cytoplasmic RNA removes basophilic nucleic acid, unmasking eosinophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that activation of enzymes under stress can lead to degradation of cytoplasmic RNA, resulting in a more eosinophilic cytoplasm due to loss of the basophilic nucleic acids on H&E. The injured tubular cells appear more pink because their blue-staining RNA has been lost, not because protein has been added.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycogen accumulation appears as clear spaces on H&E, as in Pompe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin is a yellow-to-brown pigment, not a cause of diffuse cytoplasmic eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Injured cells are not synthesizing more protein; the pinker appearance is from loss of blue RNA rather than gain of pink protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium influx activates enzymes but does not itself alter H&E staining in this way.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A section of injured kidney shows tubular cells whose nuclei are shrunken and stain intensely dark purple, with the nuclear material clumped together. Which nuclear change does this describe?

explanation.summary: Pyknosis is nuclear shrinkage with clumping, giving a shrunken, basophilic nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes three nuclear patterns of cell death: karyolysis, pyknosis, and karyorrhexis. Pyknosis is shrinkage of the nucleus that may clump nuclear material together, resulting in a shrunken, basophilic (dark purple) appearance, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cellular swelling is a cytoplasmic change of reversible injury, not a nuclear pattern of death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyaline change is a pink, glassy cytoplasmic protein accumulation, not a nuclear change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyolysis is loss of chromatin, producing fading of the usual basophilic appearance, the opposite of a dark nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Karyorrhexis is nuclear fragmentation, not a single shrunken, clumped nucleus.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A toxin damages hepatocyte membranes, and the cytosolic calcium concentration rises sharply from its normally low level. Which of the following best describes the immediate source of the excess cytosolic calcium and its principal consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Efflux across the plasma membrane; depletion of intracellular calcium stores in mitochondria and ER

choices.label: B
choices.text: Release from lysosomes; activation of acid hydrolases that lower cytosolic pH and digest organelles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Release from mitochondria and ER; activation of phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release from the Golgi; impaired glycosylation and trafficking of membrane proteins to the cell surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synthesis within the nucleus; fragmentation of chromatin by activated endonucleases

explanation.summary: Injury releases sequestered calcium from mitochondria and ER, activating destructive enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that calcium is normally low in the cytosol and ushered into the mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum; damage from ischemia and toxins increases cytosolic calcium, which leads to increased mitochondrial permeability and further release of calcium. The increased ions activate phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases, which further damage cellular constituents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Injury raises cytosolic calcium; it does not deplete intracellular stores by outward efflux.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomes are the source of acid hydrolases and nucleases, not the calcium reservoir described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick identifies mitochondria and ER, not the Golgi, as the intracellular calcium stores.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcium is an ion that is stored and released, not synthesized in the nucleus.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A patient dies of severe acute lung injury. Histology shows the walls of the alveoli lined by intensely pink, glassy, homogeneous material. A special stain performed on the same tissue turns this material red. Which of the following best characterizes this material and the special stain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulated calcium highlighted by routine eosin counterstain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulated glycogen highlighted by hematoxylin counterstain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Accumulated lipid highlighted by a cytokeratin immunostain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Accumulated melanin highlighted by Ki-67 immunostaining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Accumulated protein highlighted by periodic acid Schiff

explanation.summary: Hyaline change is abnormal protein accumulation, pink and glassy on H&E and red on PAS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes hyaline change as the light-microscopic manifestation of abnormally accumulated proteins, appearing pink, glassy, and homogeneous on H&E, and gives the example of intensely pink hyaline material lining alveolar walls in diffuse alveolar damage, a severe manifestation of lung injury. Pathologists often use periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain to further highlight such changes, which appear red on the special stain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcification appears as hard, chalky deposits, and eosin is part of routine H&E.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen appears as clear spaces, and hematoxylin is part of the routine stain, not a special stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipid accumulation appears as white, empty spaces on H&E, not pink glassy material.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanin is a brown-black pigment, and Ki-67 is an immunostain for proliferation, not for pigment.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with early-onset emphysema and chronic liver disease undergoes liver biopsy. PAS-D special stain shows numerous bright red globules within hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains the formation of these globules?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aggregation of abnormally folded alpha-1 antitrypsin protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dystrophic calcification of chronically damaged hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired lipid metabolism causing macrovesicular steatosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron accumulation as hemosiderin from chronic blood breakdown

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retention of bile pigment from impaired canalicular excretion

explanation.summary: AAT deficiency produces hyaline globules of misfolded protein that stain bright red with PAS-D.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency as a genetic disorder with impaired production of the AAT protein, resulting in aggregation of abnormally folded proteins into hyaline globules, highlighted bright red on PAS-D special stain in the liver. This is an example of protein accumulation as an intracellular accumulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dystrophic calcification produces hard, chalky deposits in damaged tissue, not intracellular protein globules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Steatosis appears as white spaces on H&E, not PAS-D positive globules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemosiderin is a yellow-to-brown iron pigment, not a red PAS-D globule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bilirubin is a yellow-brown pigment from abnormal bile excretion, not a protein globule.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use has a liver biopsy showing hepatocytes filled with large clear vacuoles. He stops drinking, and a repeat biopsy a year later shows near-normal hepatocytes. Which of the following best describes the original finding?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatty change that resolves once the toxic injury is removed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyaline change from misfolded protein aggregates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irreversible glycogen accumulation from a lysosomal defect

explanation.summary: Alcohol-induced hepatic steatosis is a reversible lipid accumulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes fatty change, or lipid accumulation, as occurring due to impairment of lipid metabolism but potentially resolving after resolution of the toxic injury. Excess alcohol causes steatosis through cellular alterations that favor lipogenesis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxidative stress in hepatocytes; lipid appears as white spaces on H&E, matching the clear vacuoles that disappeared after abstinence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracosis is black carbon pigment in the lung and lymph nodes, not liver vacuoles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaline change appears pink, glassy, and homogeneous, not as clear vacuoles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glycogen storage disease is a genetic defect and would not resolve with abstinence from alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastatic calcification deposits calcium in normal tissues due to hypercalcemia and is unrelated to alcohol-related vacuoles.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A retired coal miner dies of respiratory failure. At autopsy the lungs and hilar lymph nodes contain abundant black pigment surrounded by pink, spindled fibrosis. Which of the following best describes the pigment?

explanation.summary: Anthracosis is accumulation of inhaled exogenous carbon pigment in the lung and lymph nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that exogenous pigments such as carbon from exhaust-filled cities, tobacco smoke exposure, and coal mining accumulate as black pigment in the lung and lymph nodes, known as anthracosis. In a coal miner's lung, black anthracotic pigment with pink, spindled fibrosis is the reaction of coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bilirubin is a yellow-brown pigment related to bile excretion, seen in the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin is a yellow-to-brown blood-breakdown product, not black.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipofuscin is a brown pigment in non-dividing cells such as cardiomyocytes and neurons, not black lung pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanin is brown-black but is produced by melanocytes in skin, not inhaled into the lung.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Liver biopsies from two patients each show a yellow-brown pigment in hepatocytes. Patient 1 has a complete obstruction of bile outflow; Patient 2 has had repeated blood transfusions with breakdown of red cells. Which of the following correctly identifies the pigment in each patient?

explanation.summary: Bilirubin arises from abnormal bile excretion; hemosiderin is a blood-breakdown product.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines bilirubin as a yellow-brown pigment that results from abnormalities of bile excretion, seen in a patient who cannot eliminate bile from the liver, and hemosiderin as a yellow-to-brown pigment that is a blood-breakdown product. Bile obstruction produces bilirubin pigment, and red cell breakdown produces hemosiderin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracosis is black exogenous carbon pigment in the lung, not a hepatic pigment from bile obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the two: hemosiderin comes from blood breakdown, and bilirubin from impaired bile excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment of aging and melanin is produced by melanocytes; neither is caused by bile obstruction or transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanin and lipofuscin are unrelated to bile excretion or blood breakdown.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a parathyroid adenoma and a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL is found to have calcium deposits in the interstitium of her otherwise healthy kidneys and in the wall of her normal-appearing stomach. Which of the following best classifies these deposits?

explanation.summary: Metastatic calcification deposits calcium in normal tissues because of systemic hypercalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines metastatic calcification as the deposition of calcium in otherwise normal tissues due to disturbances of systemic calcium metabolism, such as hypercalcemia from excess parathyroid hormone. Calcium deposits in healthy kidneys and stomach in a patient with hyperparathyroidism fit this definition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged or dying tissue under normal systemic calcium homeostasis; here the tissues are normal and calcium is elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty change is lipid accumulation from impaired lipid metabolism, unrelated to calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaline change is pink, glassy protein accumulation, not calcium deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pathologic hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, such as endometrial hyperplasia, not mineral deposition.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy has a uterus many times its nonpregnant size, due largely to enlargement of individual smooth muscle cells under the influence of estrogen. Which of the following best classifies this adaptation?

explanation.summary: Hormone-driven enlargement of cells to meet a normal need is physiologic hypertrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick distinguishes pathologic hypertrophy, increased size due to functional demand such as cardiac muscle under increased workload, from physiologic hypertrophy, increased size due to hormone or growth factors. Its example is exactly this one: the uterus hypertrophies under estrogen signaling during pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pathologic hyperplasia is excessive or inappropriate proliferation, such as endometrial hyperplasia from excess estrogen; this stem describes cell enlargement in a normal state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pathologic hypertrophy is driven by abnormal functional demand, such as the heart facing hypertension, not by normal pregnancy hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physiologic atrophy is a decrease in size, such as involution of embryonic structures, the opposite of what is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is a change from one differentiated cell type to another, not enlargement of existing cells.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: During normal embryonic development, the thyroglossal duct regresses and disappears after the thyroid gland has descended to its final position. Which of the following best classifies this regression?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathologic atrophy due to decreased blood supply

explanation.summary: Involution of embryonic structures such as the thyroglossal duct is physiologic atrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines atrophy as a reduction in tissue or organ size due to decreased cell size through decreased protein synthesis or a decrease in cell number. It specifies that physiologic atrophy is a normal process, such as the involution of certain embryonic structures like the thyroglossal duct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another, not loss of a structure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased blood supply is also listed as a cause of pathologic atrophy, not of normal embryonic involution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Denervation is a cause of pathologic atrophy, a damage response, not a normal developmental process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversible injury refers to mild, transient damage from which a cell recovers; developmental regression is an adaptation, not injury.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Fibroblasts cultured from an elderly donor stop dividing after a limited number of passages, whereas fibroblasts from a young donor continue to divide for many more passages. Which of the following changes best explains why the older cells can no longer enter the cell cycle?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shortening of telomeres at chromosome ends

explanation.summary: Telomeres shorten with each division until somatic cells can no longer enter the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that somatic cells do not have unlimited regenerative and reparative capacities, and that the telomeres, DNA sequences at the end of chromosomes, shorten over time until the somatic cell can no longer enter the cell cycle, halting division. This is the mechanism limiting the older cells' replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipofuscin accumulates with aging in non-dividing cells but is not harmful and does not block cell-cycle entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue and is not a mechanism of replicative aging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick links caloric restriction and prolonged life span to mitigating, not increasing, insulin and IGF-1 signaling; increased IGF-1 signaling is not the reason division halts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is a change in epithelial cell type in response to stress, unrelated to replicative limits of fibroblasts.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man collapses with crushing substernal chest pain and dies before reaching the hospital. At autopsy, a firm, pale, wedge-shaped area is seen in the left ventricular wall. On microscopy the myocytes in this region retain their cellular outlines but have lost their nuclei, and the underlying tissue architecture is preserved. Which pattern of necrosis is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Ischemic infarction of a solid organ such as the heart produces coagulative necrosis, in which tissue architecture is preserved.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coagulative necrosis results from loss of blood supply (ischemia) and is defined by preservation of the underlying tissue architecture of the dead cells. A localized area of coagulative necrosis is an infarct, classically seen as a firm, pale wedge in the heart after a myocardial infarction, where anucleate myocytes still retain their outlines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis produces friable, cheese-like debris within a granuloma and is associated with tuberculosis, not ischemic myocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky-white saponified deposits from lipase action on adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a pattern of vessel-wall injury with deposited fibrin and immune complexes, not a myocardial infarct pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis digests dead cells into a viscous liquid and does not preserve tissue architecture; it is characteristic of the central nervous system, not the heart.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: An autopsy of a 69-year-old man with a history of atherosclerosis reveals an infarct of brain parenchyma perfused by the middle cerebral artery. The affected region is softened and has been converted into a fluid-filled cavity. Which type of necrosis is most closely associated with his cause of death?

explanation.summary: Ischemia within the central nervous system produces liquefactive necrosis, converting dead tissue into a liquid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liquefactive necrosis is dominated by digestion of dead cells, resulting in a viscous liquid of necrotic material and inflammatory cells. Unlike other organs where ischemia causes coagulative necrosis, ischemia in the central nervous system results in liquefactive necrosis, leaving a fluid-filled cavity at the infarct site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis shows a cheese-like appearance and is associated with tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections, not a bland brain infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis, in which architecture is retained, is the pattern of ischemia in most solid organs but NOT in the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinoid necrosis reflects immune-mediated vascular wall damage, not liquefaction of infarcted brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term applied to ischemic death of a limb or digits, not brain tissue.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several weeks of productive cough, night sweats, and weight loss. A chest CT shows an upper-lobe lung lesion. Biopsy demonstrates granulomas with a central area of friable, off-white material that grossly resembles cheese. Which pattern of necrosis is present?

explanation.summary: The cheese-like appearance of necrotic debris within a granuloma is caseous necrosis, classically caused by tuberculosis.
