explanation.whyCorrect: The term caseous refers to the friable, cheese-like, off-white appearance of the necrotic material. Under the microscope, ample fragmented and granular debris is enclosed within a granuloma. Caseous necrosis is commonly associated with tuberculosis infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture after ischemia and lacks the cheese-like granulomatous debris.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky-white calcium/fatty-acid deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis, not granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a vessel-wall pattern with fibrin and immune complexes, not a lung granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis creates a liquid or pus and is typical of CNS ischemia or bacterial abscess, not caseating granulomas.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with heavy alcohol use is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a markedly elevated serum lipase. During surgery, the surgeon notes multiple firm, chalky-white deposits scattered across the fat of the peritoneal cavity. Which process best explains these deposits?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in vessel walls

choices.label: B
choices.text: Digestion of dead cells into a viscous liquid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preservation of tissue architecture after ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saponification of fatty acids with calcium

explanation.summary: In acute pancreatitis, released lipases digest adipose tissue and fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky-white deposits (fat necrosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Fat necrosis occurs with breakdown of adipose tissue. In acute pancreatitis, pancreatic lipases leak into the fat-rich peritoneal cavity, and the released fatty acids combine with calcium to produce a chalky-white substance in a process called saponification. Hard, basophilic calcium deposits are seen microscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin and immune-complex deposition in vessel walls describes fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis, not the chalky fat deposits of pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Digestion into a viscous liquid describes liquefactive necrosis, seen in CNS infarcts and abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BCL2 overexpression blocks apoptosis and drives follicular lymphoma; it has nothing to do with pancreatic fat necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preservation of architecture after ischemia describes coagulative necrosis, which does not produce saponified fat.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis undergoes renal biopsy for hematuria and rising creatinine. Microscopy of a small artery shows the vessel wall replaced by a bright pink, amorphous material containing deposited fibrin and immune complexes, with associated thrombosis. Which pattern of necrosis does this represent?

explanation.summary: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes within an injured vessel wall is fibrinoid necrosis, seen in vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrinoid necrosis refers to a pattern of severe vascular injury in which fibrin and immune complexes deposit in the vessel wall, producing a bright pink appearance. It is seen in vasculitis and autoimmune diseases targeting blood vessels, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis produces cheese-like granulomatous debris associated with tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis is the pattern of ischemic infarcts in solid organs and preserves tissue architecture rather than depositing fibrin in vessel walls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky saponified deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for ischemic death of a limb or digits.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes mellitus is evaluated for several black, shriveled toes. The affected digits are dry, mummified, and mottled, and the changes extend across multiple tissue planes. There is no purulent discharge. Which term best describes this pattern of tissue death?

explanation.summary: Ischemic death of a limb or digits that crosses multiple tissue planes and appears mummified is gangrenous necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gangrenous necrosis refers to ischemic tissue death of a limb, such as the lower leg or digits, that involves multiple tissue planes. It may appear mummified or rotting. When dry, as in this patient, it lacks the wet, liquefied quality that results from bacterial degradative enzymes and host inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like debris of granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat necrosis produces chalky saponified deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinoid necrosis is a microscopic vessel-wall pattern in vasculitis, not a gross description of dead toes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis produces a viscous liquid or pus and is classically seen with CNS ischemia or bacterial abscess, not dry mummified toes.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: In response to irreparable DNA damage, a cell releases a protein from its mitochondria into the cytoplasm. This protein forms an apoptosome complex that binds and activates a critical initiator caspase, launching the executioner caspase cascade. Which caspase is activated by this mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway?

explanation.summary: In the intrinsic pathway, cytochrome c forms an apoptosome that activates caspase-9.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the outer mitochondrial membrane becomes permeable, cytochrome c is released into the cytoplasm, where it forms an apoptosome complex. This complex binds caspase-9, the critical executioner-initiating caspase of the intrinsic pathway, which then triggers a cascade of downstream executioner caspases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic effector that permeabilizes the outer mitochondrial membrane but does not act as the activated caspase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that prevents cytochrome c release; it is not a caspase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caspase-8 is the initiator caspase of the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway, activated through FADD, not by the apoptosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FADD is the adaptor protein of the extrinsic pathway that recruits caspase-8; it is not a caspase itself.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has painless generalized lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows a follicular pattern, and cytogenetics reveal a t(14;18) translocation that places the BCL2 gene adjacent to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer, causing BCL2 overexpression. Which mechanism best explains how this abnormality promotes tumor growth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced caspase-8 activation through the Fas death receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive fibrin deposition within lymph node vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of apoptosis due to sustained blockade of cytochrome c release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased outer mitochondrial membrane permeability with cytochrome c release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncontrolled necrosis with spillage of cellular contents

explanation.summary: Overexpressed BCL2 keeps the mitochondrial membrane impermeable, blocking apoptosis so that lymphoma cells accumulate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL2 keep the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable, preventing release of cytochrome c and blocking the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. In follicular lymphoma, t(14;18) places BCL2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer, causing overexpression that pathologically prevents apoptosis and facilitates lymphoma growth and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enhanced caspase-8 activation would increase death receptor apoptosis, not allow tumor cells to survive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposition in vessels describes fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis and is unrelated to BCL2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased permeability with cytochrome c release would promote apoptosis, the opposite of what BCL2 overexpression does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrosis is uncontrolled death from injury and is not the mechanism by which BCL2 overexpression drives lymphoma.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T lymphocyte recognizes a virus-infected cell and engages the target cell's Fas receptor using Fas ligand. Clustering of Fas causes the cytoplasmic death domains to form a binding site for an adaptor protein, which in turn activates an initiator caspase. Which protein is directly activated at this step of the extrinsic pathway?

explanation.summary: In the extrinsic pathway, Fas clustering recruits FADD, which activates caspase-8.
explanation.whyCorrect: When Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas, the receptors cluster and their cytoplasmic death domains form a binding site for FADD (Fas-associated death domain). FADD leads to the activation of caspase-8, which then initiates the executioner caspase cascade. Caspase-8 can also cleave BID to recruit the intrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic effector of the intrinsic pathway, not the initiator caspase of the death receptor route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein of the intrinsic pathway and is not activated by death receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caspase-9 is activated by the apoptosome in the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, not directly by FADD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome c is released by mitochondria in the intrinsic pathway and is not the caspase activated by Fas.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma begins treatment with pembrolizumab, an antibody directed against the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. Immunohistochemistry of her tumor had shown high PD-L1 expression. Which statement best describes how this drug helps eliminate the tumor?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly triggers coagulative necrosis of the tumor mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases tumor BCL2 expression to promote cell survival

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits caspase-9 to prevent apoptosis of host T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates tumor PD-L1 to enhance immune tolerance

explanation.summary: Checkpoint inhibitors block the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction so cytotoxic T cells can again drive apoptosis of tumor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: PD-L1 expressed on tumor cells binds PD-1 on T cells and blocks T-cell attack, allowing immune evasion. Checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab block this interaction, preventing PD-1/PD-L1 binding and restoring the T cell's ability to kill the cancer cell through apoptosis. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry helps select patients for this therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug works by unleashing immune-mediated apoptosis, not by directly inducing coagulative necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing BCL2 would block apoptosis and protect the tumor, the opposite of the intended effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug targets the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint, not caspase-9, and its goal is to promote tumor cell death rather than inhibit apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating PD-L1 would enhance immune evasion, not treat the cancer.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist is comparing two histologic specimens. In the first, isolated single cells are shrunken with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and fragmented nuclei, surrounded by intact neighboring cells and no inflammatory infiltrate. Which feature best identifies this process as apoptosis rather than necrosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A significant surrounding inflammatory cell infiltrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell shrinkage with a preserved plasma membrane and no inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Random degradation of DNA throughout the injured tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of the plasma membrane with spillage of cell contents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Swelling of groups of adjacent cells with karyolysis

explanation.summary: Apoptosis affects single cells with shrinkage, maintained membrane integrity, and no inflammation, distinguishing it from necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptotic cells undergo shrinkage rather than swelling, with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and controlled nuclear breakup. Membrane integrity is maintained as the cell blebs into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes ingest, so there is no robust inflammatory response. In contrast, necrosis affects groups of cells with swelling, membrane rupture, and significant inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A significant inflammatory reaction accompanies necrosis, whereas apoptosis provokes little to none.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random DNA degradation is seen in necrosis; apoptosis shows ordered internucleosomal fragmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane rupture with spilled contents is a hallmark of necrosis; apoptotic membranes remain intact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Swelling of groups of adjacent cells is characteristic of necrosis, not apoptosis.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to identify which of several processes represents physiologic apoptosis rather than pathologic necrosis. Which of the following is best classified as physiologic apoptosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bowel wall death from mesenteric ischemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiomyocyte death after coronary artery occlusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocyte death from severe thermal burn injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuronal death following a middle cerebral artery stroke

explanation.summary: Apoptosis is a normal, beneficial pathway that eliminates unneeded or self-reactive cells, whereas ischemic and thermal injury cause necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptosis is a controlled, deliberate pathway with beneficial function to the organism. It works to eliminate immature lymphocytes with faulty machinery, such as those that could mount an autoimmune reaction against the body's own tissues. This physiologic deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes is a normal role of apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bowel death from mesenteric ischemia results from loss of blood supply and is necrosis, not physiologic apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiomyocyte death from coronary occlusion is ischemic necrosis, an uncontrolled and pathologic process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A thermal burn is a physical injury that causes necrosis, not physiologic apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuronal death from a stroke is ischemic liquefactive necrosis, which is always pathologic.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with regular 28-day menstrual cycles has a normal menses. During this phase, the functional layer of the endometrium breaks down and is shed after the withdrawal of hormonal support. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of cell loss in this tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial enzymatic digestion producing a viscous liquid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Controlled, caspase-mediated self-destruction after hormone withdrawal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in spiral arteriole walls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipase-mediated saponification of stromal adipose tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Membrane rupture with release of proteolytic enzymes and cytokines

explanation.summary: Involution of hormone-dependent tissue when hormones are removed, such as endometrial breakdown during the menstrual cycle, is physiologic apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptosis is a normal pathway with beneficial function to the organism. One of its physiologic roles is to allow involution of hormone-dependent tissues when hormones are removed, the classic example being endometrial breakdown during the menstrual cycle. This is a controlled, deliberate process that follows specific steps in self-destruction and ends with activation of executioner caspases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial enzymatic digestion producing a viscous liquid describes liquefactive necrosis, a pathologic process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin and immune-complex deposition in vessel walls is fibrinoid necrosis, seen in vasculitis, not in normal menstruation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saponification of fat by lipases is fat necrosis, as in acute pancreatitis, and is unrelated to endometrial involution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Membrane rupture with spillage of contents and an inflammatory reaction describes necrosis, which is always pathologic and does not account for normal menstrual shedding.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A cultured fibroblast is exposed to ionizing radiation that produces extensive DNA damage. Within hours, a family of regulated apoptosis initiators is upregulated and the cell proceeds toward death through the mitochondrial pathway. Which of the following best describes the direct action of these upregulated initiator proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antagonize BCL2 and stimulate BAX and BAK

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bind cytochrome c to assemble the apoptosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly cleave and activate executioner caspases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintain impermeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recruit FADD to clustered cytoplasmic death domains

explanation.summary: BH3-only proteins, upregulated by DNA damage or ER stress, block BCL2 and stimulate the pro-apoptotic proteins BAX and BAK.
explanation.whyCorrect: A group of regulated apoptosis initiators known as BH3-only proteins are upregulated in response to DNA damage and endoplasmic reticulum stress from misfolded and abnormally aggregated proteins. These BH3-only proteins block the function of BCL2 and also stimulate two key pro-apoptotic proteins, BAX and BAK, which increase the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome that binds caspase-9 after it is released; BH3-only proteins act upstream by activating BAX and BAK.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Executioner caspases are activated downstream through the caspase cascade initiated by caspase-9, not directly by BH3-only sensors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keeping the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable is the function of anti-apoptotic BCL2, which the BH3-only proteins oppose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FADD recruitment to death domains is the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway triggered by Fas or TNFR1, not the DNA-damage-driven intrinsic pathway.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A research group engineers a cell line that lacks both BAX and BAK. When these cells are treated with a DNA-damaging agent, BH3-only sensor proteins are appropriately upregulated, yet the cells fail to undergo apoptosis. Which of the following steps is most likely blocked in these cells?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clustering of Fas receptors in the plasma membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Release of cytochrome c into the cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stimulation of BCL2 by growth factor signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of BH3-only proteins by DNA damage

explanation.summary: BAX and BAK increase outer mitochondrial membrane permeability; without them, cytochrome c cannot be released to initiate the caspase cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the intrinsic pathway, BH3-only proteins stimulate BAX and BAK, which increase the permeability of the outer mitochondrial membrane, allowing leakage of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic proteins into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c then forms the apoptosome that binds caspase-9. Without BAX and BAK, the membrane remains impermeable and cytochrome c is not released, so apoptosis is not triggered despite intact upstream sensing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caspase-8 activation through FADD is an extrinsic pathway event initiated at the plasma membrane, independent of BAX and BAK.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fas receptor clustering belongs to the extrinsic pathway and does not depend on BAX or BAK.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth factor stimulation of BCL2 is a survival signal; loss of BAX and BAK does not block it, and it would not be the missing pro-apoptotic step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stem states BH3-only proteins are appropriately upregulated; that step is intact, and it lies upstream of BAX and BAK.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: Hematopoietic progenitor cells are maintained in culture with a growth factor. When the growth factor is withdrawn from the medium, the cells shrink, their chromatin condenses, and they fragment into membrane-bound bodies. Which of the following best describes the initiating event of this cell death?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of PD-L1 to PD-1 on the cell surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clustering of TNFR1 death domains with FADD recruitment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Engagement of Fas by Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of pro-survival signaling that stimulates BCL2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the plasma membrane with spillage of contents

explanation.summary: Lack of growth factor (survival) signals removes stimulation of BCL2 and triggers the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Growth factors and pro-survival signals help stimulate BCL2 to keep the cell alive by keeping the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable. When survival signals are lacking, this protection is lost: BH3-only proteins are activated, BAX and BAK increase mitochondrial permeability, cytochrome c leaks into the cytoplasm, and caspases are activated. Cessation of survival signals such as growth factors is therefore a trigger of the intrinsic, not the extrinsic, pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PD-L1/PD-1 binding is a T-cell regulatory checkpoint and is not the trigger for progenitor cell death after growth factor withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TNFR1 death domain signaling is the extrinsic death receptor pathway, which is not what growth factor withdrawal activates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas-FasL engagement by a cytotoxic T cell initiates the extrinsic pathway; no T cells are present in this culture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Membrane rupture with spillage of contents is necrosis; the shrinkage and membrane-bound bodies described are apoptotic.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: In an experiment, a virus-infected cell is exposed to a cytotoxic T cell expressing Fas ligand. Investigators observe activation of caspase-8 and, shortly thereafter, leakage of cytochrome c from the mitochondria of the target cell. Which of the following proteins, activated by caspase-8, most directly explains the mitochondrial event?

explanation.summary: Caspase-8 activates BID, a BH3-only protein, producing cross-talk that secondarily activates the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways are thought of as separate, there is cross-talk between them. Caspase-8, activated through Fas and FADD in the extrinsic pathway, activates BID, a BH3-only protein. Like other BH3-only proteins, BID antagonizes BCL2 and stimulates BAX and BAK, increasing outer mitochondrial membrane permeability and releasing cytochrome c, thereby secondarily engaging the intrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCL2 is anti-apoptotic and keeps the mitochondrial membrane impermeable; its activation would prevent, not cause, cytochrome c release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caspase-9 is activated by the apoptosome after cytochrome c release; it is downstream of, not the cause of, the mitochondrial leak.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytochrome c is the protein released from the mitochondria; it does not explain why the release occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FADD is the adaptor upstream of caspase-8 that links Fas death domains to caspase-8 activation; it is not activated by caspase-8.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A newly characterized member of the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor family is found on the plasma membrane of immune cells. Structural analysis shows that, unlike TNFR1 and Fas, this receptor lacks a cytoplasmic death domain. Which of the following functions is this receptor most likely to serve?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antagonism of BCL2 at the mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Assembly of the apoptosome with caspase-9

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recruitment of FADD and activation of caspase-8

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria

explanation.summary: TNF receptor family members that lack a cytoplasmic death domain do not relay pro-apoptotic signals and instead activate inflammatory pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The TNF receptor family of proteins are important plasma membrane proteins that feature a cytoplasmic death domain that relays pro-apoptotic signals. TNFR1 and Fas are classic death receptors. However, some family members lack a cytoplasmic death domain and instead function to activate inflammatory pathways. A receptor without a death domain therefore cannot serve as a death receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antagonism of BCL2 is the role of BH3-only proteins in the intrinsic pathway, not of a TNF receptor family member.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The apoptosome forms in the cytoplasm from released cytochrome c and binds caspase-9; it is not assembled by a membrane receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FADD recruitment and caspase-8 activation require clustered cytoplasmic death domains, which this receptor lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome c release is a mitochondrial event of the intrinsic pathway, not a direct function of a plasma membrane TNF receptor.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A protein located within the mitochondria normally functions as a member of the electron transport chain for ATP production through aerobic respiration. When it escapes into the cytoplasm, however, it becomes an important initiator of cell death through activation of executioner caspases. Which of the following is this protein?

explanation.summary: Cytochrome c is both an electron transport chain member and, once released into the cytoplasm, an initiator of caspase-mediated apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytochrome c is an important member of the electron transport chain for ATP production through aerobic respiration. Under stress, the mitochondrial outer membrane becomes more permeable and cytochrome c is released into the cytoplasm, where it forms part of the apoptosome complex that binds caspase-9 and triggers the executioner caspase cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic protein that increases outer mitochondrial membrane permeability; it has no role in the electron transport chain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that keeps the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable and does not participate in ATP production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caspase-8 is the initiator caspase of the death receptor pathway and is not part of the electron transport chain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FADD is a cytoplasmic adaptor of the extrinsic pathway that links Fas death domains to caspase-8; it is not a mitochondrial respiratory protein.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A cell in which both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways have converged now has fully active executioner caspases. Which of the following findings is most likely to be observed in this cell as a direct result of executioner caspase activity?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophil recruitment with pro-inflammatory cytokine release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organelle swelling with rupture of the plasma membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein denaturation with loss of cytoplasmic RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random DNA degradation with spillage of cytoplasm

explanation.summary: The executioner caspase cascade mediates the final steps of apoptosis: proteolysis, cytoskeleton breakdown, DNA degradation, and nuclear fragmentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both the intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic (death receptor-initiated) pathways funnel into the final executioner caspase cascade. This cascade mediates the final steps of cell death, including proteolysis, breakdown of the cytoskeleton, DNA degradation, and fragmentation of the nucleus, all carried out in a controlled manner with membrane integrity maintained.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophil recruitment with cytokine release is the significant inflammatory reaction of necrosis; apoptosis provokes no inflammatory reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Organelle swelling and plasma membrane rupture characterize necrosis; apoptotic cells shrink and keep their membranes intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deep eosinophilia from protein denaturation and loss of cytoplasmic RNA is a feature of necrotic cells, not a caspase-mediated event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random DNA degradation with spillage of cytoplasm is the necrotic pattern; apoptosis shows nonrandom DNA fragmentation without spillage.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist notes numerous scattered apoptotic cells in a tissue section, yet there is no inflammatory infiltrate and neighboring viable cells appear undamaged. Which of the following best explains the absence of injury to adjacent cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: BCL2 sequesters the signals that attract phagocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caspases inactivate cytokines before they can be released

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell swelling dilutes cytoplasmic contents before rupture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Membrane-enclosed bodies are phagocytosed before contents leak

choices.label: E
choices.text: The nucleus remains intact, so no DNA is ever exposed

explanation.summary: Apoptotic bodies retain their membrane coating and are consumed by phagocytes before contents are released, preventing propagation of injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptosis disposes of dead cells in a neat and tidy manner. Cells break into apoptotic bodies containing cytoplasm, organelles, and sometimes nuclear fragments. These apoptotic bodies are easily consumed by phagocytes such as macrophages before cellular contents are released from their membrane coating, preventing propagation of harmful substances or signals that could damage nearby viable cells. Apoptotic cells also release signals to phagocytes to promote elimination with a limited inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCL2 keeps the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable; apoptotic cells actually release signals that recruit phagocytes rather than sequestering them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caspases execute proteolysis, cytoskeletal breakdown, and DNA degradation within the dying cell; the brick does not describe them neutralizing cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Swelling and rupture describe necrosis; apoptotic cells shrink and maintain membrane integrity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The apoptotic nucleus condenses and breaks apart in a controlled manner; the protection comes from membrane integrity, not an intact nucleus.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A skin biopsy shows a single squamous cell with intensely pink, hypereosinophilic cytoplasm that is shrunken relative to its neighbors, with no surrounding inflammatory response. Which of the following nuclear findings is most consistent with the process affecting this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromatin condensed and aggregated beneath the nuclear membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fading of chromatin from progressive endonuclease action

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the nucleus with a preserved cellular outline in the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear swelling with dispersion and clumping of chromatin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random degradation of DNA with plasma membrane rupture

explanation.summary: In apoptosis, chromatin condenses and aggregates under the nuclear membrane before the nucleus breaks apart in a controlled manner.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cell described, with shrunken, dense, hypereosinophilic cytoplasm, single-cell involvement, and no inflammatory response, is undergoing apoptosis. In apoptotic cells the chromatin condenses and aggregates under the nuclear membrane, and the nucleus may begin to break apart in a controlled manner, giving the condensed nuclear appearance seen in comparison with surrounding squamous cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fading of chromatin from endonuclease action is karyolysis, a nuclear change of necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the nucleus with preserved outlines describes cells in coagulative necrosis within an infarct, which involves groups of cells with inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear swelling accompanies the cellular swelling of acute injury and necrosis, not the shrinkage of apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random DNA degradation with membrane rupture is the necrotic pattern; apoptosis shows nonrandom fragmentation with membrane integrity maintained.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist examines tissue from an area of necrosis. Some nuclei have shrunk into small, dense, dark masses. Others have faded, and still others have broken into fragments. Which of the following terms describes the nuclei that have shrunk into small dense masses?

explanation.summary: Pyknosis is shrinking of the nucleus; karyolysis is fading of chromatin; karyorrhexis is fragmentation of the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nuclear changes in necrosis include fading of chromatin (karyolysis) due to endonuclease action, shrinking of the nucleus (pyknosis), and fragmentation of the nucleus (karyorrhexis). The shrunken, small, dense nuclei described are pyknotic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apoptotic bodies are membrane-bound fragments of apoptotic cells, not a term for nuclear shrinkage in necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyolysis is the fading of chromatin caused by endonuclease action, corresponding to the pale, faded nuclei in the stem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyorrhexis is fragmentation of the nucleus, corresponding to the nuclei that have broken into fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Saponification is the combination of fatty acids with calcium in fat necrosis; it is not a nuclear change.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A section through a 3-day-old renal infarct shows tubular epithelial cells that are much more deeply pink on hematoxylin and eosin stain than the viable cells at the edge of the lesion. Which of the following best explains the increased eosinophilia of the necrotic cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of calcium soaps within the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Condensation of chromatin beneath the nuclear membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of cytoplasmic RNA and denaturation of proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phagocytosis of neutrophils into the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Necrotic cells are deeply eosinophilic partly because of loss of cytoplasmic RNA and denatured proteins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dying cells from necrosis are often deeply eosinophilic, partly due to loss of cytoplasmic RNA (which is basophilic) and denatured proteins, which bind the pink eosin dye. This accompanies the nuclear changes of karyolysis, pyknosis, and karyorrhexis and the preserved tubular architecture of coagulative necrosis in an infarct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcium soaps are the chalky, basophilic deposits of fat necrosis in adipose tissue, and calcium deposits stain basophilic (blue), not eosinophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromatin condensation under the nuclear membrane is a nuclear change of apoptosis and does not explain cytoplasmic eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin and immune-complex deposition occurs in vessel walls in fibrinoid necrosis, not inside infarcted tubular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inflammatory cells react to necrotic debris from outside the dead cells; they are not phagocytosed into the cytoplasm of necrotic cells.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is evaluated for crushing chest pain that began 4 hours ago. Serum troponin is markedly elevated. Which of the following features of the cell death occurring in his myocardium best explains why this contractile protein can be detected in the blood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caspase-mediated cleavage that releases troponin fragments

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin within coronary vessel walls

choices.label: C
choices.text: Packaging of contractile proteins into apoptotic bodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of cell membranes with spillage of cytoplasmic contents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saponification of myocyte membranes by calcium

explanation.summary: Necrosis is uncontrolled; membranes rupture and spill intracellular contents, including troponins, into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Troponins are contractile proteins present in cardiac muscle. During a myocardial infarction, cardiomyocytes undergo necrosis. Because necrosis is an uncontrolled process, membranes rupture and cells spill their cytoplasmic contents, including troponins, which are then measurable in the blood and are clinically useful in the monitoring and management of patients with myocardial infarction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caspase activation is the mechanism of apoptosis; ischemic myocardial death is necrosis, in which cells do not have time for an organized signaling pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposition in vessel walls is fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis; it does not explain leakage of myocyte proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Apoptotic bodies retain their membrane coating and are phagocytosed before contents are released; this would keep troponin out of the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Saponification is the combination of fatty acids with calcium in fat necrosis of adipose tissue, not a mechanism of myocyte content release.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of substernal chest pressure. An electrocardiogram is concerning for an acute myocardial infarction, but her initial serum troponin is within the reference range. Which of the following statements best guides interpretation of this troponin result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal value at presentation excludes myocardial necrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Troponin is released only after liquefaction of the infarct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Troponin remains within apoptotic bodies until they are phagocytosed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Troponin rises only when cardiomyocytes die by apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Troponin typically becomes measurable about 2 hours after necrosis

explanation.summary: Troponins released by necrotic cardiomyocytes can be measured in the blood about 2 hours following necrosis, so a very early value may be normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiomyocytes undergoing necrosis spill their intracellular contents, including troponins. These troponins can be measured in the blood 2 hours following necrosis and are clinically useful in the monitoring and management of patients with myocardial infarction. At 30 minutes after symptom onset, necrosis may not yet have released a measurable amount, so a normal early value should be interpreted in light of this timing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Because troponin becomes measurable roughly 2 hours after necrosis, a normal value 30 minutes after symptom onset does not exclude necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ischemic myocardial death is coagulative, not liquefactive, necrosis; troponin release results from membrane rupture, not liquefaction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Apoptotic bodies are a feature of apoptosis; infarcted myocardium undergoes necrosis, in which contents leak through ruptured membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Troponin release reflects necrosis with spillage of contents; apoptosis maintains membrane integrity and would not spill troponin.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman develops occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery. Over the following days, the zone of bowel-wall necrosis expands to involve cells that were initially outside the ischemic territory. Which of the following best explains this spread of injury to neighboring cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptotic bodies transfer death signals to adjacent cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: BH3-only proteins diffuse into neighboring cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytochrome c is secreted and taken up by nearby cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: FADD is activated in adjacent cells by released Fas ligand

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inflammatory cells release proteolytic enzymes and cytokines

explanation.summary: In necrosis, inflammatory cells reacting to dying cells and debris release proteolytic enzymes and pro-inflammatory cytokines that damage nearby cells, propagating injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cells undergoing necrosis rupture their membranes, spill cytoplasmic contents, and denature proteins. Inflammatory cells react to dying cells and debris with additional proteolytic enzymes and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Damage from this inflammation can spread to nearby cells, resulting in propagation of injury and necrosis, which is why necrosis affects groups of neighboring cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed before contents leak, preventing propagation of harmful signals; they do not spread injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BH3-only proteins are intracellular sensors of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway; the brick does not describe them diffusing between cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytochrome c is released from mitochondria into the cytoplasm of the same cell during apoptosis; it is not a secreted signal that kills neighbors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FADD is an intracellular adaptor of the extrinsic pathway; propagation of necrosis is driven by inflammation, not by death receptor signaling.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with a painful, red, fluctuant swelling on his thigh following a bacterial skin infection. Incision releases a creamy, yellow liquid composed of necrotic material and inflammatory cells. Which pattern of necrosis is present?

explanation.summary: Pus, a creamy yellow liquid of necrotic material and inflammatory cells, is the product of liquefactive necrosis in a bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liquefactive necrosis is dominated by the digestion of dead cells, resulting in a viscous liquid. Pus is a creamy, yellow liquid of necrotic material and inflammatory cells, the hallmark of liquefactive necrosis caused by bacterial infection. Liquefactive necrosis is also the pattern of ischemia within the central nervous system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis produces friable, cheese-like, off-white debris within a granuloma, classically in tuberculosis, not a fluctuant pus-filled abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture, as in an infarct; it does not produce a liquid collection of pus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky-white saponified deposits in adipose tissue, as in acute pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a pattern of vessel-wall injury with fibrin and immune-complex deposition, seen in vasculitis.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease has a black, ischemic forefoot. Unlike a dry, mummified appearance, the tissue is swollen, moist, and foul-smelling, with purulent drainage. Which of the following best explains the wet character of this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrin deposition within the walls of dermal vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liquefaction by bacterial enzymes and host inflammatory cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preservation of tissue architecture after ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saponification of subcutaneous fat by leaked lipases

explanation.summary: Wet gangrene results from greater contributions of liquefactive necrosis from bacterial degradative enzymes and the host inflammatory counter-attack.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for ischemic tissue death of a limb or digits involving multiple tissue planes; it may appear mummified or rotting. Wet gangrene results from greater contributions of liquefactive necrosis from the degradative enzymes of bacteria and the counter-attack of host inflammatory cells, which digest dead tissue into a liquid and account for the moist, purulent appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin deposition in vessel walls is fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis and does not explain liquefaction of a gangrenous foot.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomas with cheese-like debris describe caseous necrosis, associated with tuberculosis, not gangrene of an ischemic limb.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preservation of architecture is coagulative necrosis, which underlies the dry, mummified form rather than the wet, liquefied form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Saponification of fat by lipases is fat necrosis, as in acute pancreatitis; it produces chalky-white deposits, not a wet, purulent limb.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old mountaineer sustains a severe freezing injury to his toes, which become black and necrotic across skin, subcutaneous tissue, and bone. A pathologist notes that the term used for this lesion, unlike the other named patterns of necrosis, is defined by its clinical context rather than by a distinct microscopic appearance. Which term is being described?

explanation.summary: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for ischemic death of a limb or digits across multiple tissue planes, and frostbite is a classic cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for ischemic tissue death of a limb, such as the lower leg or digits, that involves multiple tissue planes; it is commonly used in the context of the limbs and digits. Frostbite, a severe freezing injury, may result in gangrene. The other patterns listed are defined by their histologic or gross appearance rather than by the clinical setting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis is defined by its cheese-like appearance and granular debris within a granuloma, typically in tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat necrosis is defined by saponification of adipose tissue with chalky-white deposits, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinoid necrosis is a microscopic pattern of fibrin and immune-complex deposition in vessel walls in vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis is defined by digestion of dead cells into a viscous liquid, as in CNS infarcts and abscesses.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with gallstones develops acute pancreatitis. At laparotomy, a biopsy of peripancreatic adipose tissue shows necrotic fat cells with hard, basophilic deposits scattered among them. Which of the following enzymes is most directly responsible for initiating the process that produced these deposits?

explanation.summary: In acute pancreatitis, leaked pancreatic lipases digest adipose tissue, freeing fatty acids that combine with calcium to form hard, basophilic deposits.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fat necrosis occurs with the breakdown of adipose tissue. In acute pancreatitis, pancreatic lipases leak into the fat-rich peritoneal cavity and digest adipose tissue, freeing fatty acids that combine with calcium in a process called fat saponification. Under the microscope, hard and basophilic calcium deposits are commonly seen in this type of necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial degradative enzymes contribute to liquefactive necrosis and wet gangrene, not to sterile fat necrosis of pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caspase-9 is the intrinsic-pathway initiator caspase of apoptosis and has no role in the breakdown of adipose tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endonuclease action causes fading of chromatin (karyolysis) in necrotic nuclei; it does not digest fat or generate calcium deposits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proteolytic enzymes from inflammatory cells propagate necrotic injury but are not the lipases that free fatty acids from fat.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A renal biopsy from a 48-year-old man with an autoimmune vasculitis shows a small vessel whose wall is replaced by bright pink fibrinoid material with surrounding inflammation and no viable endothelial cells. A thrombus fills the lumen. Which of the following best describes the relationship between the thrombus and the vessel-wall necrosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The thrombus is a cluster of apoptotic bodies awaiting phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thrombus is caseous debris shed from a granuloma

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thrombus is embolized saponified fat from the pancreas

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thrombus is secondary to damage from the vasculitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The thrombus is the primary cause of the fibrinoid change

explanation.summary: In autoimmune vasculitis, the luminal thrombus is a consequence of vessel-wall damage rather than the cause of the fibrinoid necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrinoid necrosis is a pattern of severe vascular injury in which fibrin and immune complexes deposit in the vessel wall, seen in vasculitis such as autoimmune diseases targeting blood vessels. The wall shows inflammation and loss of viable endothelial cells. A thrombus, or blood clot, may be seen in the lumen; in this setting the thrombus is secondary to damage from the autoimmune vasculitis rather than the cause of the fibrinoid necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apoptotic bodies are membrane-bound fragments of single apoptotic cells; the luminal material here is a blood clot in a necrotic vessel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseous debris is the cheese-like material within granulomas of tuberculosis and is not the content of a vessel lumen in vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Saponified fat is a feature of fat necrosis in adipose tissue during pancreatitis and does not form intravascular thrombi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fibrinoid change results from immune-mediated injury to the vessel wall; the clot forms because the damaged wall lacks viable endothelium, not the reverse.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A surgical pathology report on a resected colon states that on gross examination a 4-cm tumor was identified. A medical student asks what the word gross means in this context. Which of the following is the best answer?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A finding that requires light microscopy to identify

choices.label: C
choices.text: A finding visible at the organ level without a microscope

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clinical term for ischemic necrosis of a limb

choices.label: E
choices.text: The physical cutting and sampling of the specimen

explanation.summary: In pathology, gross refers to an appearance or finding seen at the organ level without the aid of a microscope; grossing is the physical processing of a specimen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pathologists use the term gross to refer to an appearance or finding that can be seen at the organ level without the aid of a microscope. The related verb grossing means the physical processing of an organ in the surgical pathology laboratory, such as cutting and sampling a large tumor present in a resected length of colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immunohistochemistry, such as scoring PD-L1 expression in tumor cells, is a laboratory stain, not what gross means.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Findings requiring light microscopy are histologic or microscopic, the opposite of gross.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The clinical term for ischemic necrosis of a limb or digits is gangrene, not gross.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The physical cutting and sampling of a specimen is grossing, the verb, rather than the meaning of a gross finding.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with metastatic carcinoma undergoes tumor biopsy. Immunohistochemistry shows that the tumor cells strongly express PD-L1. Tumor-infiltrating T cells that contact these cancer cells show reduced function and many undergo programmed cell death. Which of the following best explains the fate of these T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PD-L1 antagonizes BH3-only proteins within the T cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: PD-L1 binds T-cell PD-1, decreasing function and inducing apoptosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: PD-L1 blocks FADD recruitment inside the tumor cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor BCL2 is transferred to T cells and blocks caspase activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor cells phagocytose T cells as apoptotic bodies

explanation.summary: Binding of tumor PD-L1 to PD-1 on T cells decreases T-cell function and leads to T-cell apoptosis, allowing the tumor to evade the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Programmed Death-1 (PD-1) is a receptor on T cells important to normal immune regulation, preventing T-cell attack of host cells. Binding of PD-1 to PD-L1 decreases T-cell function and leads to apoptosis. Cancer cells can upregulate PD-L1 to prevent an anti-tumor immune response, which is why PD-L1 expression on tumor cells leads to reduced T-cell function and T-cell apoptosis. Quantifying PD-L1 by immunohistochemistry helps pathologists determine treatment selection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PD-L1 acts at the cell surface through PD-1 signaling; the brick does not describe it antagonizing BH3-only proteins inside the T cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The effect of PD-L1 is on the T cell through PD-1, not on FADD signaling within the tumor cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: BCL2 is an intracellular anti-apoptotic protein; it is not transferred between cells, and blocking caspases would prevent, not cause, T-cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagocytes such as macrophages consume apoptotic bodies; tumor cells do not kill T cells by phagocytosing them.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A hepatocyte is exposed to a toxin that causes a marked, sustained rise in cytoplasmic calcium concentration. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this change in the injured cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of multiple cellular enzymes and increased mitochondrial permeability

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of pro-apoptotic proteins by accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER

choices.label: C
choices.text: Damage to lipids, proteins, and nuclear DNA by reactive oxygen species

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enzymatic digestion of cellular components by released lysosomal enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of cellular components through a damaged, leaky plasma membrane

explanation.summary: Increased cytoplasmic calcium activates multiple cellular enzymes and increases mitochondrial permeability.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the mechanisms of cell injury, increased cytoplasmic calcium leads directly to activation of multiple cellular enzymes and to increased mitochondrial permeability. Increased mitochondrial permeability in turn permits leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins, linking calcium overload to cell death.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Activation of pro-apoptotic proteins is the consequence of protein misfolding and DNA damage, a distinct injury mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Damage to lipids, proteins, and DNA is the direct consequence of reactive oxygen species, a separate mechanism of injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enzymatic digestion of cellular components follows lysosomal membrane damage, not a rise in cytoplasmic calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of cellular components is the consequence of plasma membrane damage, not the direct effect of increased cytoplasmic calcium.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A chemical injury damages the lysosomal membranes of a renal tubular cell. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this membrane damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Depletion of ATP with multiple downstream effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins from the mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of cellular components through the plasma membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of BH3-only proteins by DNA damage

explanation.summary: Damage to the lysosomal membrane releases lysosomal enzymes, causing enzymatic digestion of cellular components.
explanation.whyCorrect: Membrane damage is one of the principal mechanisms of cell injury, and its consequences depend on which membrane is affected. Damage to the lysosomal membrane leads to enzymatic digestion of cellular components, whereas damage to the plasma membrane leads to loss of cellular components.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP depletion is a separate mechanism of injury with multiple downstream effects; it is not the direct result of lysosomal membrane damage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins is the consequence of mitochondrial damage, not lysosomal membrane injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of cellular components is the consequence of plasma membrane damage, the other membrane target of injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BH3-only proteins are upregulated in response to DNA damage and ER stress, not to lysosomal membrane rupture.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist examines tissue and organs that were removed from patients during operative procedures, evaluating them under the microscope to diagnose disease and guide treatment selection. This work is the primary domain of which subspecialty of anatomic pathology?

explanation.summary: Surgical pathology evaluates tissues and organs procured by a surgical procedure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines surgical pathology as the branch of anatomic pathology that evaluates tissues and organs procured by a surgical procedure, generated through biopsies, excisions, and resections. Evaluating operatively removed tissue under the microscope to diagnose disease is exactly this discipline.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytopathology focuses on diagnosis at the level of individual cells rather than intact tissues and organs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forensic pathology and medical autopsy address cause of death, not routine evaluation of operatively procured tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematopathology deals with blood products, which the brick specifically excludes from anatomic (and cytopathology) practice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular pathology involves specialized molecular tests for treatment selection rather than routine microscopic tissue evaluation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: During an operative procedure for cancer, a surgeon notices a suspicious nodule in the mesentery. If the nodule is cancerous, the surgeon will alter the operation. Which of the following would be most helpful to rapidly determine the identity of the lesion during the surgery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excise the nodule for formalin-fixed paraffin embedding

explanation.summary: A frozen section provides rapid intraoperative diagnosis, usually in under 20 minutes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the frozen section as a rapid intraoperative evaluation in which the pathologist freezes the tissue, evaluates it, and calls back a preliminary result, usually in under 20 minutes. This lets the surgeon obtain the identity of the lesion while the operation is still ongoing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Formalin-fixed paraffin embedding (FFPE) requires significant processing in the histology laboratory and is not a means of rapid intraoperative evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Special stains are also performed on processed sections and cannot provide an answer during the surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry is generally performed on routine FFPE sections and would not be available until after laboratory processing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular testing may be performed in certain cases but takes significant time to yield results.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a suspicious cyst on her forearm. The surgeon removes the entire lesion in a single procedure, both to establish a diagnosis and to treat the patient by removing the abnormal tissue. Which of the following best describes this procedure?

explanation.summary: An excision (excisional biopsy) removes the entirety of the abnormal tissue and can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that excisions, including excisional biopsies, are performed with the intent of removing the entirety of the abnormal tissue, possibly curing the disease process. As such, an excisional biopsy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic and is less extensive than a resection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A core biopsy uses a needle to sample a core of tissue for diagnosis and does not remove the whole lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incisional biopsy removes only a portion of the abnormal tissue for diagnostic sampling, not the entire lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A punch biopsy uses a cylindric blade to remove a small tissue sample, again for sampling rather than complete removal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A resection is a major surgery that removes part or all of an organ and is more extensive than an excision of a small cyst.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with gastric adenocarcinoma undergoes a major surgery in which the diseased stomach is removed. Which of the following terms names this resection?

explanation.summary: A gastrectomy is the resection of the stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches resection terminology in which the procedure is named for the organ removed: a gastrectomy is a resection of the stomach. Resections are major surgeries often performed for malignancies such as gastric cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A colectomy is a resection of the colon, not the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hepatectomy is removal of the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mastectomy is removal of the breast.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A nephrectomy is removal of a kidney and does not describe removal of the stomach.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: After a routine breast biopsy specimen is grossed, it is placed in fixative and processed by the histology laboratory into tissue blocks that are then stored for at least 10 years in case future evaluation is necessary. Which of the following best describes these archived blocks?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stained cytology smears on glass slides

explanation.summary: Routine surgical specimens are processed into formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) blocks stored for at least 10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that after grossing, surgical pathology specimens are typically processed into formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks, and that these FFPE blocks are stored for at least 10 years in case future evaluation is necessary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoalveolar lavage is a cytopathology sampling method for cells from the airways, not a tissue-block preservation method.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fresh, unfixed tissue is not preserved and would not survive years of storage; the formalin fixation and paraffin embedding are what allow archiving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frozen section blocks are prepared for rapid intraoperative evaluation, not for long-term archival of routine specimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytology smears are used in cytopathology to evaluate individual cells, not to embed and archive tissue blocks.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A tissue section is stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic evaluation. Under the microscope, one of the dyes stains the nucleus and nuclear material a dark blue-to-purple color. Which dye is responsible for this staining?

explanation.summary: Hematoxylin stains the nucleus and nuclear material dark blue to purple.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that in the routine H&E stain, hematoxylin appears dark blue or purple and is useful for visualizing the nucleus and nuclear material, whereas eosin stains cytoplasmic components pink.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin appears pink and stains cytoplasmic components, not the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver is a special stain that highlights fungal organisms gray-to-black, not a routine nuclear stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunohistochemical stains target specific molecular antigens (often appearing brown), not general nuclear material in H&E.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Masson trichrome is a special stain used to visualize fibrosis, not to stain nuclei in the routine H&E.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 55-year-old immunocompromised man has a lung nodule, and the pathologist suspects a fungal infection. Which of the following stains would be most helpful to highlight fungal organisms in the tissue section?

explanation.summary: The Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) special stain highlights fungal organisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes special stains as dyes or chemicals with an affinity for a certain tissue component, and specifically states that the Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain is used to highlight fungal organisms, staining them gray to black.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin alone stains cytoplasmic components pink and does not selectively highlight fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin identifies epithelial (carcinoma) cells, not fungal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Masson trichrome is a special stain used to visualize fibrosis, not fungal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hematoxylin and eosin is the routine stain for general tissue architecture and is not the special stain used to highlight fungi.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hepatologist requests evaluation of a liver biopsy to assess the degree of fibrosis (scarring). Which of the following special stains is most helpful for visualizing fibrosis?

explanation.summary: Masson trichrome is a special stain helpful for visualizing fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists special stains and specifically notes that Masson trichrome is helpful for visualizing fibrosis, making it the appropriate choice for assessing the degree of scarring in a liver biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin alone stains cytoplasm pink and does not specifically demonstrate collagen deposition in fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver is used to highlight fungal organisms, not fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematoxylin and eosin is the routine stain and is not the dedicated special stain for fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin identifies epithelial-origin (carcinoma) cells, not areas of fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A poorly differentiated tumor is difficult to classify on routine H&E. The pathologist performs immunohistochemistry, which is positive (brown) for cytokeratin, an intermediate filament found in epithelial cells. This result most strongly supports which of the following diagnoses?

explanation.summary: Cytokeratin positivity indicates epithelial origin, confirming a carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that immunohistochemistry directed against cytokeratins, intermediate filaments in epithelial cells, is often used to confirm a tumor as a carcinoma, a malignant tumor of epithelial origin. A cytokeratin-positive tumor is therefore best classified as a carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrosis is scarring visualized with Masson trichrome and is not a cytokeratin-positive epithelial tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fungal infection is identified with special stains such as GMS, not with an epithelial immunostain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lymphoma arises from lymphoid cells and is identified by lymphoid markers, not cytokeratin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sarcoma is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin and would not be defined by epithelial cytokeratin positivity.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A medical student wants to know the size of a hepatocellular carcinoma as measured in the pathology laboratory. In which section of the surgical pathology report would this information most likely be found?

explanation.summary: The measured size of a tumor is documented in the gross description.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the gross description is the physical description of the specimen and documentation of how it was processed, and that the size of the primary tumor (which determines the T stage) is found in the gross description.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An addendum details additional information after finalization that does not change the diagnosis, not the measured tumor size.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical information may reference a radiologic size, but the size measured in the laboratory is recorded in the gross description.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The comment is where the pathologist gives an opinion on the case, not where the specimen measurements are listed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The microscopic description details cellular and tissue-level observations under the microscope rather than the gross measured size.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: After a surgical pathology report has been finalized and signed out, an ordered immunostain result becomes available. It supports and does not change the original diagnosis. The pathologist incorporates this new result into the report. This addition is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: An addendum is a minor modification, such as incorporating later test results that do not change the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an addendum as a minor modification to the report, such as the incorporation of testing results that were not previously available and do not change the diagnosis. That matches a supporting immunostain added after sign-out.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An amendment is a major change made after finalization; a change in diagnosis would warrant an amendment, which did not occur here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The final diagnosis is the top diagnostic line naming the disease, not a post-finalization addition of new test results.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gross description documents the specimen's physical appearance and processing, not newly available test results.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synoptic report is a structured report of prognostic information included in certain cancer cases, not a late modification.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule sampled by fine needle aspiration (FNA), and individual cells are evaluated by cytopathology. Compared with a surgical pathology specimen, which of the following is a disadvantage of this cytopathologic approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be used to sample nodules of the thyroid gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more invasive than a surgical resection specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not optimal for evaluating tissue architecture

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is unable to detect frankly cancerous cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires removal of the entire affected organ

explanation.summary: Because cytopathology evaluates individual cells rather than intact tissue, it is not optimal for assessing tissue architecture.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a disadvantage of cytopathology is that it is not optimal for the evaluation of tissue cytoarchitecture, and that fewer cells are available for evaluation compared with many surgical pathology specimens. FNA sampling of a thyroid nodule illustrates this limitation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FNA is specifically described as commonly used for thyroid nodules and salivary gland tumors, so it can indeed sample thyroid nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick lists minimal invasiveness as an advantage of cytopathology, so it is not more invasive than a resection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytopathology can identify worrisome or malignant cells (for example, on a Pap smear), so it is not unable to detect cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytopathology samples cells without removing an entire organ; whole-organ removal describes a resection, not FNA.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A first-year medical student on a hospital tour asks what unifies the many subspecialties of pathology, from surgical pathology to hematopathology. Which of the following best describes the role of pathology as a medical discipline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administering chemotherapy according to tumor stage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Counseling patients on lifestyle modification for chronic disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Imaging lesions to guide the placement of biopsy needles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Performing the surgical resection of malignant tumors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Providing diagnostic information to patients and clinicians

explanation.summary: Pathology is the medical discipline that provides diagnostic information to patients and clinicians.
explanation.whyCorrect: The College of American Pathologists defines pathology as the medical discipline that provides diagnostic information to patients and clinicians, impacting nearly all aspects of patient care from diagnosing cancer to managing chronic diseases through accurate laboratory testing. Every subspecialty, anatomic or clinical, shares this diagnostic role.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Treatment such as chemotherapy is selected by the clinical team; pathology informs that choice with diagnostic information rather than delivering therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lifestyle counseling is a clinical management task, not the diagnostic function that defines pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imaging to guide biopsies is the work of interventional radiology, which procures the specimen that pathology then evaluates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resections are performed by the surgeon; the pathologist evaluates the tissue that the surgeon removes.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hospital laboratory receives five items in one afternoon: a colectomy specimen, a cervical Pap smear, a sputum sample submitted for bacterial culture, a thyroid fine needle aspiration, and a skin punch biopsy. Which of the following is evaluated by clinical pathology rather than anatomic pathology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical Pap smear for cytologic screening

choices.label: C
choices.text: Skin punch biopsy for histologic examination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid fine needle aspiration for cytology

explanation.summary: Microbiology and other laboratory testing belong to clinical pathology, whereas tissues and cells are evaluated by anatomic pathology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pathology is divided into anatomic pathology and clinical pathology. Anatomic pathology is the study of patient cells, tissues, and organs for disease diagnosis and treatment selection. Clinical pathology deals with blood products, microbiology, and other aspects of laboratory testing, so a sputum sample sent for bacterial culture is a clinical pathology (microbiology) specimen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A Pap smear collects cervical cells for cytopathology, which is part of anatomic pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A colectomy is a resection specimen evaluated by surgical pathology, a subspecialty of anatomic pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A punch biopsy generates tissue for surgical pathology (dermatopathology), within anatomic pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fine needle aspiration of a thyroid nodule is a cytopathology sample, an anatomic pathology discipline.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history has a 2-cm nodule in the right upper lobe on chest CT. An interventional radiologist performs a core biopsy of the nodule under imaging guidance. Which of the following best describes the intent of this procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obtain individual cells rather than tissue for cytologic evaluation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Provide a rapid preliminary result during an ongoing operation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relieve the burden of disease in the affected lobe of the lung

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remove the entirety of the nodule in order to cure the disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sample a portion of the nodule to determine whether it is cancerous

explanation.summary: Incisional, punch, and core biopsies are performed for sampling, not for therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The intent of most biopsies is to sample a portion of the lesion to investigate the histologic findings and hopefully arrive at a diagnosis; the brick's own example is an interventional radiologist biopsying a lung nodule to determine whether it is a cancerous growth. Core biopsies utilize a needle to sample tissue and, like incisional and punch biopsies, are not performed for therapeutic purposes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A core biopsy samples tissue with a needle; obtaining individual cells describes fine needle aspiration in cytopathology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rapid preliminary evaluation during surgery describes a frozen section, not an image-guided core biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relief of disease burden is a therapeutic purpose; core biopsies are sampling procedures and are not therapeutic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removal of the entirety of abnormal tissue with possible cure is the intent of an excision or excisional biopsy, not a core biopsy.
