questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a pigmented lesion on her upper back. The dermatologist presses a small instrument with a cylindric blade against the skin, rotates it, and removes a small column of tissue for evaluation. Which of the following procedures was performed?

explanation.summary: A punch biopsy uses a cylindric blade to remove a small sample of tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines punch biopsies as procedures that use a cylindric blade to remove tissue, illustrated by a punch biopsy of the skin. This is a sampling biopsy, performed to evaluate a portion of the lesion rather than to treat it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A core biopsy uses a needle, not a cylindric blade, to sample tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An excisional biopsy removes the entire lesion with a safety margin of normal skin, not a small column of tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fine needle aspiration uses a needle to pull cells from a lesion for cytopathology and does not remove intact tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A resection is a major surgery removing part or all of an organ, far more extensive than a skin punch.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a new ulcerated lesion on the lateral tongue. Rather than proceeding directly to a glossectomy, the surgeon performs an incisional biopsy in clinic. Which of the following best explains the rationale for choosing this procedure at this stage of the patient's evaluation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Incisional biopsy is more extensive than a glossectomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incisional biopsy is performed to relieve the burden of disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incisional biopsy removes the entire lesion and may cure it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incisional biopsy yields a preliminary result within 20 minutes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its result guides decisions such as the need for additional surgery

explanation.summary: Sampling biopsies are used early in a disease's evaluation, and their results influence management decisions such as the need for further surgery or treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because incisional, punch, and core biopsies sample rather than treat, they are often utilized in the early stages of a disease's evaluation. The results of the biopsy then influence management decisions, such as the need for additional surgeries or treatments; here the biopsy determines whether a glossectomy is warranted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biopsies and excisions are less extensive than resections such as a glossectomy, not more extensive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Incisional biopsies are not performed for therapeutic purposes; they are performed for sampling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Removing the entire lesion with possible cure describes an excisional biopsy; an incisional biopsy incises only a portion of the abnormal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A preliminary result in under 20 minutes is the frozen section, an intraoperative evaluation, not a clinic incisional biopsy.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a large squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx undergoes a laryngectomy, and the entire larynx containing the tumor is sent to the pathology laboratory. Which of the following best characterizes this procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frozen section for rapid intraoperative evaluation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A punch biopsy removing tissue with a cylindric blade

choices.label: C
choices.text: A resection removing all or part of an organ with the diseased tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: An excisional biopsy that is both diagnostic and therapeutic

choices.label: E
choices.text: An incisional biopsy sampling a portion of the abnormal tissue

explanation.summary: A resection is a major surgery that removes part or all of an organ, including the diseased tissue, often for malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a resection as a major surgery that removes part or all of an organ including the diseased tissue, and gives a laryngectomy for a large squamous cell carcinoma as its example. Resections are often performed for malignancies as well as for advanced disease processes affecting an organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A frozen section is a laboratory evaluation performed on tissue during surgery, not the surgical removal of an organ.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A punch biopsy removes a small tissue sample with a cylindric blade and is a sampling procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An excisional biopsy removes a lesion such as a cyst or suspicious lump and is less extensive than a resection of an entire organ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incisional biopsy samples only a portion of abnormal tissue rather than removing the organ.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A colectomy specimen arrives in the surgical pathology laboratory. A resident documents the tissue's physical appearance and size and then cuts the specimen into pieces that can be further processed by the laboratory. Which of the following terms best describes this step?

explanation.summary: In the gross room, the specimen is grossed, or cut, into pieces after its physical appearance and size are documented.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gross room, or surgical pathology laboratory, receives the specimen and evaluates it, including documentation of the tissue's physical appearance and size. The specimen is then grossed, or cut, into pieces that can be further processed by the laboratory.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accessioning refers to assigning the specimen number that identifies the case in the report.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fixation refers to placing the specimen in a preservative such as formalin, not to cutting and describing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A frozen section is a rapid intraoperative evaluation, not the routine cutting of a specimen for processing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunohistochemistry is an antibody-based stain performed later on processed tissue sections.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A skin excision is placed in a container of liquid medium immediately after removal so that the tissue is preserved until it can be processed. Which of the following is the preservative most commonly used for this purpose?

explanation.summary: Formalin is a commonly used preservative for surgical pathology specimens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a specimen may remain fresh or be placed in various liquid mediums, such as formalin, a commonly used preservative. Formalin fixation is also the first step in producing formalin-fixed paraffin embedded blocks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin is a dye that stains cytoplasmic components pink, not a preservative.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematoxylin is a dye that stains nuclear material dark blue in the H&E stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paraffin is the embedding medium for processed tissue blocks, not a liquid preservative for fresh specimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Saline solution is used for bronchoalveolar lavage washings to collect cells, not as a tissue preservative.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: During a thyroidectomy, the pathologist freezes a portion of a nodule, evaluates it, and calls the operating room with a result of "favor carcinoma." Two days later, after routine processing, a report is issued with a final diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following best describes the relationship between the intraoperative result and the report?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The final report is issued only when the frozen section result was incorrect

choices.label: B
choices.text: The frozen section eliminates the need for formalin fixation and paraffin embedding

choices.label: C
choices.text: The frozen section result is preliminary, and the final diagnosis follows evaluation of FFPE sections

choices.label: D
choices.text: The frozen section result is recorded in the synoptic report rather than the diagnostic line

choices.label: E
choices.text: The frozen section result is the final diagnosis, and the later report is an addendum

explanation.summary: A frozen section yields a preliminary result; the final diagnosis is issued after routine FFPE processing and evaluation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a frozen section, the pathologist freezes the tissue, evaluates it, and calls back a preliminary result, usually under 20 minutes. Surgical pathology specimens are then typically processed into formalin-fixed paraffin embedded tissue blocks, and the pathologist issues the report with the final diagnosis, usually within 2 days for routine cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A final report is issued for every specimen regardless of whether the preliminary result matched.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Frozen sections are for rapid intraoperative decision-making; the tissue is still processed into FFPE blocks for final evaluation and archiving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The final diagnosis is given on the top diagnostic line; a synoptic report is a structured section of prognostic information in certain cancer cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The intraoperative result is explicitly preliminary; an addendum is a minor modification made after a report is finalized, which is not what a routine final report represents.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A pathologist orders two additional tests on a lung biopsy: a Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain and an immunohistochemical stain for cytokeratin. Which of the following correctly distinguishes the mechanism of the immunohistochemical stain from that of the special stain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry highlights fungal organisms with a silver dye, whereas special stains identify epithelial tumors with specific antibodies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry is performed intraoperatively on the same day, whereas special stains require several days of processing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry is performed only on frozen tissue sections, whereas special stains can be run only on FFPE blocks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry is visualized as gray to black deposits, whereas special stains are visualized as a brown chromogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immunohistochemistry uses an antibody against a molecular antigen, whereas special stains use dyes with affinity for a tissue component

explanation.summary: Special stains rely on dyes or chemicals with affinity for a tissue component; immunohistochemistry relies on an antibody directed against a specific molecular antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes special stains as dyes or chemicals that have an affinity for a certain tissue component (for example, GMS highlighting fungal organisms). Immunohistochemistry instead uses an antibody directed against a specific molecular antigen, which is visualized under the microscope as a certain color, usually brown.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the roles: GMS (a special stain) highlights fungal organisms, and cytokeratin immunohistochemistry confirms epithelial tumors (carcinomas).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neither test is intraoperative; both are ordered as needed on processed tissue and are not available during surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both tests are generally performed on routine FFPE sections after laboratory processing; neither is specific to frozen tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the colors: GMS stains fungi gray to black, whereas immunohistochemistry is usually visualized as brown.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman undergoes a routine punch biopsy of a rash on her forearm and asks the clinician when the pathology results will be available. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Approximately 2 weeks for every routine specimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after immunohistochemistry has been completed

choices.label: C
choices.text: The same day, before leaving the clinic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Usually within 2 days, longer for complex cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Usually within 20 minutes, as for a frozen section

explanation.summary: Surgical pathology reports are usually issued within 2 days for routine biopsies, with complex cases requiring additional time.
explanation.whyCorrect: After evaluating the specimen, the surgical pathologist issues a report, usually within 2 days for routine biopsies, though some complex cases require additional time for study. A routine skin punch biopsy falls into the routine category.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two weeks overstates the typical turnaround; routine biopsies are usually reported within 2 days.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunohistochemistry is performed only as needed and is not a prerequisite for issuing a routine report.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Routine specimens must be grossed, fixed, processed, cut, and stained before evaluation, which is not completed during the clinic visit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A result in under 20 minutes describes a frozen section requested during an operation, not a routine clinic biopsy that must be processed into FFPE blocks.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman reads her surgical pathology report on the patient portal before her follow-up visit and is upset because she cannot understand terms such as "nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio." Which of the following best explains this situation and the appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reports are released only to the clinical team, so she should not have received it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reports are written in lay language, so no clinician explanation should be expected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reports use technical language for medical professionals, so the clinician should review it with her

choices.label: D
choices.text: She should wait for an amendment that rewrites the report in patient-friendly language

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pathologist cannot be contacted, so the clinician must interpret it without assistance

explanation.summary: Pathology reports are written in technical language for medical professionals but are released to patients as well, so thoughtful communication is needed to interpret them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surgical reports are written in technical language for medical professionals; however, they are released not only to the clinical team but also to the patient. Thoughtful communication is therefore necessary for interpreting and discussing pathology reports with patients who want clarification on their findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reports are released to the patient as well as the clinical team, so her access is expected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reports are written for medical professionals, not in lay language, which is exactly why patients may need clarification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An amendment is a major change in the report after finalization, such as a change in diagnosis, not a rewrite for patient readability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pathologist for any given case can be contacted for additional clarification and discussion.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A clinician is reviewing the sections of a surgical pathology report for a skin biopsy. Which of the following items is found in the patient identifiers and clinical information section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Location of the specimen source, such as "left arm"

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measured size of the resected tumor in centimeters

choices.label: C
choices.text: Results of immunohistochemical and special stains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Structured prognostic data reported for a cancer case

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pathologist's opinion on the difficult case

explanation.summary: The identifiers section includes name, date of birth, medical record number, specimen (accessioning) number, and limited clinical information such as the specimen location.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient identifiers and clinical information section contains the patient's name, date of birth, medical record number, and specimen number (also called an accessioning number). Limited clinical information, such as the location of the specimen source ("left arm"), is also given there.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The size of a tumor as measured in the laboratory is documented in the gross description.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemical and special stain results are often included in the comment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Structured prognostic information for cancer cases is provided in the synoptic report.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The comment is where the pathologist gives an opinion on the case.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A pathologist evaluates a liver biopsy but, after review of the H&E sections and special stains, cannot assign a specific disease to the process. Which of the following best describes how the final diagnosis section of the report is most likely handled?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A synoptic report is substituted for the diagnostic line

choices.label: B
choices.text: The case is finalized as an addendum rather than as a report

choices.label: C
choices.text: The diagnostic line summarizes the important pathologic findings

choices.label: D
choices.text: The microscopic description is omitted and only the gross description is given

choices.label: E
choices.text: The report is issued with the diagnostic line left blank pending clinical correlation

explanation.summary: When the disease process remains equivocal, the diagnostic line summarizes the important pathologic findings.
explanation.whyCorrect: The final diagnosis is a top-line text, known as the diagnostic line, that names the disease. If the disease process remains equivocal, the diagnostic line may instead summarize the important pathologic findings, and the clinician can contact the pathologist for further discussion and clarification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A synoptic report is a structured section of prognostic information in certain cancer cases, not a replacement for the diagnostic line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An addendum is a minor modification to an already finalized report, not a way of finalizing an equivocal case.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Equivocal cases are exactly where documenting microscopic findings is useful; omitting them would not help the clinician.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A diagnostic line is still provided; it summarizes findings rather than being left blank.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A resident reviewing a thyroidectomy report finds no separately labeled "microscopic description" section, yet the report mentions nuclear enlargement, overlap, and clearing that support the diagnosis of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Microscopic findings are documented only in the synoptic report

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microscopic findings can be reported only as an addendum after finalization

choices.label: C
choices.text: Such findings belong in the gross description, so a microscopic section is never used

choices.label: D
choices.text: The microscopic description is optional and its findings are often included in the comment

choices.label: E
choices.text: The report is incomplete and must be amended to add the missing section

explanation.summary: The microscopic description is an optional section; in common practice its findings are often included in the comment rather than as a separate part of the report.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microscopic description describes what is seen under the microscope, for example nuclear clearing in papillary thyroid carcinoma. The brick notes it is optional: in common practice, the microscopic findings are often included in the comment and not as a separate part of the report, or may not be given at all in straightforward cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The synoptic report provides structured prognostic information in cancer cases; it is not the designated home for microscopic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An addendum incorporates results not previously available; it is not the mechanism for reporting routine microscopic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The gross description documents the physical appearance and processing of the specimen, not cellular features seen under the microscope.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The absence of a separate microscopic section is normal practice, not a deficiency requiring an amendment, which is reserved for major changes such as a change in diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A pathology report on a lung biopsy contains the statement: "The findings are concerning for an infectious process; clinical correlation and cultures are recommended." In which section of the surgical pathology report does this statement most likely appear?

explanation.summary: The comment is where the pathologist gives an opinion and may recommend additional testing or clinical correlation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The comment is where the pathologist gives an opinion on the case, such as favoring an infectious process. Recommendations for additional testing or clinical correlation may be included there, along with immunohistochemical and special stain results and pertinent aspects of the microscopic description.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The gross description is the physical description of the specimen and how it was processed, not an interpretive opinion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pathology signature identifies the reading pathologist electronically and contains no interpretive text.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This section contains name, date of birth, medical record number, specimen number, and specimen location, not recommendations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synoptic report is a structured summary of prognostic information in certain cancer cases.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A surgeon compares two colon reports. The report for an adenocarcinoma resection includes a structured section listing prognostic information for patient care, whereas the report for a benign polyp biopsy from another patient contains no such section. Which of the following names the section present only in the cancer report?

explanation.summary: A synoptic report is included in certain cancer cases and provides important prognostic information.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the synoptic report as a section included in certain cancer cases that gives important prognostic information for patient care. It is not part of reports for benign specimens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An addendum is a minor post-finalization modification and is not specific to cancer cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A comment gives the pathologist's opinion and can appear in any report, benign or malignant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A gross description is part of every surgical pathology report, including the benign polyp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Every report carries the electronic signature of the reading pathologist.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A clinician wants to telephone the pathologist who evaluated a patient's breast biopsy to discuss the findings. Where in the surgical pathology report is the name of the reading pathologist identified?

explanation.summary: The name of the reading pathologist can be identified in the electronic signature.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists the pathology signature as a component of the report and states that the name of the reading pathologist can be identified in the electronic signature. The pathologist for any given case can be contacted for additional clarification and discussion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An addendum incorporates later test results that do not change the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical information gives the specimen source location and patient identifiers, not the pathologist's name.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gross description documents the specimen's physical appearance and processing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The synoptic report contains structured prognostic data for cancer cases.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A surgical pathology report is finalized with a diagnosis of carcinoma. One week later, additional immunohistochemistry demonstrates that the tumor is actually a lymphoma, and the pathologist changes the diagnosis in the report. Which of the following best describes this modification?

explanation.summary: An amendment is a major change in the report after finalization, such as a change in diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an amendment as a major change in the report after finalization and states specifically that a change in diagnosis would warrant an amendment. Changing carcinoma to lymphoma is a change in diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An addendum is a minor modification, such as incorporating results that do not change the diagnosis; here the diagnosis changed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The comment is the section where the pathologist gives an opinion, not a mechanism for altering a finalized report.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A frozen section is a rapid intraoperative evaluation unrelated to modifying a finalized report.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synoptic report is structured prognostic information in cancer cases, not a post-finalization change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a painless, slowly enlarging mass of the parotid (salivary) gland. Before deciding on surgery, the clinician wants a minimally invasive diagnostic sample of the lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate procedure?

explanation.summary: Fine needle aspiration is a minimally invasive cytopathology technique commonly used for salivary gland tumors and thyroid nodules.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cytopathology, lesions may be directly sampled with fine needle aspiration, a technique in which a needle is used to pull cells from the tissue. FNA sampling is commonly used for salivary gland tumors and thyroid nodules, and an advantage of cytopathology is that it is minimally invasive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoalveolar lavage uses saline washings to obtain cells from the airways, not from a salivary gland mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An excisional biopsy removes the entire lesion and is a surgical, not minimally invasive, procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A frozen section is an intraoperative evaluation and requires that surgery already be underway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An incisional biopsy incises tissue surgically and is more invasive than needle sampling of cells.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman undergoes routine cervical screening with a Pap smear. On cytopathologic evaluation, a cluster of cells in one area is flagged as worrisome for a pre-malignant or malignant lesion. Compared with a normal intermediate squamous cell, which of the following features would be expected in the worrisome cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio with nuclear membrane irregularity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio with abundant cytoplasm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oblong hyphae and oval yeast forms staining gray to black

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small round nuclei with smooth nuclear membranes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniform intermediate squamous morphology with small nuclei

explanation.summary: Worrisome cells on a Pap smear show high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, nuclear enlargement, and nuclear membrane irregularity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pap smears collect cervical cells to screen for malignant and pre-malignant lesions. The brick's Pap smear example shows worrisome cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, nuclear enlargement, and nuclear membrane irregularity, contrasted with a normal intermediate squamous cell that has abundant cytoplasm and a small nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A low nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio with abundant cytoplasm describes the normal intermediate squamous cell, not the worrisome cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyphae and yeast forms staining gray to black describe fungal organisms on a GMS special stain, not abnormal cervical epithelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Small nuclei with smooth membranes are features of normal cells; worrisome cells show enlarged, irregular nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uniform intermediate squamous morphology is the normal comparison cell in the example, not the abnormal cluster.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 60-year-old immunocompromised man has bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. A pulmonologist passes a bronchoscope into the airways, instills saline solution, and withdraws the fluid, which is sent to cytopathology. Which of the following procedures was performed?

explanation.summary: Bronchoalveolar lavages use saline solution washings to obtain cells from the airways for cytopathology.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes bronchoalveolar lavage as a cytopathology sampling method that uses saline solution washings to obtain cells from the airways. The cells recovered in the fluid are evaluated at the level of the individual cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A core biopsy uses a needle to obtain a core of tissue for surgical pathology, not a fluid sample of cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fine needle aspiration uses a needle to pull cells directly from a lesion such as a thyroid nodule, not saline washings of the airways.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A Pap smear collects cervical cells to screen for malignant and pre-malignant lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A punch biopsy uses a cylindric blade to remove tissue, typically from the skin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A man presents for removal of a lump on the back of his neck. The surgeon excises the abnormal tissue and sends it to the pathology laboratory, where the pathologist finds a benign tumor composed of mature fat. Which of the following best describes the diagnosis and the expected next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carcinoma of epithelial origin; additional surgery is needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carcinoma, a malignant epithelial tumor; the excision is curative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipoma, a benign tumor of mature fat; a resection is still required

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipoma, a benign tumor of mature fat; the excision is curative

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lipoma, a malignant tumor of fat; molecular testing guides therapy

explanation.summary: A lipoma is a benign tumor of mature fat; excision of the lipoma is curative and no additional treatment is needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the brick's case, the pathologist diagnoses the excised neck lump as a lipoma, a benign (non-cancerous) tumor of mature fat. Because excisions remove the entirety of the abnormal tissue, the surgeon explains that the excision was curative and that no additional treatment will be needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The tumor is benign fat, not an epithelial malignancy, and no additional surgery is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A carcinoma is a malignant tumor of epithelial origin, not a benign tumor of mature fat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The excision already removed the entire lesion and was curative; a resection of an organ is not required for a benign lipoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A lipoma is benign, not malignant, and no further therapy is needed, so molecular testing for treatment selection is not indicated.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A clinician receives a surgical pathology report whose diagnostic line summarizes findings without naming a specific disease, and the clinician is unsure how to explain the result to the patient. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact the pathologist for discussion and clarification

choices.label: B
choices.text: Order a frozen section on the archived tissue block

choices.label: C
choices.text: Request an amendment that changes the diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Submit a new specimen so the case can be grossed again

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wait for a synoptic report to be added to the case

explanation.summary: For equivocal cases or reports needing additional explanation, the clinician can contact the pathologist for further discussion and clarification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that the pathologist for any given case can be contacted for additional clarification and discussion. For equivocal cases or reports needing additional explanation, one can contact the pathologist for further discussion in the clinical setting before communicating findings to the patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A frozen section is a rapid intraoperative evaluation performed during surgery, not a tool for clarifying a finalized report.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An amendment is issued by the pathologist for a major change such as a new diagnosis; a clinician cannot request one simply to obtain clarification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The specimen has already been grossed and processed into FFPE blocks; a repeat specimen is not the way to clarify the existing report.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synoptic report provides prognostic information in certain cancer cases and would not resolve an equivocal diagnosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops swelling and redness of the lower jaw 24 hours after a dental infection. A biopsy of the involved tissue is most likely to show an abundance of which cell type, given that these are the first cells to arrive at a site of acute inflammation and that their response typically peaks about 24 hours after injury?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are the most abundant WBC and the first responders in acute inflammation, peaking around 24 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils are the paramedics of acute inflammation and are the first cells to arrive at the scene. They are the most abundant white blood cells, making up about 60 percent of the total WBC count, and their response peaks about 24 hours after injury or infection. They kill microorganisms by phagocytosis and by releasing antimicrobial proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are associated with parasitic infection and allergy, not the initial acute inflammatory response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts participate in later tissue repair and scarring, not the early acute inflammatory infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages become the predominant cell type only later, about 48 to 72 hours after injury, not first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are antibody-producing cells of the adaptive response and are not the first cells at an acute site.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Three days after a soft-tissue injury, the predominant leukocyte at the site is a large phagocyte that also takes up antigen, presents it to T and B lymphocytes, and secretes cytokines to help mount an adaptive immune response. Which cell is being described?

explanation.summary: Macrophages predominate at 48 to 72 hours, act as antigen-presenting cells, and secrete cytokines linking innate and adaptive immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophages are leukocytes found throughout the body tissues that become the predominant cell type roughly 48 to 72 hours (2 to 3 days) after injury. Besides killing microorganisms and clearing cellular debris by phagocytosis, they secrete cytokines and act as antigen-presenting cells that help T and B lymphocytes mount an adaptive immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils release mediators such as histamine but do not become the predominant phagocytic, antigen-presenting cell at 2 to 3 days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cells kill virally infected and tumor cells but are not the predominant phagocyte or the antigen-presenting cell described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils arrive first and peak at about 24 hours; they are not the main antigen-presenting cell described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets contribute to clotting and release mediators but are cell fragments, not antigen-presenting phagocytes.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman scrapes her knee, and within minutes the surrounding skin becomes red and warm to the touch. These two cardinal signs are produced by the first vascular reaction of acute inflammation. Which change most directly explains the redness and warmth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clotting within the microvessels around the wound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased local blood flow from vasodilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leakage of protein-rich fluid into the interstitium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration of neutrophils along a chemokine gradient

explanation.summary: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the injured area, producing the redness (rubor) and heat (calor) of acute inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first vascular reaction is an increase in vascular diameter (vasodilation), which increases blood flow to the injured area. Redness and heat are caused by this increase in local blood flow, making them among the earliest visible cardinal signs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clotting in the microvessels helps contain infection but does not produce the redness and heat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leakage of protein-rich fluid causes swelling (tumor), not primarily the redness and warmth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil migration along a chemokine gradient recruits cells but is not the cause of the warmth and redness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sloughing of necrotic tissue describes ulceration, a morphologic pattern, not the mechanism of redness and heat.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient develops visible swelling of a finger after a small puncture wound. The swelling results from accumulation of fluid and protein in the interstitial space. Which of the following is most directly responsible for this fluid accumulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin within the extracellular space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diapedesis of leukocytes across the vessel wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of adhesion molecules on the endothelial surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to the area

explanation.summary: Increased vascular permeability lets fluid and molecules leave the vessel, producing swelling (tumor).
explanation.whyCorrect: In response to inflammatory stimuli, endothelial cells contract and widen the endothelial cell junction, increasing vascular permeability. This lets fluid, specialized cells, and molecules reach the site of injury, and the resulting accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space causes the visible swelling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin deposition characterizes fibrinous inflammation and is not the mechanism of the interstitial swelling here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis is the passage of leukocytes between endothelial cells, not the primary cause of the edema fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adhesion molecule expression helps leukocytes stick to the endothelium but does not itself cause interstitial fluid accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute inflammation causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, and reduced flow would not cause fluid to accumulate in tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A student is asked to place the steps of leukocyte extravasation in the order in which a neutrophil leaves the bloodstream and reaches an infected tissue. Which of the following is the correct sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding, margination and rolling, migration, diapedesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diapedesis, binding, margination and rolling, migration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Margination and rolling, binding, diapedesis, migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Margination and rolling, diapedesis, binding, migration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migration, diapedesis, binding, margination and rolling

explanation.summary: Leukocyte extravasation proceeds as margination and rolling, then binding, then diapedesis, then migration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocyte extravasation involves four steps in order: margination and rolling (the cell moves to the vessel wall and rolls along the endothelium), binding (the cell is firmly stopped and fixed in place), diapedesis (the endothelial junction is pulled apart so the cell slips into the interstitium), and migration (the cell moves up a chemokine gradient toward the site).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding cannot precede margination and rolling, and migration comes after diapedesis, so this order is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis is the third step and cannot come first; the leukocyte must first marginate and bind.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding must occur before diapedesis, because the leukocyte must be firmly fixed before it squeezes between endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the true order; margination and rolling is the first step, not the last.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy has a history of delayed umbilical cord separation, poor wound healing, and recurrent bacterial infections that characteristically produce little or no pus. Neutrophils are abundant in the blood but fail to accumulate at sites of infection. A defect in which of the following steps of neutrophil extravasation best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firm binding of leukocytes to the endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of neutrophils in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs the binding step, so neutrophils cannot firmly adhere and cross the endothelium to reach the tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the binding step, adhesion molecules firmly fix the leukocyte to the endothelium. Patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency have defects in this leukocyte adhesion, so neutrophils cannot fix in place, extravasate, and reach the site of injury. This leads to impaired wound healing, recurrent infections, and a characteristic absence of pus despite blood neutrophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired complement opsonization is a different immune defect and does not explain the failure of neutrophils to accumulate at sites of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are actually increased in the blood, so bone marrow production is not the defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The failure is in leukocyte adhesion, not in macrophage cytokine secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasodilation is intact in this disorder; the problem is that leukocytes cannot adhere and leave the vessel.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: During the final step of leukocyte recruitment, a neutrophil that has entered the interstitium must locate and move toward the site of injury. This directional movement up a concentration gradient is driven by which class of mediators?

explanation.summary: Migration is guided by chemokines, whose concentration gradient directs leukocyte chemotaxis toward the injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the migration step, the leukocyte must locate and move toward the site of injury. This is facilitated by chemokines, chemical signals whose binding to receptors on the leukocyte surface promotes directional movement up the chemokine concentration gradient, a process called chemotaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulins are antibodies of the adaptive response and are not the chemotactic gradient that directs migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kinins increase vascular permeability and cause pain but do not direct leukocyte chemotaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandins contribute to vasodilation, pain, and fever rather than guiding chemotactic migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selectins mediate the earlier rolling step by tethering leukocytes to the endothelium, not directional migration through tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with gram-negative bacteremia develops high fever and hypotension progressing to shock. These systemic effects are largely mediated by tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6 released by macrophages. Which class of mediators is responsible?

explanation.summary: Cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 cause local endothelial activation and systemic fever, metabolic changes, and hypotensive shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytokines (including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6) are produced by macrophages, endothelial cells, and mast cells. Locally they cause endothelial activation, and systemically they cause fever, metabolic abnormalities, and hypotension that can progress to shock, exactly the picture seen with severe bacteremia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement drives chemotaxis and membrane attack complex killing, not the TNF/IL-1/IL-6 systemic shock syndrome described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability locally but is not the mediator of systemic fever and shock.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukotrienes increase vascular permeability and promote chemotaxis but do not produce this systemic fever and hypotensive shock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins contribute to vasodilation, pain, and fever but are not the TNF/IL-1/IL-6 cytokines named in the stem.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with an insect sting rapidly develops a red, raised, itchy wheal as mast cells degranulate. The chief mediator released causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability with endothelial activation. Which mediator is primarily responsible?

explanation.summary: Histamine, released chiefly by mast cells, causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and endothelial activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histamine is a vasoactive amine released by mast cells, basophils, and platelets. Its principal actions are vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and endothelial activation, which together produce the wheal and flare seen after mast cell degranulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin maintains plasma oncotic pressure and is not a mediator of vasodilation or permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen is a positive acute-phase reactant that aids clotting and repair, not the mast cell mediator producing the wheal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin regulates iron handling in macrophages and does not cause vasodilation or increased permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin is an iron-transport protein and a negative acute-phase reactant, not a vasoactive mediator.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with bacterial pneumonia has a lung biopsy showing alveolar spaces filled with a thick, protein- and cell-rich fluid containing abundant neutrophils that reduces the area available for gas exchange. Which morphologic pattern of acute inflammation does this represent?

explanation.summary: A neutrophil-rich, protein-rich exudate forming pus is the hallmark of purulent (suppurative) inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An exudate contains protein and cellular elements and arises from increased vascular permeability that lets neutrophils enter the tissue. The buildup of leukocytes produces pus, defining purulent (suppurative) inflammation. In bacterial pneumonia, pus fills the alveolar spaces and reduces the area available for gas exchange.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinous inflammation is characterized by fibrin deposition in the extracellular space, not by a neutrophil-rich pus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pseudomembranous inflammation refers to a debris membrane in the colon (for example, C. difficile), not alveolar pus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serous inflammation is a watery, protein-poor transudate, such as a skin blister, not the pus-filled exudate described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative inflammation is a local defect of a skin or mucosal surface from sloughing of necrotic tissue, not alveolar pus.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man after a myocardial infarction develops chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. At autopsy the pericardial surface is covered by a shaggy pink meshwork of fibrin. This finding is characteristic of which morphologic pattern, which typically involves the lining of body cavities?

explanation.summary: Fibrinous inflammation deposits fibrin in the extracellular space and characteristically involves body cavity linings such as the pericardium.
explanation.whyCorrect: When vascular permeability increases enough for large molecules such as fibrinogen to leak out, fibrinogen deposits as fibrin in the extracellular space, forming a fibrinous exudate. This occurs when vascular leaks are large or there is a local procoagulant stimulus, and it is characteristic of inflammation in the lining of body cavities such as the meninges, pericardium, and pleura.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous inflammation is a chronic pattern with epithelioid macrophages, not the acute fibrinous pattern shown here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Purulent inflammation produces neutrophil-rich pus, not the fibrin deposition described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serous inflammation is a watery transudate, not a fibrin meshwork on the pericardium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative inflammation is a surface defect from sloughed necrotic tissue, not a fibrinous exudate over a cavity lining.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with an acute infection has laboratory testing. During acute inflammation, most plasma proteins made by the liver rise, but a few drop below their normal levels and are called negative acute-phase reactants so that amino acids can be conserved for the positive reactants. Which of the following is a negative acute-phase reactant?

explanation.summary: Albumin and transferrin fall during acute inflammation and are the negative acute-phase reactants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative acute-phase reactants are proteins that drop below their normal levels during acute inflammation. Albumin, the primary protein maintaining plasma oncotic pressure, is produced in lower amounts to conserve amino acids for the positive acute-phase reactants, making it a negative acute-phase reactant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant that rises and helps recognize and eliminate pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant whose serum level rises to sequester iron during inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen is a positive acute-phase reactant that increases and promotes tissue repair and RBC rouleaux.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin is a positive acute-phase reactant that rises and acts as a gatekeeper for iron stored in macrophages.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a long-standing autoimmune disorder has had ongoing low-level inflammation of her joints for several years. Which of the following statements best distinguishes this process from acute inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It generally lasts only a few days before resolving

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an essential and beneficial part of the body's defense system

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is limited to the vascular reactions of vasodilation and permeability

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is mediated mainly by neutrophils arriving within 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is not beneficial and leads to tissue damage and chronic disease

explanation.summary: Chronic inflammation is an ongoing low-level process lasting weeks to years that, unlike acute inflammation, is not beneficial and damages tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are two types of inflammation, acute and chronic. Acute inflammation is an essential part of the body's defense system and generally lasts a few days. Chronic inflammation involves ongoing low-level inflammation that lasts for weeks, months, or even years; unlike acute inflammation it is not beneficial, leads to tissue damage, and is linked to the development of many chronic diseases including diabetes, cancer, and autoimmune disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lasting only a few days describes acute inflammation, not the years-long process in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Being an essential, beneficial defense is the description of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is not beneficial.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The vascular reactions of vasodilation and increased permeability are features of the acute response, and chronic inflammation is not defined by them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils arriving and peaking at about 24 hours characterize the acute response, not chronic inflammation.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man sustains a deep laceration of the forearm contaminated with soil. Within minutes, clots form at the site of injury as part of the acute inflammatory response. In addition to halting the flow of blood out of the injured area and providing a framework for tissue repair, this clotting serves which of the following purposes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creates a physical barrier that contains the spread of infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delivers effector molecules and immune cells to the wound

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directs leukocytes up a chemokine concentration gradient to the site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increases blood flow to the injured tissue by vasodilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widens the endothelial cell junctions of nearby postcapillary venules

explanation.summary: The second major role of acute inflammation, clotting at the site of injury, stops blood loss, provides a repair framework, and walls off infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute inflammation has three major roles. The second role is causing blood to clot at the site of injury; this halts the flow of blood out of the injured area, provides a framework for tissue repair, and creates a physical barrier that contains the spread of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Delivery of effector molecules and cells to the site is the first role of inflammation (recruiting help), not a function of clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Directional movement up a chemokine gradient is chemotaxis during the migration step of leukocyte extravasation, not a function of clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased blood flow results from vasodilation, the first vascular reaction, not from clot formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widening of endothelial junctions is the mechanism of increased vascular permeability, not a purpose of clotting.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a healthy adult shows a cell with a multilobed nucleus that makes up about 60 percent of the white blood cells. This cell is classified as a granulocyte. Which of the following is the basis for that classification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ability to present antigen to T and B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peak activity 48 to 72 hours after injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Presence of specific granules in the cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residence within body tissues rather than blood

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are granulocytes because of the specific granules present in their cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells, about 60 percent of the total WBC count. They are classified as granulocytes because of the presence of specific granules in their cytoplasm, and they kill microorganisms by phagocytosis and by releasing antimicrobial proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen presentation to T and B lymphocytes is a property of macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells, not the basis for calling a cell a granulocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peak activity at 48 to 72 hours describes macrophages; neutrophils peak at about 24 hours, and timing does not define a granulocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histamine release characterizes mast cells, basophils, and platelets; it is not why neutrophils are termed granulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophages are the leukocytes found throughout body tissues; neutrophils circulate in blood, and tissue residence is not the granulocyte criterion.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: During intravital microscopy of a small vessel, a fine needle is used to injure the surrounding tissue. Immediately after the injury the vessel narrows briefly for 1 to 2 seconds, and only then does it begin to widen. Which of the following best explains the initial narrowing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A transient smooth muscle shock response to the injury

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of endothelial cells that widens their junctions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of sticky cell-adhesion molecules on the endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Initiation of clot formation in the surrounding microvessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of histamine from degranulating mast cells

explanation.summary: The very first vascular response to acute injury is a brief 1 to 2 second constriction, likely a smooth muscle shock response, before the four key vascular reactions begin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood vessels react within seconds to acute tissue injury. The very first thing vessels do in response to acute injury is constrict; this lasts for 1 to 2 seconds and is likely a smooth muscular shock response. Only afterward do the first molecular mediators prompt the four key responses, beginning with vasodilation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Endothelial cell contraction widens the endothelial junctions and increases permeability; it does not narrow the vessel lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cell-adhesion molecules becoming sticky helps leukocytes locate the site; it does not constrict the vessel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clotting in microvessels locks the doors against spread of infection but is not the cause of the transient vessel narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine causes vasodilation and increased permeability, the opposite of the brief constriction observed.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with a deep skin abscess has a temperature of 39.2 C, shivering, and a rapid pulse. A complete blood count shows a markedly increased white blood cell count. Which of the following terms describes this laboratory finding as a systemic sign of inflammation?

explanation.summary: Leukocytosis, an increased white blood cell count on CBC, is one of the systemic signs of inflammation alongside fever, rigors, chills, and increased pulse and blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Other systemic signs of inflammation include fever, leukocytosis (increased white blood cell count on CBC), increased pulse and blood pressure, rigors (shivering), and chills (a search for warmth). The elevated WBC count in this febrile, shivering patient is leukocytosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extravasation is the passage of leukocytes out of the vessel into tissue, not the term for an increased blood WBC count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphadenitis is secondary inflammation and enlargement of draining lymph nodes, not an elevated WBC count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Margination is the movement of leukocytes to the vessel wall as blood flow slows, a step of extravasation rather than a CBC finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rouleaux are stacks of red blood cells that settle faster in the ESR test; they are not a white blood cell count finding.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A complete blood count with differential is performed on a healthy 28-year-old woman. Which of the following leukocytes represents roughly 5 percent of circulating white blood cells and is the blood counterpart of the tissue macrophage?

explanation.summary: Monocytes make up about 5 percent of blood WBCs, and the macrophage is their tissue equivalent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monocytes represent about 5 percent of white blood cells in the blood, and the macrophage is the tissue equivalent of the monocyte. Macrophages are the leukocytes found throughout body tissues that become predominant at 48 to 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils constitute less than 1 percent of blood WBCs and are not the precursor of the tissue macrophage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils represent about 3 percent of blood WBCs and increase with allergies and parasitic infections; they are not related to macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells occur in tissue, not in blood, so they do not appear on a blood differential.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs at about 60 percent and are granulocytes, not the blood form of the macrophage.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has an infected puncture wound of the hand. On examination, the lymph nodes at the elbow and in the axilla on the same side are enlarged and tender. Which of the following best explains the lymph node findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of a watery transudate from increased hydrostatic pressure in the nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin within the lymph node sinuses from a local procoagulant stimulus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased lymphatic drainage carrying fluid, leukocytes, debris, and pathogens to the nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue within the lymph node cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction of nodal vessels causing ischemic swelling of the lymph nodes

explanation.summary: During acute inflammation, increased lymphatic drainage delivers fluid, white blood cells, cell debris, and pathogens to draining nodes, which become secondarily inflamed and enlarged (lymphadenitis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphatics normally drain the small amount of extravascular fluid that seeps out of capillaries. During inflammation the amount of fluid draining to the lymphatics increases, and white blood cells, cell debris, and pathogens can make their way through the lymphatics to draining lymph nodes. For this reason lymph nodes can become secondarily inflamed and enlarged during acute inflammation, a process called lymphadenitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hydrostatic transudate characterizes serous inflammation and systemic diseases like heart failure, not the drainage-related enlargement of nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposition from a procoagulant stimulus describes fibrinous inflammation of body cavity linings, not the mechanism of lymphadenitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sloughing of necrotic tissue produces an ulcer on a skin or mucosal surface, not enlarged draining lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasoconstriction is only a 1 to 2 second initial response to injury and does not cause nodal enlargement.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: In an inflamed venule, leukocytes that were previously free-flowing in the center of the stream begin to come into close contact with the vessel wall. Although vasodilation has increased the total blood flow reaching the tissue, which of the following changes most directly permits this margination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A decrease in the speed of blood flow within the widened vessel

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reduction in the total volume of blood reaching the injured tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: A rise in plasma oncotic pressure that pulls cells toward the endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: An increase in the velocity of fluid moving through the vessel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Constriction of the vessel that squeezes cells toward the wall

explanation.summary: Although vasodilation increases total flow, the fluid and its components move more slowly, and this slowing lets leukocytes contact the vessel wall (margination).
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood vessels dilate to increase the blood volume (total flow) reaching injured tissue. Although total flow and blood volume are increased via vasodilation, the actual fluid and the components within it move more slowly. This decrease in the speed of blood flow allows free-flowing leukocytes to come into close contact with the vessel wall, a process known as margination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Total blood volume reaching the tissue is increased by vasodilation, not reduced.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oncotic pressure governs fluid movement in transudate formation and does not pull leukocytes toward the endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluid velocity decreases, not increases, in the dilated vessel; faster flow would keep leukocytes in the central stream.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vessel is dilated during margination; vasoconstriction is only a brief 1 to 2 second initial response.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A child has recurrent infections. Studies show that his neutrophils lack the sialyl-Lewis X antigen and therefore cannot interact with selectins expressed on the vessel wall. Which step of leukocyte extravasation is most directly impaired?

explanation.summary: Rolling depends on selectins on the vessel wall attaching to sialyl-Lewis X antigens on the leukocyte.
explanation.whyCorrect: After margination, rolling occurs due to expression of selectins on the vessel wall attaching to sialyl-Lewis X antigens on the leukocyte, tethering the cell so that it travels along the surface of the vascular endothelium. Without sialyl-Lewis X, this selectin interaction and therefore rolling cannot occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding is firm arrest mediated by cell-adhesion molecules attaching to CD11/CD18 integrins on the leukocyte, not selectin interactions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis, squeezing through the endothelial junction, is aided by PECAM-1 rather than selectins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Migration is the final step and is guided by chemokines, not by selectin binding to sialyl-Lewis X.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phagocytosis is how neutrophils kill microorganisms after reaching the tissue; it is not a step of extravasation.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A neutrophil has been firmly arrested on the endothelium of an inflamed vessel. With the help of PECAM-1, it next squeezes through the endothelial cell junction and enters the interstitium. Which of the following names this step?

explanation.summary: Diapedesis is the step in which the endothelial cell junction is pulled apart and the leukocyte slips through into the interstitium, aided by PECAM-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the step called diapedesis, the endothelial cell junction is pulled apart, allowing the leukocyte to slip through the opening and enter the interstitium. Diapedesis follows binding and involves the leukocyte squeezing through the endothelial cell junction with the help of PECAM-1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemotaxis is directional movement up a chemokine gradient during migration, which happens after the cell has already entered the interstitium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Margination is the earlier movement of leukocytes into close contact with the vessel wall as flow slows.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is not one of the four steps of leukocyte extravasation described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rolling is travel along the endothelial surface via selectin tethering, before firm binding, not passage through the junction.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with an acutely inflamed knee has fever and marked joint pain. A drug is given that blocks production of a lipid-derived mediator released by mast cells and leukocytes that is responsible for vasodilation, pain, and fever. Which of the following mediators is targeted?

explanation.summary: Prostaglandins are lipid products from mast cells and leukocytes whose actions are vasodilation, pain, and fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: The principal mediators of inflammation include the lipid products prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Prostaglandins are produced by mast cells and leukocytes, and their actions are vasodilation, pain, and fever, matching the febrile, painful presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemokines come from leukocytes and activated macrophages and cause chemotaxis and leukocyte activation, not fever.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is produced in the liver and acts through chemotaxis, membrane attack complex killing, and mast cell stimulation, not pain and fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine is a vasoactive amine causing vasodilation, permeability, and endothelial activation, but it is not a lipid product and does not cause fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kinins are plasma proteins produced in the liver, not lipid products of mast cells, and their listed actions do not include fever.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A lipid mediator released by mast cells and leukocytes during an asthma exacerbation increases vascular permeability and promotes chemotaxis along with leukocyte adhesion and activation, but is not listed as a cause of fever. Which of the following is this mediator?

explanation.summary: Leukotrienes are lipid products of mast cells and leukocytes that increase vascular permeability and drive chemotaxis, leukocyte adhesion, and activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukotrienes, like prostaglandins, are lipid products produced by mast cells and leukocytes. Their actions are increased vascular permeability, chemotaxis, and leukocyte adhesion and activation, which distinguishes them from prostaglandins, whose actions are vasodilation, pain, and fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokines are proteins from macrophages, endothelial cells, and mast cells causing endothelial activation and systemic fever and shock, not lipid mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine is a vasoactive amine causing vasodilation, permeability, and endothelial activation, not chemotaxis or leukocyte activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kinins are plasma proteins made in the liver that cause permeability, smooth muscle contraction, vasodilation, and pain; they are not lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins are the other lipid product from the same sources, but their actions are vasodilation, pain, and fever rather than chemotaxis and adhesion.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a bacterial infection has bacteria lysed directly by a membrane attack complex assembled from proteins that circulate in plasma. The same mediator system also stimulates mast cells to produce vasodilation and promotes leukocyte chemotaxis. Where are these proteins produced?

explanation.summary: Complement proteins are plasma mediators produced in the liver that cause chemotaxis, direct target killing via the membrane attack complex, and vasodilation through mast cell stimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complement is a plasma-derived mediator produced in the liver. Its actions are leukocyte chemotaxis and activation, direct target killing through the membrane attack complex, and vasodilation via mast cell stimulation, all of which match the description.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activated macrophages produce cytokines and chemokines, not the complement proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endothelial cells are a source of cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6, not complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mast cell granules are the source of histamine, not the plasma proteins that form the membrane attack complex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets release histamine but do not produce the plasma complement system.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A plasma-derived inflammatory mediator produced in the liver increases vascular permeability, causes vasodilation and pain, and additionally triggers smooth muscle contraction. Which of the following is this mediator?

explanation.summary: Kinins are plasma mediators produced in the liver that cause increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, vasodilation, and pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kinins are listed among the principal mediators of inflammation with a source of plasma (produced in the liver). Their actions are increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, vasodilation, and pain; smooth muscle contraction is the distinguishing feature.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemokines are produced by leukocytes and activated macrophages and cause chemotaxis and leukocyte activation, not pain or permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is also produced in the liver, but its actions are chemotaxis, membrane attack complex killing, and vasodilation via mast cells, not smooth muscle contraction or pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Platelet-activating factor comes from leukocytes and mast cells and drives leukocyte adhesion, degranulation, and oxidative burst, not smooth muscle contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins are lipid products from mast cells and leukocytes, not liver-derived plasma proteins, and they cause fever rather than smooth muscle contraction.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A mediator released by leukocytes and mast cells causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability and also promotes leukocyte adhesion and chemotaxis. Uniquely among the principal mediators, it also triggers leukocyte degranulation and the oxidative burst. Which of the following is this mediator?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokines such as TNF and IL-1

explanation.summary: Platelet-activating factor, from leukocytes and mast cells, causes vasodilation, permeability, leukocyte adhesion, chemotaxis, degranulation, and oxidative burst.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelet-activating factor is produced by leukocytes and mast cells. Its actions are vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, leukocyte adhesion, chemotaxis, degranulation, and oxidative burst; degranulation and oxidative burst are the features that set it apart from the other mediators.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement is a plasma protein system producing chemotaxis and membrane attack complex killing, not leukocyte degranulation and oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytokines cause local endothelial activation and systemic fever, metabolic abnormalities, and shock rather than degranulation and oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine causes vasodilation, permeability, and endothelial activation but is not listed as causing degranulation or oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukotrienes cause permeability, chemotaxis, and leukocyte adhesion and activation, but not vasodilation, degranulation, or oxidative burst.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with a dental abscess reports that her lower jaw is exquisitely painful and visibly swollen. Which of the following best explains the pain (dolor) she is experiencing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clot formation within microvessels that mechanically compresses the sensory nerves

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin in the extracellular space surrounding peripheral nerves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firm binding of leukocytes to the endothelium of inflamed jaw vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased local blood flow delivering heat to exposed sensory nerve endings

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral nerve response to pressure from swelling and to inflammatory cytokines

explanation.summary: Pain in acute inflammation results from the peripheral nervous response to physical stimuli such as pressure from swelling and to chemical stimuli such as inflammatory cytokines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The perception of pain results from the peripheral nervous response to physical stimuli, such as pressure due to swelling, or chemical stimuli, such as inflammatory cytokines from pathogens or damaged tissue. Both the swelling and the infectious cause in this patient contribute to her pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clotting in microvessels locks the doors against spread of infection; it is not described as the cause of pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposition characterizes fibrinous inflammation of body cavity linings and is not the mechanism of pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding of leukocytes to endothelium is a step of extravasation and is not the cause of pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased local blood flow causes the redness and heat of inflammation, not the pain.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy with a sore throat is examined with a tongue depressor. The pharynx is bright red, and several small red-purple spots are seen on the palate. Which of the following best describes what the small spots represent?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrin deposits on the mucosal surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local defects produced by sloughing of necrotic tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pus collecting beneath the mucosal surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serous fluid accumulating beneath the epithelium

explanation.summary: Petechiae are small red or purple spots caused by bleeding into the mucosa; erythema is redness.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a patient presents with pharyngitis, the physician uses a tongue depressor to look for the cardinal signs of acute inflammation. Palatal petechiae are small red or purple spots caused by bleeding into the mucosa, and pharyngeal erythema is redness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposits form the fibrinous exudates typical of body cavity linings, not petechial spots.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Local surface defects from sloughing necrotic tissue are ulcers, not petechiae.
