whyWrongByChoice.D: A collection of pus would represent purulent inflammation, not the small red-purple spots of petechiae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serous fluid accumulating beneath the epithelium describes a blister of serous inflammation, not a petechia.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with congestive heart failure develops a watery, protein-poor fluid collection in the lungs. Which of the following best explains why this fluid is a transudate rather than an exudate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A local procoagulant stimulus produced a large vascular leak

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased hydrostatic pressure in lung vessels forced fluid out of the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased vascular permeability allowed neutrophils to enter the tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leakage of fibrinogen led to fibrin deposition in the extracellular space

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sloughing of necrotic tissue released fluid into the alveoli

explanation.summary: Transudates arise from an imbalance between hydrostatic and oncotic pressure, as when heart failure raises hydrostatic pressure in the lung vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: A transudate passes through a membrane that filters out many solid components, so it is more watery than an exudate. Transudates arise from an imbalance in the hydrostatic pressure that forces fluid out of circulation and the oncotic pressure that pulls fluid back in, and they occur in systemic diseases affecting these forces. Congestive heart failure causes increased hydrostatic pressure in the vessels of the lung because the heart cannot circulate blood effectively, leading to transudative leak.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A local procoagulant stimulus with a large leak produces a fibrinous exudate, not a transudate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased permeability with neutrophil entry produces a protein- and cell-rich exudate, the opposite of this watery fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen leakage and fibrin deposition describe fibrinous inflammation, an exudative process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sloughing of necrotic tissue produces an ulcer and is not the mechanism of transudate formation.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman burns her palm on a hot pan and within hours develops a tense, clear, fluid-filled blister. Histologically, the epidermis is separated from the dermis by a collection of watery, cell-poor fluid. Which morphologic pattern of inflammation is present?

explanation.summary: A skin blister from a burn or viral infection is serous inflammation, an accumulation of cell-poor serous fluid (transudate) within or beneath the epidermis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serous inflammation is marked by exudation of cell-poor fluid (transudate) into spaces created by cell injury. A skin blister resulting from a burn or viral infection represents accumulation of serous fluid within or beneath the damaged epidermis, with the epidermis separated from the dermis by a local collection of serous effusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinous inflammation involves fibrin deposition and is characteristic of body cavity linings such as the pericardium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pseudomembranous inflammation is a pattern in the colon during Clostridium difficile infection, not a skin blister.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Purulent inflammation is a neutrophil-rich exudate forming pus, not the clear, cell-poor fluid of a blister.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative inflammation is a surface defect from sloughing of necrotic tissue, not an intact fluid-filled blister.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with chronic epigastric pain undergoes endoscopy, which shows a crater-like defect in the duodenal mucosa. Biopsy shows an acute inflammatory exudate at the base of the crater. Which of the following processes produced this mucosal defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of serous fluid beneath the mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Buildup of neutrophils forming a pocket of pus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin on the mucosal surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of a debris membrane on the mucosa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue from the surface

explanation.summary: An ulcer is a local defect of the skin or a mucosal surface produced by sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulcerative inflammation produces an ulcer, which is a local defect of the skin or a mucosal surface produced by the sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. A duodenal ulcer crater with an acute inflammatory exudate in its base is the classic example.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serous fluid accumulation beneath an epithelium describes serous inflammation such as a blister, not a mucosal crater.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A pus-filled collection is purulent (suppurative) inflammation, not a surface defect from tissue loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrin deposition characterizes fibrinous inflammation of body cavity linings such as the pericardium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A debris membrane over the mucosa describes pseudomembranous inflammation of the colon with Clostridium difficile.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: During an acute infection, the liver increases production of several positive acute phase reactants. Which of the following reactants has functions related to attenuating the acute inflammatory response rather than promoting pathogen clearance, clotting, or iron handling?

explanation.summary: Serum amyloid A is a liver-produced positive acute phase reactant with functions related to attenuating the acute inflammatory response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The positive acute phase reactants increase when inflammation is present. Serum amyloid A is produced by the liver and has several functions related to attenuating the acute inflammatory response, which distinguishes it from the other positive reactants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C-reactive protein helps the body recognize and eliminate invading pathogens rather than dampening the response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin stores iron in cells and its serum level rises to help sequester iron during inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinogen aids tissue repair and influences endothelial cell adhesion and proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin acts as a gatekeeper for iron stored in macrophages; it is an iron-handling protein.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a prolonged bacterial infection has elevated serum ferritin and hepcidin with a decreased transferrin level. Which of the following best explains the shared purpose of these three changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhancing endothelial cell adhesion and proliferation for tissue repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing the amino acids available for positive acute phase reactants

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promoting rouleaux formation to speed red blood cell sedimentation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raising plasma oncotic pressure to limit fluid leakage from vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestering iron inside cells because iron supports microbial metabolism

explanation.summary: Increased ferritin and hepcidin with decreased transferrin all work to hide iron inside cells, because iron is an important component of microbial metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: The changes in serum levels of ferritin, hepcidin, and transferrin during acute inflammation all work toward the same goal of sequestering iron inside cells. This occurs because iron is an important component of microbial metabolism, so the body hides iron during inflammation in case the inflammation is due to an infectious cause. Transferrin falls because it is internalized by macrophages, and prolonged states of these changes can lead to iron deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influencing endothelial adhesion and proliferation for repair is a function of fibrinogen, not of ferritin, hepcidin, or transferrin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Conserving amino acids for positive reactants is the reason albumin production falls, not the purpose of the iron protein changes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rouleaux formation and faster sedimentation are driven mainly by fibrinogen, not by the iron-handling proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maintaining plasma oncotic pressure is the role of albumin, which is unrelated to iron sequestration.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A blood sample from a 60-year-old man with an active infection is placed in a tall, thin tube, and the red blood cells settle at 45 mm/h. Which of the following best explains the accelerated settling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C-reactive protein binds red cell membranes and causes them to clump together

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased albumin lowers plasma oncotic pressure, shrinking the red cells so they settle faster

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated fibrinogen neutralizes negative surface charges so red cells stack into rouleaux

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased hepcidin traps iron within macrophages, making the red cells denser

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leukocytosis increases the total cellular mass of the blood sample in the tube

explanation.summary: Pro-sedimentation factors, most importantly fibrinogen, neutralize the negative charges on RBCs so they stack into rouleaux that settle faster.
explanation.whyCorrect: Red blood cells are studded with negatively charged surface proteins, causing them to repel each other. Pro-sedimentation factors neutralize these negative charges and allow RBCs to stick together in stacks like poker chips, called rouleaux, which settle at a faster rate. This is due to increased levels of acute phase proteins, most importantly fibrinogen, and ESR correlates most reliably to fibrinogen levels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C-reactive protein helps recognize and eliminate pathogens; ESR is tied to fibrinogen, not CRP binding to red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Albumin falls as a negative acute phase reactant to conserve amino acids, but red cell shrinkage is not the mechanism of a raised ESR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepcidin gatekeeps iron in macrophages as part of iron sequestration; it does not alter red cell sedimentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leukocytosis is a systemic sign of inflammation on CBC but is not the described mechanism of faster RBC settling.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is evaluated 6 hours after a severe crush injury. Laboratory testing shows a markedly elevated C-reactive protein, yet his erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 8 mm/h. Which of the following best explains the discordant results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CRP is falsely elevated because ESR is the more rapid marker

choices.label: B
choices.text: The CRP reflects fibrinogen levels, which change before the ESR

choices.label: C
choices.text: The ESR generally does not rise until 24 to 48 hours after injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ESR is above the normal male range and confirms active inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ESR is disease-specific and does not detect trauma-related inflammation

explanation.summary: CRP is the most rapidly seen marker of acute inflammation, whereas ESR generally will not be elevated until 24 to 48 hours after the initial injury or infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinically, the most important and most rapidly seen marker of acute inflammation is increased C-reactive protein. A limitation of ESR is that it generally will not be elevated, even in the setting of acute inflammation, until 24 to 48 hours after the initial injury or infection, and its elevation occurs more slowly than changes in CRP. An ESR of 8 mm/h is within the normal male range of 0 to 15 mm/h.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CRP, not ESR, is the more rapid marker, so an early CRP rise is expected rather than false.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is the ESR, not CRP, that correlates most reliably with fibrinogen, and that elevation occurs more slowly than CRP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal ESR for male patients is 0 to 15 mm/h, so 8 mm/h is within the normal range, not elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The ESR is not disease-specific; it can detect active inflammation due to cancer, infection, and autoimmune disease.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis undergoes synovial biopsy of a chronically swollen knee. The pathologist notes that the process has been ongoing for years rather than days. Which of the following morphologic features is most characteristic of chronic, rather than acute, inflammation?

explanation.summary: Chronic inflammation is proliferative and heals by fibrosis, unlike the exudative, neutrophil-driven pattern of acute inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that chronic inflammation is proliferative in nature and that the body attempts repair by adding connective tissue, producing fibrosis and, at times, granulomas. Because damaged tissue cannot be repaired normally, fibroblasts secrete collagen that expands connective tissue, so healing by fibrosis is a hallmark of the chronic process.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A neutrophil-predominant infiltrate is the main cell pattern of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute inflammation begins within minutes to hours; chronic inflammation typically takes over about 48 hours after injury and lasts weeks to years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pus and abscess formation are classic results of acute inflammation, not chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular changes and edema are exudative features of acute inflammation, whereas chronic inflammation is proliferative.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a soft-tissue biopsy taken 3 days after a penetrating wound that failed to clear. The infiltrate is now dominated by large mononuclear cells that phagocytose debris, secrete cytokines, and appear to be organizing the response into a walled-off collection. Which of the following cells is the predominant cell type at this stage and orchestrates the transition from acute to chronic inflammation?

explanation.summary: Macrophages become the predominant cell about 48-72 hours after injury and orchestrate the acute-to-chronic transition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that macrophages become the predominant cell type approximately 48-72 hours (2-3 days) after injury or infection, kill microorganisms through phagocytosis, and secrete cytokines. They orchestrate the transition from acute to chronic inflammation and can form the 'wall' of a granuloma that isolates foreign substances.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are associated with allergic and parasitic responses and are not the predominant cell described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts secrete collagen during repair but are not the phagocytic cell that orchestrates the transition to chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils dominate the first 48 hours of acute inflammation, not the later organizing phase described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells produce antibody but are not described as the predominant cell that drives the acute-to-chronic transition.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old sandblaster who has worked without respiratory protection for 25 years develops progressive dyspnea, and lung biopsy shows chronic inflammation with particle-laden macrophages. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how his occupational exposure produced chronic inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A resistant intracellular microbe evades macrophage killing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages consume silica particles they cannot break down

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophils rapidly clear the particles, resolving inflammation within days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated mechanical wear exceeds the tissue's capacity to heal

choices.label: E
choices.text: The immune system mistakes lung cells for foreign antigens

explanation.summary: Inhaled silica is engulfed by macrophages that cannot digest it, keeping them in a chronic 'processing' state that sustains inflammation (silicosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that with ongoing toxin exposure some particles simply cannot be destroyed; alveolar macrophages consume inhaled silica but cannot break it down, and these particle-filled cells release inflammatory signals that cause a chronic inflammatory disease called silicosis. Macrophages consuming indigestible substances get stuck in 'processing' mode, leading to chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A resistant intracellular microbe describes infectious causes such as tuberculosis, not silica dust.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick emphasizes that these particles cannot be destroyed, so the response is prolonged rather than resolved within days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mechanical wear exceeding healing describes persistent injury such as osteoarthritis, not inhaled-toxin exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Attacking self antigens describes autoimmune disease (e.g., sarcoidosis), not the indigestible-particle mechanism of silicosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who recently emigrated from Russia is admitted to the intensive care unit with fulminant respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction. Despite aggressive antibiotics and supportive care he dies. At autopsy, the lungs contain numerous large granulomas with central areas of caseous necrosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these lesions?

explanation.summary: Caseating (necrotic) granulomas are the hallmark of infectious granulomatous disease, classically Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that M. tuberculosis is a highly resistant intracellular pathogen the body contains by forming granulomas, and that the granulomas seen in tuberculosis characteristically have a central necrotic (caseating) core with surrounding multinucleated giant cells. Central necrosis distinguishes these infectious granulomas from noninfectious ones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crohn disease can produce granulomas in the gut wall but is not the classic cause of large caseating pulmonary granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV promotes chronic inflammation by evading immune killing but does not itself form caseating granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sarcoid granulomas characteristically lack central necrosis (non-caseating), the opposite of what is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silica exposure causes silicosis with particle-laden macrophages, not caseating infectious granulomas.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with several months of dry cough, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort, and pulmonary function testing shows restrictive lung disease. Lung biopsy reveals well-formed granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells and lymphocytes but no central necrosis. Which of the following best characterizes this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A non-caseating granulomatous process traditionally regarded as autoimmune

choices.label: B
choices.text: An abnormal passageway between two hollow organs or the skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: An infectious granulomatous process caused by a resistant acid-fast mycobacterium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipid-laden plaque formation within the wall of a muscular artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scarring that replaces the liver's normal stromal framework

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis produces non-caseating (necrosis-free) granulomas and is traditionally viewed as an autoimmune disorder, often causing restrictive lung disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes sarcoidosis as a noninfectious cause of granulomas that has traditionally been viewed as autoimmune, in which the body is tricked into treating its own cells as foreign. Sarcoid granulomas lack the central necrosis seen in tuberculosis and, when they accumulate in the lungs, lead to impaired respiration and restrictive lung disease with dry cough, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An abnormal passageway between organs defines a fistula, not a granulomatous lung process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An infectious mycobacterial granuloma (tuberculosis) shows central caseating necrosis, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arterial lipid plaques describe atherosclerosis, not a non-caseating granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver stromal scarring describes hepatic fibrosis, not a pulmonary granulomatous disease.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with long-standing Crohn disease develops recurrent urinary tract infections and is found to have an abnormal channel connecting a loop of inflamed bowel to the urinary bladder. Which of the following terms best describes this abnormal connection?

explanation.summary: A fistula is an abnormal passageway between two hollow organs or between an organ and a surface, a classic complication of Crohn disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a fistula as an abnormal passageway between two hollow or tubular organs or between an organ and the body surface, most commonly in the GI tract. In Crohn disease, prolonged transmural inflammation drives fibroblasts to tunnel through the bowel wall; an enterovesical fistula between the GI tract and urinary bladder can present as recurrent urinary tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abscess is a localized collection of pus, a feature of acute inflammation, not an abnormal channel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An exudate is protein-rich fluid of acute inflammation, not an abnormal organ-to-organ passage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fibrous cap covers the lipid core of an atherosclerotic plaque and is unrelated to a bowel-to-bladder connection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A granuloma is a walled-off mass of macrophages, not a passageway connecting two organs.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 6-month history of diarrhea and abdominal pain is found to have transmural, granulomatous inflammation throughout her GI tract and is diagnosed with Crohn disease. Her physician explains that one cell type coordinates the inflammatory response by releasing cytokines that alter the behavior of nearby macrophages and fibroblasts. Which of the following cells is most responsible for this cytokine secretion?

explanation.summary: T lymphocytes coordinate chronic inflammation by producing cytokines that reprogram nearby cells such as macrophages and fibroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the T cell's major role in chronic inflammation is the production of inflammatory cytokines that alter the behavior of nearby cells, including macrophages and fibroblasts. T cells react on antigen recognition and are central coordinators of the chronic inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells give rise to plasma cells and produce antibody; the cytokine-driven coordination is attributed to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages phagocytose pathogens and secrete cytokines too, but the brick identifies the T cell as the major cytokine producer that alters other cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are the main effector cell of acute inflammation and are not the primary coordinators of chronic cytokine signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells secrete antibody, not the coordinating cytokines described.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A peripheral tissue biopsy from a patient with a chronic autoimmune disease shows numerous antibody-producing cells. On high power, each cell has an eccentric nucleus with coarsely clumped chromatin, deeply basophilic cytoplasm, and a pale zone beside the nucleus. Which of the following cells is being described?

explanation.summary: The plasma cell is a mature, differentiated B cell with an eccentric nucleus, clumped chromatin, blue cytoplasm, and a perinuclear hof.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the plasma cell as a mature differentiated B cell that produces a specific antibody, and shows that it has a nucleus at the side of the cell (eccentric), characteristically clumped chromatin, blue cytoplasm, and a lighter space beside the nucleus called a perinuclear hof. In autoimmune disease, plasma cells make antibodies that target the body's own cells, driving continuous inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibroblasts secrete collagen and are spindle-shaped, lacking the described antibody-producing morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages are large phagocytic cells that form granuloma walls; they do not show an eccentric nucleus with a perinuclear hof.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are fused macrophages within granulomas and have many nuclei, not a single eccentric nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils have multilobed nuclei and are cells of acute inflammation, not antibody producers.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a long history of heavy daily alcohol use develops new-onset abdominal distention from ascites. Liver biopsy shows regenerating hepatocytes surrounded by dense bands of fibrosis. Which of the following consequences most directly results from these fibrotic bands?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete restoration of normal liver architecture

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of caseating granulomas in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased resistance in the hepatic portal system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Narrowing of coronary arteries from lipid plaques

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid, reversible recovery of hepatocyte function

explanation.summary: Fibrotic bands in the liver raise resistance in the hepatic portal system, producing portal hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that chronic inflammation from alcohol damages the liver's structural framework so that regeneration is not possible and tissue is replaced by fibrotic lesions (scarring). It specifically states that fibrotic bands increase resistance in the hepatic portal system, causing portal hypertension, and that liver function is progressively and irreversibly reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick emphasizes that once the framework is destroyed, regeneration is not possible and normal architecture is not restored.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas are a feature of tuberculosis, not alcohol-induced hepatic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coronary artery narrowing from lipid plaques describes atherosclerosis, a different chronic inflammatory lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver function is progressively and irreversibly reduced, not rapidly and reversibly recovered.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a long smoking history experiences sudden crushing chest pain and is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. Angiography shows an occlusive thrombus overlying a disrupted atherosclerotic lesion. Which of the following best explains how chronic inflammation in the vessel wall led to this acute event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A caseating granuloma eroded through the arterial wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fistula formed between two adjacent coronary arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrosis of the myocardium regenerated the vessel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils formed an abscess that occluded the artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the plaque's fibrous cap released lipids and mediators

explanation.summary: Atherosclerotic plaques are sites of chronic inflammation; rupture of the fibrous cap releases lipids and mediators that cause a thrombus, blocking the vessel and causing infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes atherosclerosis as narrowing of arteries from lipid-laden plaques formed by the immune system's ineffective attempts to clear lipids in vessel walls damaged by smoking or diabetes, creating an environment of chronic inflammation. It states that rupture of the fibrous cap releases lipids and inflammatory mediators into the blood, forming a clot that can block the lumen and cause myocardial infarctions and strokes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseating granulomas are features of tuberculosis, not atherosclerotic plaque rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fistula is an abnormal passageway between organs, not the cause of thrombotic coronary occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis produces scarring and loss of function, not regeneration of a healthy vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abscess formation is a feature of acute inflammation and is not the mechanism of plaque-related coronary occlusion.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studying a solid tumor observes that systemic chronic inflammation stimulates the growth of new blood vessels around the mass, providing an ideal environment for tumor growth and hematogenous spread. A drug is being developed to block this process and starve the tumor. Which of the following processes is the drug designed to inhibit?

explanation.summary: Angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, can be driven by chronic inflammation and feeds tumor growth and metastasis; anti-angiogenic drugs block this.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes angiogenesis as the growth of new blood vessels in response to increased metabolic demand and explains that in cancer, systemic chronic inflammation leads to formation of new vessels around a tumor that feed it and provide an ideal environment for growth and hematogenous metastasis. It notes that drugs designed to inhibit angiogenesis are used to treat certain cancers by blocking the tumor's source of nutrients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseous necrosis is the central necrosis of tuberculous granulomas, not a target for anti-tumor vascular therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis is collagen scarring; it is a separate consequence of chronic inflammation and not the vessel-forming process being blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isotype switching is a change in antibody class and is unrelated to tumor vascularization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagocytosis is engulfment of particles by macrophages, not the formation of tumor-feeding blood vessels.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a decades-long smoking history develops a chronic productive cough and progressive airflow obstruction. Biopsy of the airways shows thickened walls with luminal narrowing that obstructs airflow, and arterial blood gas reveals reduced oxygen saturation with carbon dioxide retention. Which consequence of chronic inflammation best accounts for these structural airway changes?

explanation.summary: Tissue remodeling from chronic exposure to airway irritants thickens the airway wall and narrows the lumen, as in chronic bronchitis, causing CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that tissue remodeling occurs when chronic inflammation alters tissue structure to suit the inflammatory environment. It gives the example of chronic exposure to airborne irritants such as cigarette smoke leading to chronic bronchitis, in which persistent inflammation thickens the airway and narrows the lumen, obstructing airflow; the end result is reduced oxygen saturation and increased carbon dioxide retention that can cause respiratory acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abscess formation is a localized pus collection of acute inflammation, not chronic structural airway remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels, not the airway-wall thickening and luminal narrowing described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caseating granulomas are features of tuberculosis and do not explain diffuse airway wall thickening from smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Portal hypertension results from hepatic fibrosis, not from remodeling of the airways.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis undergoes thyroid biopsy that shows a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells. On examination, the thyroid is not warm, red, tender, or visibly swollen. Which of the following best describes the classic signs of inflammation in this process?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Present only during the first 24 hours

explanation.summary: Chronic inflammation is often subtle in presentation, and the classic signs of heat, redness, pain, and swelling are only sometimes present.
explanation.whyCorrect: A lymphocyte- and plasma-cell-rich infiltrate in an autoimmune disease is chronic inflammation. The brick's Table 1 lists the classic signs of inflammation as 'usually present' in acute inflammation but only 'sometimes present' in chronic inflammation, and the text notes that chronic inflammation is often subtle in presentation, which is why it can be difficult to identify, diagnose, and treat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The classic signs are not absent in every case of chronic inflammation; the brick says they are sometimes present.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick does not restrict the classic signs to the first 24 hours; acute inflammation predominates for roughly the first 48 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are the main cell type of acute inflammation, but the brick does not tie the classic signs exclusively to a neutrophil-predominant infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 'Usually present' describes the classic signs in acute inflammation, not the chronic process seen here.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who has worked for 25 years unloading heavy freight develops progressive pain and limited motion in both knees. Imaging shows loss of joint cartilage, and he is diagnosed with osteoarthritis. Which of the following categories of cause best explains the chronic inflammation in his joints?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ineffective clearance of lipids from vessel walls

explanation.summary: Persistent injury from chronic exposure to harmful forces causes wear and tear that makes healing difficult, as in osteoarthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists persistent injury as one of the causes of chronic inflammation. Repeated impact forces on the arms and legs, such as those experienced by athletes or manual laborers, damage cartilage in the joints, resulting in osteoarthritis; the body's efforts to repair the injury lead to chronic inflammation of the affected joint with pain and functional deficits of the limb.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune diseases involve the body mistakenly identifying its own cells as foreign; the brick attributes osteoarthritis to repeated mechanical injury, not autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxin exposure such as inhaled silica causes chronic inflammation when particles cannot be destroyed; there is no toxin in this occupational history.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ineffective lipid clearance in damaged vessel walls describes atherosclerosis, not joint cartilage damage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistant microorganisms such as HIV, hepatitis viruses, and M tuberculosis cause chronic inflammation by evading immune killing, not by mechanical damage to cartilage.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection has laboratory evidence of persistent, low-level immune activation for several years. Which of the following best explains why this infection produces chronic rather than acute inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies mark the patient's own cells for destruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrophages ingest the virus but cannot break it down

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeated mechanical injury prevents tissue healing

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus evades immune killing, so infection is lifelong

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus induces caseating granulomas in the lungs

explanation.summary: Some pathogens, including HIV, successfully evade the immune system's attempts to kill them, resulting in lifelong infection and a long-lasting inflammatory response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation names HIV, hepatitis viruses, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis as examples of microbes that evade the immune system's attempts at killing them. When an organism is resistant to clearance, the result can be lifelong infection, leading to a long-lasting inflammatory response that is potentially very harmful over time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies marking the body's own cells describes autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, not a resistant infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages stuck in 'processing' mode after consuming indigestible substances describes silicosis and asbestosis, not viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeated mechanical injury describes persistent injury as in osteoarthritis, not a viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of tuberculosis; the brick's review material states HIV is not characterized by granuloma formation.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea and weight loss, and small-intestinal biopsy shows persistent inflammation. She is told that her condition results from her immune system mistakenly identifying some of her own cells as foreign. Which of the following diagnoses is most consistent with this mechanism?

explanation.summary: Celiac disease is one of the common autoimmune diseases the brick lists, in which the body attacks otherwise healthy tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune diseases are characterized by the body mistakenly identifying some of its own cells as foreign, causing an immunological attack against otherwise healthy tissues with persistent immune activation, chronic inflammation, and tissue damage. The brick lists rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and celiac disease as common autoimmune diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic bronchitis is tissue remodeling caused by chronic exposure to airborne irritants such as cigarette smoke.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoarthritis results from persistent injury caused by repeated impact forces that damage cartilage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Silicosis results from exposure to an indigestible toxin (inhaled silica), not from an autoimmune attack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculosis is an infection by a resistant microorganism, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a chronically inflamed, nonhealing wound undergoes biopsy that shows marked expansion of connective tissue at the site. Which of the following provides the strength of this newly expanded connective tissue?

explanation.summary: Connective tissue added during chronic inflammation gets its strength from collagen, which is secreted by fibroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that chronic inflammation is proliferative, associated with the addition of cells, most commonly the expansion of connective tissue used to contain a pathogen or provide structure to tissue that cannot be repaired normally. This connective tissue gets its strength from collagen, which is secreted by specialized cells called fibroblasts, and excessive expansion is known as fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies tag pathogens for destruction by phagocytes; they are not a structural component of connective tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T-cell cytokines alter the behavior of nearby macrophages and fibroblasts but do not themselves provide the structural strength of connective tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipid accumulation within vessel walls describes atherosclerotic plaque, not the strength of connective tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Angiogenesis supplies nutrients and immune cells to inflamed tissue but does not provide the tensile strength of connective tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man sustains a minor injury confined to a tissue with a high capacity for renewal. The underlying tissue framework is intact and there is no persistent inflammatory stimulus. According to the pathways of tissue response to injury, which of the following outcomes is most likely?

explanation.summary: After injury, renewing tissues undergo complete regeneration, whereas wounds heal with scar formation and chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Figure 1 diagrams the responses to injury from normal homeostasis: renewing tissues follow the regeneration pathway to complete regeneration of tissues, a wound follows the repair pathway to wound healing with scar formation, and chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis. A minor injury to a renewing tissue with intact framework and no ongoing inflammatory stimulus regenerates completely.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abscess formation is a result of acute inflammation with pus, not a regenerative response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis is the end result of the chronic inflammation pathway, which requires a persistent inflammatory stimulus that is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas form when macrophages wall off foreign substances or resistant pathogens, not after a minor injury to a renewing tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Scar formation is the outcome of wound healing, not of regeneration in a renewing tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A biopsy of a chronically inflamed tissue shows numerous newly formed blood vessels. In addition to meeting the increased nutritional requirements of the inflamed tissue, which of the following is a function of these new vessels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carrying accumulated lipids out of the tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the influx of immune cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolating the pathogen within a granuloma

explanation.summary: New vessels formed by angiogenesis in chronic inflammation both meet nutritional demand and increase the influx of immune cells trying to resolve the inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that new blood vessels may be added during chronic inflammation, a process known as angiogenesis, to meet the increased nutritional requirements of the inflamed tissue. It adds that these new vessels also function to increase the influx of immune cells that are attempting to resolve the inflammatory condition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick does not describe new vessels clearing lipids; lipid accumulation in vessel walls is the problem in atherosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Collagen is secreted by fibroblasts, not by blood vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isolating pathogens is the role of the macrophage 'wall' of a granuloma, not of new blood vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular changes and edema are manifestations of acute inflammation; the brick does not assign new vessels a role in removing exudate.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman sustains a deep laceration of the forearm that becomes contaminated. Using the brick's useful rule of thumb, at approximately what time after the injury does chronic inflammation typically take over from acute inflammation?

explanation.summary: Acute inflammation predominates for about the first 48 hours after injury; after the 48-hour mark, chronic inflammation typically takes over.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that although the exact duration of acute inflammation can vary, 48 hours is a useful rule of thumb. In most cases acute inflammation predominates for the first 48 hours after an injury, and after the 48-hour mark chronic inflammation typically takes over. Table 1 likewise lists the onset of chronic inflammation as approximately 48 hours after injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two weeks is far beyond the 48-hour rule of thumb the brick gives for the transition.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six hours falls within the window of acute inflammation, which begins within minutes to hours and predominates for about 48 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seven days is well past the transition; by then macrophages have long been the predominant cell type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick's review material specifically notes that chronic inflammation begins around 48 hours, not within 24 hours.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy shows a tumor-like cluster of cells with a central collection of large activated macrophages, some of which have fused into multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes. Which of the following terms describes the activated macrophages at the center of this lesion?

explanation.summary: Granulomas contain activated macrophages called epithelioid cells, which often fuse into multinucleated giant cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes granulomas as tumor-like masses of cells that form because of a chronic inflammatory response. These cell clusters contain activated macrophages, termed epithelioid cells, which often fuse into multinucleated giant cells and are surrounded by T lymphocytes that support the structure via cytokine secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen-presenting cells are the cells T cells contact during antigen recognition; the brick's name for the activated macrophages within a granuloma is epithelioid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibroblasts secrete collagen; they are not the fused, activated macrophages at the center of a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are the main cell type of acute inflammation and are not the centralized cells of a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are antibody-producing differentiated B cells with an eccentric nucleus; they are not the activated macrophages of a granuloma.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who received a kidney transplant develops chronic inflammation within the graft. His physician explains that a specific lymphocyte subtype first encounters a foreign antigen displayed by another cell and then reacts to the graft. With which of the following cells do these lymphocytes come into contact before mounting the response?

explanation.summary: In conditions such as viral infection and tissue-graft rejection, T cells contact antigen-presenting cells and react on antigen recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in some chronic inflammatory conditions, such as viral infection and tissue-graft rejection, T cells come in contact with antigen-presenting cells. On antigen recognition, the T cell reacts to the foreign invader, leading to an inflammatory response, and its major role is the production of inflammatory cytokines that alter the behavior of nearby cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts secrete collagen and are targets of T-cell cytokines, not the cells that present antigen to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are fused macrophages within granulomas; the brick names antigen-presenting cells as the T cell's contact in graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are cells of acute inflammation and are not described as presenting antigen to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are mature B cells that produce antibody; the brick does not describe them presenting antigen to T cells.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has had symmetric joint swelling for 8 years despite treatment. Synovial tissue shows abundant plasma cells. Which of the following best explains how these cells sustain the ongoing inflammatory response in her joints?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They engulf indigestible particles and remain in processing mode

choices.label: B
choices.text: They fuse into multinucleated giant cells that wall off the joint

choices.label: C
choices.text: They produce antibodies that mark her own cells for destruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: They secrete collagen that thickens the synovial lining

choices.label: E
choices.text: They tunnel through the joint capsule into adjoining tissue

explanation.summary: In autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, plasma cells produce antibodies that mark the body's own cells as targets, causing continuous recruitment of inflammatory cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that antibodies have sticky 'arms' that attach to pathogens, tagging them for destruction by phagocytic cells such as macrophages. In some autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, plasma cells produce antibodies that mark the body's own cells as targets for destruction, resulting in continuous recruitment of inflammatory cells and an ongoing inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Engulfing indigestible particles and becoming stuck in processing mode describes macrophages in silicosis and asbestosis, not plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fusion into multinucleated giant cells is a property of activated macrophages in granulomas, not of plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Collagen is secreted by fibroblasts, not plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tunneling through a wall into adjoining tissue describes fibroblast proliferation in fistula formation, not plasma-cell activity.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 38-year-old nurse has a positive screening test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. She has no cough, fever, or weight loss and feels entirely well. Which of the following best explains why she is infected yet has no symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies have neutralized the bacteria in the bloodstream

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophils have completely eradicated the bacteria

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bacteria are contained within granulomas

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bacteria have been cleared from macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: The bacteria have spread hematogenously to distant sites

explanation.summary: In latent tuberculosis, the bacteria hide within granulomas, which is why not everyone infected with M tuberculosis is symptomatic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick asks why not everyone infected with M tuberculosis is symptomatic and answers: granulomas. Although macrophages cannot destroy and eradicate the bacterial cells, they contain the infection by inducing granuloma formation. In latent tuberculosis, the bacteria hide within granulomas until the opportunity for escape arises.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes containment within granulomas, not antibody neutralization, as the reason infected people can be asymptomatic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M tuberculosis is highly resistant to the immune system's attempts to destroy it; the brick emphasizes that the body can contain but not eradicate the bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M tuberculosis is an intracellular pathogen that persists after being phagocytosed by macrophages; the bacteria are not cleared.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hematogenous spread describes cancer metastasis in the brick; it would not explain an asymptomatic contained infection.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with a fully functioning immune system is found to harbor Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a pulmonary granuloma. Which of the following properties of this organism best explains its ability to evade destruction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It depletes T lymphocytes from the granuloma

choices.label: B
choices.text: It remains extracellular to avoid macrophage uptake

choices.label: C
choices.text: It secretes collagen to build its own capsule

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates plasma cells to make autoantibodies

choices.label: E
choices.text: It survives inside macrophages after phagocytosis

explanation.summary: M tuberculosis is an intracellular pathogen; being phagocytosed by macrophages is part of its 'plan,' and it survives within them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that M tuberculosis bacteria have the ability to evade destruction even when the immune system is functioning perfectly. It is an intracellular pathogen, meaning it is part of its 'plan' to get phagocytosed by macrophages; although macrophages cannot destroy the bacteria, they can contain the infection by inducing granuloma formation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T lymphocytes surround and support the granuloma via cytokines; the brick does not describe the bacterium depleting them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The opposite is true: the organism is intracellular and is taken up by macrophages as part of its survival strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Collagen is secreted by host fibroblasts; the bacterium is contained by a host granuloma, not a self-made capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autoantibody production describes autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, not the survival mechanism of M tuberculosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis has a lung biopsy showing a granuloma with a central necrotic core surrounded by macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and lymphocytes. Which of the following best explains the development of the necrotic core?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Death of immune cells overcome by the pathogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fusion of activated macrophages into giant cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of a fibrous cap over the lesion

explanation.summary: When pathogens gain the upper hand in the granuloma 'battlefield,' the immune cells working to clear the infection die, forming a necrotic core.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes infectious granulomas as a battlefield where an ongoing war takes place between bacteria and the immune system. If the pathogens gain the upper hand, immune cells working to clear the infection will die, which causes a necrotic core to develop within the center of the granuloma; this is a common feature of M tuberculosis infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Undigested inhaled particles describe silicosis, in which the review material notes granulomas lack central necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Collagen deposition by fibroblasts produces fibrosis, not central necrosis of a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fusion of activated macrophages produces multinucleated giant cells at the granuloma's periphery; it does not create the necrotic center.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrous cap rupture describes atherosclerotic plaque and the resulting clot, not granuloma necrosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with Crohn disease undergoes colonoscopy with biopsy, and the pathologist reports granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following best describes the expected location and appearance of these granulomas?

explanation.summary: Crohn granulomas form within the gut wall and, being noninfectious, lack the central necrosis seen in tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that in Crohn disease, formation of granulomas within the gut wall is not uncommon, and Figure 8 shows granulomatous inflammation within the transmurally inflamed bowel wall. The review material adds that Crohn granulomas would be gastrointestinal, not pulmonary, and would not have central necrosis, which distinguishes them from the caseating granulomas of tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crohn granulomas lack central necrosis; a necrotic core signifies an infectious granuloma such as tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crohn disease affects the GI tract; the brick does not describe granulomas in joint cartilage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary granulomas with central necrosis are characteristic of tuberculosis, not Crohn disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary granulomas without necrosis describe sarcoidosis; Crohn granulomas are in the gut wall.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with long-standing Crohn disease develops a tract connecting the ileum to the skin of the abdominal wall. Histologic examination of the tract shows that a proliferating cell type has created a tunnel through the intestinal wall into adjoining tissue. Which of the following cells is most responsible for creating this tunnel?

explanation.summary: In Crohn disease, fibroblasts proliferating to replace eroded intestinal wall create the tunnel that becomes a fistula.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that fistulas are a major complication of Crohn disease. Prolonged inflammation causes intestinal epithelium and resident fibroblasts to attempt repair; as immunocytes attack the gut mucosa and erode the intestinal wall, fibroblasts proliferate to replace the destroyed tissue, creating a tunnel through the intestinal wall and into the adjoining tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells; they are not described as creating the fistula tract.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are fused macrophages found in granulomas, not the cells that tunnel through the bowel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are the main cell of acute inflammation and pus; the brick attributes the fistula tunnel to fibroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells produce antibody; they do not proliferate to form the tunnel of a fistula.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A medical student is asked where fistulas, abnormal passageways between hollow or tubular organs or between an organ and the body surface, most commonly occur. Which of the following is the correct answer?

explanation.summary: Fistulas most commonly occur in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a fistula as an abnormal passageway between two hollow or tubular organs or between an organ and the body surface and states that fistulas most commonly occur in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, where they are a major complication of Crohn disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coronary arteries are narrowed by atherosclerotic plaques; they are not described as a site of fistulas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver is the site of hepatic fibrosis in the brick, not of fistulas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lungs are the site of granulomas in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis, not the most common site of fistulas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The urinary bladder can be one end of an enterovesical fistula, but the brick identifies the GI tract as the most common site.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a single, brief exposure to a substance that damages only his hepatocytes while leaving the liver's underlying stromal framework intact. He has no ongoing infection or toxin exposure afterward. Which of the following is the most likely long-term outcome for his liver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dense fibrotic bands replacing healthy tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granuloma formation around the damaged cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Portal hypertension from increased hepatic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive, irreversible loss of liver function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regeneration of hepatocytes with restored function

explanation.summary: The liver can regenerate after injuries that damage only hepatocytes and leave the stromal framework intact; fibrosis occurs when chronic inflammation destroys that framework.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the liver has an incredible capacity for regeneration after certain types of injury, particularly injuries that only damage hepatocytes and leave the underlying stromal framework intact. Only when chronic inflammation from infection or chronic toxin exposure damages the structural framework does regeneration become impossible, leaving scarring (fibrosis) as the only repair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrotic bands form when the structural framework is damaged so that regeneration is not possible, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomas form to wall off resistant pathogens or indigestible substances, not in response to a brief hepatocyte-only injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal hypertension results from fibrotic bands increasing resistance in the hepatic portal system, a consequence of chronic, framework-destroying injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive, irreversible reduction of liver function occurs as healthy tissue is replaced by fibrotic lesions, not after a regenerable injury.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a 20-year history of hepatitis C infection undergoes liver biopsy that shows regenerating hepatocytes surrounded by dense bands of fibrosis. He does not drink alcohol. Which of the following categories of cause best accounts for the chronic inflammation that produced these findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune attack on the liver's own hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infection by a microorganism that evades clearance

explanation.summary: Hepatitis viruses evade immune killing, producing lifelong infection whose chronic inflammation can destroy the liver's framework and cause hepatic fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names viruses that cause hepatitis among the pathogens that successfully evade the immune system's attempts at killing them, resulting in lifelong infection and a long-lasting inflammatory response. It also states that chronic inflammation caused by infection, as well as by toxins such as alcohol, can damage the liver's structural framework so that repair is only possible by fibrosis, and Figure 9 shows exactly these findings in a patient with hepatitis C.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atherosclerosis narrows arteries through lipid-laden plaques; it is not the cause of hepatic fibrosis in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune disease involves the body identifying its own cells as foreign; hepatitis C is an infectious cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Indigestible particles such as silica cause lung disease when macrophages cannot break them down; this is not the mechanism of hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Persistent mechanical injury describes repeated impact forces damaging joint cartilage, not viral liver disease.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a 40-pack-year smoking history has stable exertional chest pain. Coronary angiography shows narrowing of a coronary artery by a lipid-laden plaque, without rupture or thrombus. Which of the following best explains how this plaque formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies tagged the arterial endothelium as foreign

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibroblasts tunneled through the damaged arterial wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune cells failed to clear lipids from a damaged wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages walled off an intracellular pathogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: New vessels grew into the arterial wall to feed a tumor

explanation.summary: Atherosclerotic plaques form from the immune system's ineffective attempts to clear accumulated lipids in vessel walls damaged by factors such as smoking or diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines atherosclerosis as narrowing of arteries due to accumulation of lipid-laden plaques within the vessel wall. These plaques are formed by the immune system's ineffective attempts to clear accumulated lipids in the walls of vessels damaged by factors such as smoking or diabetes, and ongoing efforts to clear these fats create an environment of chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies tagging the body's own cells describes autoimmune disease; the brick attributes plaque to lipid accumulation in damaged vessel walls.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts tunneling through a wall describes fistula formation in Crohn disease, not plaque formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages walling off an intracellular pathogen describes granuloma formation in tuberculosis, not atherosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Angiogenesis feeding a tumor is the brick's cancer example; it is not the mechanism of coronary plaque.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with a 15-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has steadily declining kidney function. Renal biopsy shows fibrosis of the glomeruli. Which of the following best describes the sequence that produced this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fistula formed between the renal collecting system and the bowel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caseating granulomas developed around the glomerular capillaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated glucose inflamed the glomerulus, which became fibrotic

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indigestible glucose crystals lodged in macrophages within the glomeruli

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plaque rupture caused ischemic necrosis of the glomeruli

explanation.summary: In poorly controlled diabetes, elevated blood glucose inflames the glomerulus, and chronic inflammation of this fragile boundary leads to glomerular fibrosis and diabetic nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in chronic systemic inflammatory disease such as diabetes, fibrosis evolves in multiple organ systems. In patients with poorly controlled diabetes, elevated blood glucose leads to inflammation of the glomerulus, the functional unit of renal filtration; inflammation of this fragile boundary between the kidney and systemic circulation eventually leads to glomerular fibrosis and reduced kidney function, a condition known as diabetic nephropathy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fistulas most commonly occur in the GI tract and are complications of Crohn disease, not of diabetic kidney disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas are a feature of tuberculosis, not diabetic nephropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages stuck processing indigestible particles describes silicosis and asbestosis; the brick does not describe glucose crystals in glomerular macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plaque rupture with ischemia is the brick's mechanism for myocardial infarction and stroke, not for glomerular fibrosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy is counseled that the same inflammatory and fibrotic process affecting his kidneys can damage the vessels supplying another organ, causing a second well-known diabetic complication. Which of the following structures is at risk?

explanation.summary: The same process that causes diabetic nephropathy can affect the vessels supplying the retina, producing diabetic retinopathy and vision loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: In its clinical correlation on fibrosis, the brick states that the same process that produces glomerular fibrosis in diabetic nephropathy can also affect the vessels that supply blood to the retina, leading to diabetic retinopathy and associated vision loss. The summary lists diabetic retinopathy among the health complications of fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Airway thickening is the brick's example of tissue remodeling from cigarette smoke (chronic bronchitis), not a diabetic vascular complication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bowel-wall inflammation and fistulas belong to Crohn disease in the brick, not to diabetic vascular disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diabetes damages vessel walls and promotes atherosclerosis, but the brick's stated retinal complication that parallels nephropathy is diabetic retinopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Joint cartilage damage from repeated impact forces produces osteoarthritis, not a complication of diabetes.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man cuts his hand while cooking. Within 2 hours the wound is red, warm, swollen, and painful. Assuming the wound is cleaned and heals normally, which of the following best describes the expected duration of this acute inflammatory phase?

explanation.summary: Acute inflammation begins within minutes to hours of injury and lasts hours to days, in contrast to chronic inflammation lasting weeks, months, or years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Table 1 lists the onset of acute inflammation as within minutes to hours after injury and its duration as hours to days; the text notes that acute inflammation generally lasts a few days and is characterized by the classical signs of heat, redness, pain, and swelling. With rest and proper care, an injury such as cutting a finger heals effectively without progressing to chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lifelong inflammation is described for infections by microbes that evade immune clearance, not for a simple cut.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Minutes to hours describes the onset of acute inflammation, not its duration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Months to years describes chronic inflammation, an ongoing low-level process, not a normally healing cut.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Weeks to months is within the duration of chronic inflammation, which follows if the problem cannot be fixed by normal defenses.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who has consumed five alcoholic beverages daily since college presents with new-onset ascites and asks how this could have developed so quickly when she had no symptoms for decades. Which of the following best explains the long symptom-free interval?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute inflammation with classic signs was present but went unnoticed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol was fully cleared before reaching the hepatocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Angiogenesis preserved perfusion until vessels regressed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granulomas walled off the alcohol until they ruptured

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ongoing regeneration compensated until it became impossible

explanation.summary: Chronic alcohol use causes silent, low-level liver damage; the liver repairs itself for years until regeneration becomes impossible and fibrosis produces ascites.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case connection explains that even without symptoms, behind the scenes there was silent, chronic damage to the liver cells from daily alcohol use. The liver can repair itself, but over the years the ability to regenerate new healthy cells becomes impossible once the structural framework is damaged; this leads to fibrosis of the liver and the ascites that finally appears, all attributable to years of chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic inflammation is often subtle and its classic signs only sometimes present; the brick attributes her silent course to chronic, not acute, inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes ongoing damage to hepatocytes from alcohol, not clearance of alcohol before it reached the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Angiogenesis is described in the context of tumors and inflamed tissue, not as the reason for a silent course in alcoholic liver disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas wall off resistant pathogens or indigestible particles; the brick does not describe granulomas in alcoholic liver damage.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man survives a large anterior myocardial infarction. Several weeks later, the infarcted region of myocardium has been replaced by a dense collagenous scar rather than by new cardiac muscle, because cardiac myocytes are permanent (nondividing) cells. Which of the following cell types shares this same regenerative classification?

explanation.summary: Permanent (nondividing) tissues such as cardiac muscle and neurons cannot regenerate and heal only by scarring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurons, like cardiac myocytes, are permanent tissue: they are nondividing and lack the ability to regenerate, so lost cells are replaced by connective tissue scar rather than by new functional cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basal keratinocytes of the skin are labile tissue that continuously divide to renew the epidermis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematopoietic precursors of the bone marrow are labile tissue that divide continuously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colonic surface epithelium is labile (continuously dividing) tissue that regenerates readily when the ECM is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent) tissue that can regenerate once primed to re-enter the cell cycle.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman undergoes colonoscopy with biopsy of the colonic mucosa. Two weeks later the biopsy site has fully regenerated with normal, functioning epithelium and no scar. Which property of colonic epithelium best explains this complete regeneration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a labile tissue whose cells continuously divide

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a permanent tissue that heals only by scarring

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a stable tissue that must be primed before it can divide

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks an underlying basement membrane and extracellular matrix

choices.label: E
choices.text: It relies entirely on myofibroblast contraction to close defects

explanation.summary: Labile tissues are continuously dividing and regenerate completely when the extracellular matrix remains intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonic columnar epithelium is a labile tissue that divides continuously; with an intact ECM/basement membrane scaffold it can fully regenerate the lost cells, restoring normal architecture without scar formation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Permanent tissues (e.g., cardiac muscle, neurons) are nondividing and heal only by scarring, unlike labile epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stable tissues such as hepatocytes are quiescent and must be primed to divide; colonic epithelium divides continuously without such priming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epithelium sits on a basement membrane; this intact ECM is precisely what permits regeneration rather than preventing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myofibroblast contraction closes large open wounds by secondary intention; it is not the mechanism of epithelial regeneration.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 45-year-old living liver donor undergoes resection of approximately 60% of his liver. Over the following weeks the remaining liver regenerates to nearly its original mass as hepatocytes leave a resting state and re-enter the cell cycle. Hepatocytes are best classified as which of the following tissue types?

explanation.summary: The liver is the classic stable tissue: normally quiescent hepatocytes must be primed to divide but retain a remarkable regenerative capacity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent, G0) cells that do not divide continuously; following injury or loss they are primed by signals such as HGF and move from G0 into the proliferating G1 stage, allowing the liver to regenerate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulation tissue is a temporary reparative tissue of fibroblasts and new vessels, not a hepatocyte classification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The interstitial matrix is a component of the ECM between cells, not a category of tissue regenerative capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Labile tissues (e.g., gut epithelium, bone marrow) divide continuously without needing to be primed; hepatocytes are normally quiescent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Permanent tissues cannot regenerate at all; the liver's robust regeneration excludes this category.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: An 80-year-old bed-bound woman in a nursing home develops a non-healing ulcer over the sacrum after prolonged, unrelieved pressure to the area. Examination shows loss of the overlying epithelium with underlying granulation tissue. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this chronic wound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the epidermal basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess collagen deposition confined to the wound margins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reopening of a previously closed surgical incision

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained compression compromising local blood flow

explanation.summary: Pressure sores are areas of skin ulceration and necrosis caused by prolonged compression that compromises blood flow, typically in immobile patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sustained pressure over a bony prominence in a bed-bound patient reduces perfusion and oxygen delivery, producing ischemic necrosis and a non-healing ulcer with loss of epithelium and underlying granulation tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune basement-membrane destruction describes blistering diseases, not a compression-related pressure sore.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess collagen confined to the wound describes a hypertrophic scar, not an ischemic ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myofibroblast contraction produces contractures over joints, not a sacral pressure ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reopening of a closed incision defines wound dehiscence, a postsurgical complication.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: During the later stages of wound healing, one growth factor both stimulates fibroblasts to synthesize collagen and extracellular matrix and dampens the inflammatory response so that it does not damage the healing tissue. Which of the following growth factors has these dual actions?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta stimulates fibroblast collagen/ECM synthesis while suppressing inflammation during the later, remodeling phase of repair.
