Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

explanation.summary: DIC is a thrombohemorrhagic disorder that produces simultaneous microvascular thrombosis and bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes DIC as uncontrolled activation of coagulation that forms microthrombi throughout small vessels while consuming platelets and clotting factors, so the patient bleeds and clots at the same time. It commonly complicates sepsis and presents with oozing from IV sites plus cyanosis of the extremities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute myocardial infarction causes substernal chest pain radiating down the left arm, not diffuse bleeding with thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder in which patients bleed into muscles and joints, and it is not triggered by sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deep venous thrombosis presents with a swollen, painful lower extremity, not bleeding from the gums and IV sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding but does not produce the cyanotic extremities or consumptive picture described.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman develops a pulmonary embolism arising from a deep vein thrombus in her leg. Follow-up evaluation reveals a Factor V Leiden mutation. Which component of Virchow's triad does this genetic finding represent?

explanation.summary: Factor V Leiden is an inherited cause of hypercoagulability, one of the three factors in Virchow's triad.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists hypercoagulability as an abnormally high tendency of the blood to clot from a genetic disorder such as Factor V Leiden or a prothrombin gene mutation, distinct from endothelial injury and abnormal blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No vascular injury is described; endothelial injury involves exposure of tissue factor and von Willebrand factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased fibrinolysis promotes clot breakdown and bleeding, the opposite of a prothrombotic mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stasis is a form of abnormal blood flow, not the inherited clotting tendency represented by Factor V Leiden.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Turbulent blood flow is another category of abnormal flow, not a genetic hypercoagulable state.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man sustains a femoral shaft fracture in a motorcycle collision. Two days later he becomes acutely dyspneic and confused, and laboratory studies show a low platelet count. Which type of embolism most likely accounts for his presentation?

explanation.summary: Fat embolism follows long-bone fractures and can produce fat embolism syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that fat embolism results from microscopic fat globules and bone marrow entering the vasculature after fractures of long bones. Symptomatic patients develop fat embolism syndrome with pulmonary insufficiency, neurologic symptoms, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Air embolism arises from communication with outside air during procedures or chest wall injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amniotic fluid embolism occurs during labor or the postpartum period, not after a limb fracture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Foreign body embolism occurs when an object such as a bullet enters a vessel, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A leg-vein thromboembolus is possible after trauma but does not explain the fat-globule syndrome with thrombocytopenia following a fracture.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews a hemorrhagic (red) infarct on autopsy. Red infarcts are most likely to occur in which of the following organs?

explanation.summary: Red infarcts occur in tissues with a dual circulation, such as the lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that red infarcts occur in tissues with dual circulation, including the lung, liver, and small intestine, where blood from the unobstructed parallel supply flows into the necrotic zone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain has an end-arterial circulation and is not the classic site of red infarcts described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The heart has a single, end-arterial circulation and develops white infarcts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The kidney has an end-arterial supply and develops pale white infarcts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen has an end-arterial supply and develops white infarcts.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is placed on prolonged bed rest after abdominal surgery and develops a swollen, painful calf. Which component of Virchow's triad is most directly responsible for his venous thrombosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endothelial injury from tissue factor exposure

explanation.summary: Prolonged immobilization causes venous stasis, a form of abnormal blood flow that predisposes to thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that abnormal blood flow includes stasis, which disrupts normal laminar flow and brings platelets into contact with the endothelium. Stasis is emphasized in prolonged bed rest and the post-operative setting, and venous thrombi begin at sites of stasis in the lower extremity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No direct vascular injury exposing tissue factor is described; the immobility is the key factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased fibrinolysis breaks down clots and would predispose to bleeding, not thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing indicates an inherited clotting tendency such as Factor V Leiden.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recanalization is a fate of an existing thrombus, not a predisposing factor for a new one.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: Several weeks after a lower-extremity thrombus formed, histology of the affected vessel shows fibroblasts and collagen deposition within the old clot along with several small new channels through the mass, partially restoring blood flow. Which fate of the thrombus does this describe?

explanation.summary: Organization and recanalization form new channels through a thrombus that partially restore flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes organization and recanalization as a process in which fibroblasts grow and deposit collagen fibers within the vessel (organization) and new lumina develop through the thrombus (recanalization), partially restoring flow in the blood vessel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Calcification is not one of the fates of a thrombus taught in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dissolution is complete breakdown of the thrombus by fibrinolysis, not incorporation into the wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Embolization is detachment of a fragment that travels to a distant site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Propagation is enlargement of the thrombus by additional platelets and fibrin, not channel formation.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman receiving heparin after surgery develops a falling platelet count and a new deep venous thrombosis on day 6 of therapy. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An antibody forms against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited Factor V Leiden mutation is unmasked by exposure to heparin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excessive plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis consumes circulating platelets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparin directly lyses circulating platelets by disrupting their membranes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shiga-like toxin from an enteric infection damages the endothelium

explanation.summary: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is driven by antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex that activate platelets and cause thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in HIT heparin binds platelet factor 4 (PF4) on the platelet surface, and an antibody develops against the heparin-PF4 complex. Platelets become activated and aggregated, lowering the platelet count while forming clots, with thrombosis (commonly DVT or PE) as the major complication.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIT is an acquired antibody-mediated disorder, not an unmasked inherited Factor V Leiden mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The thrombocytopenia is from platelet activation and aggregation, not excessive fibrinolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heparin does not directly lyse platelets; the platelet drop results from antibody-mediated activation and consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shiga-like toxin endothelial damage is the mechanism of hemolytic uremic syndrome, not HIT.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a recent large anterior myocardial infarction develops sudden pain and pallor of the right leg. Imaging shows a mural thrombus in the left ventricle. This clinical picture is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fat embolus from bone marrow

choices.label: B
choices.text: A venous embolus traveling to the lungs

choices.label: C
choices.text: An air embolus from a chest wall injury

explanation.summary: Arterial emboli predominantly originate from mural thrombi in the heart and lodge in distal arteries such as those of the limbs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that arterial emboli predominantly originate from mural thrombi in the heart (thrombus in the heart chambers or aortic lumen) and continue along the flow of blood until they end up in a smaller artery, most commonly in the lower extremities and brain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fat emboli arise from long-bone fractures or trauma, not a cardiac mural thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A venous embolus travels through the right heart to the lungs, causing pulmonary embolism, not limb ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Air embolism follows communication with outside air, not a ventricular mural thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amniotic fluid embolism occurs during labor or the postpartum period.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has sudden occlusion of a renal artery, and the kidney later shows a sharply demarcated, pale (white) area of necrosis. Which property of the kidney best explains why this infarct is white rather than red?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dual blood supply with parallel circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: High resistance of renal tissue to hypoxia

explanation.summary: White infarcts occur in organs with a single, end-arterial circulation such as the kidney.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that white infarcts occur in tissues with single, end-arterial circulation, including the heart, spleen, and kidney, because no parallel supply can flow blood into the necrotic zone. The names refer to the color seen macroscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dual blood supply produces red infarcts, seen in the lung, liver, and small intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tissue hypoxia tolerance affects whether infarction occurs, not the red-versus-white color.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tissue density relates to red infarcts in loose tissue, but the defining feature here is the end-arterial supply.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rate of occlusion influences whether an infarct forms, not its color; this occlusion was sudden.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A researcher compares how quickly different tissues suffer irreversible damage during ischemia. Which tissue is most vulnerable, undergoing irreversible injury after only a few minutes of hypoxia?

explanation.summary: Neural tissue is the most sensitive to hypoxia, dying within minutes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists tissue vulnerability to hypoxia as a factor in infarction, noting that brain tissue undergoes irreversible damage after only a few minutes of hypoxia, whereas heart muscle starts to die after 20-30 minutes and skeletal muscle may survive a few hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiac muscle begins to die after 20-30 minutes of ischemia, longer than the brain's few minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The liver has a dual blood supply and is comparatively protected from thromboembolic infarction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lung has a dual blood supply and is not the most hypoxia-vulnerable tissue described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skeletal muscle may survive a few hours before dying, making it relatively resistant.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman becomes acutely dyspneic and cyanotic and then goes into shock during delivery, followed by seizures. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her sudden deterioration?

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but often fatal complication of labor and the immediate postpartum period.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes amniotic fluid embolism as infusion of amniotic fluid or fetal tissue into the maternal circulation through a tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins, presenting with dyspnea, cyanosis, and shock followed by neurologic impairment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A deep venous thrombosis presents with a swollen, painful leg rather than acute peripartum collapse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foreign body embolism results from an introduced object such as a bullet, not childbirth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fat embolism follows long-bone fractures or trauma, not delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Air embolism arises from communication with outside air during procedures or chest wall injury.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child develops bloody diarrhea followed by thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and acute renal failure after eating undercooked ground beef. This thrombotic microangiopathy is most commonly caused by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited Factor V Leiden mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shiga-like toxin from E. coli O157:H7

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncontrolled release of tissue factor in sepsis

explanation.summary: Hemolytic uremic syndrome is typically caused by Shiga-like toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that HUS, a thrombotic microangiopathy on the differential with DIC, is typically associated with gastroenteritis caused by Shiga-like toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7. The toxin is absorbed from the gastrointestinal mucosa and damages endothelial function, causing platelet activation, bloody diarrhea, and acute renal failure, especially in children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic fluid embolism is an obstetric emergency, unrelated to this child's illness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor V Leiden is an inherited hypercoagulable state, not the cause of toxin-mediated HUS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies against heparin-PF4 cause HIT, not the post-diarrheal renal failure described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncontrolled tissue factor release triggers DIC, which is a distinct disorder from toxin-mediated HUS.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and untreated hypercholesterolemia develops a thrombus over a damaged segment of his coronary artery endothelium. Which of the following best describes how injury to the endothelium initiates clot formation at this site?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of laminar flow to stasis and turbulence within the lumen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exposure of underlying tissue factor for binding of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of an antibody against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inherited resistance of mutant Factor V to inactivation by protein C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of fibrinolytic plasminogen activators from the endothelial surface

explanation.summary: Endothelial injury triggers thrombosis by exposing subendothelial tissue factor for von Willebrand factor binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that injury to the endothelium triggers clot formation by exposing underlying tissue factor for binding of von Willebrand factor. It adds that inflammation and noxious stimuli such as toxins absorbed from cigarette smoke and metabolic abnormalities like hypercholesterolemia damage the endothelium by shifting its gene expression toward a prothrombotic pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stasis is a separate component of Virchow's triad (abnormal blood flow), not the direct consequence of endothelial injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An antibody against the heparin-PF4 complex is the mechanism of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, not endothelial injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor V Leiden is an inherited hypercoagulable state, a distinct arm of Virchow's triad from endothelial injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrinolysis breaks clots down (dissolution); it is not how injured endothelium initiates a thrombus.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has severe atherosclerotic narrowing of her internal carotid artery. A thrombus forms just downstream of the narrowed segment even though she is fully ambulatory and has no inherited clotting disorder. Which form of abnormal blood flow most directly promoted thrombus formation at this site?

explanation.summary: Turbulence, as at an atherosclerotic vessel narrowing, is a form of abnormal blood flow that promotes thrombosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's Virchow's triad figure lists abnormal blood flow as either stasis (e.g., atrial fibrillation, bed rest) or turbulence (e.g., atherosclerotic vessel narrowing). Stasis or turbulent flow disrupts normal laminar flow and brings platelets into contact with the endothelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal laminar flow is protective; it is the disruption of laminar flow that predisposes to thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced venous return relates to venous stasis, not to an arterial atherosclerotic narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Atrial fibrillation is an example of stasis in the heart; no arrhythmia is described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The patient is fully ambulatory, so immobility-related stasis is not the driver here.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with widely metastatic pancreatic cancer develops a deep venous thrombosis of the left leg. He is active, has no history of vascular injury, and genetic testing for Factor V Leiden and the prothrombin gene mutation is negative. His thrombosis is best attributed to which of the following?

explanation.summary: Disseminated cancer is an acquired cause of hypercoagulability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines hypercoagulability as an abnormally high tendency of the blood to clot through either a genetic disorder (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation) or an acquired disorder, listing smoking, pregnancy, cancer, and oral contraceptive use. The triad figure specifically names disseminated cancer as an acquired example.

whyWrongByChoice.B: No vascular injury or trauma is described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genetic testing for the inherited causes named in the brick is negative.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The patient is active, so immobility-related stasis is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Turbulence is an arterial flow abnormality; this is a venous thrombosis in a patient with no vessel narrowing described.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman is recovering from hip surgery and will be unable to walk for several days. In addition to prescribing a blood thinner, which of the following interventions is most appropriate to reduce her risk of venous thrombosis in the legs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevation of the head of the bed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sequential compression devices on the legs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strict bed rest with the legs kept still

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm compresses applied to both calves

explanation.summary: Post-operative patients who cannot ambulate can receive sequential compression devices to reduce venous thrombosis risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that stasis is a concern with prolonged bed rest, particularly post-operatively, and that in patients who cannot ambulate extra interventions can be considered, namely blood thinners and sequential compression devices (SCD), which are stockings used to reduce the risk of venous thrombosis in the leg.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevating the head of the bed is not a described intervention against venous thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluid restriction is not a measure the brick describes for preventing venous stasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keeping the legs still worsens stasis; the brick encourages walking or lower extremity exercises when possible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm compresses do not address stasis of blood flow in the leg veins.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with extensive atherosclerosis develops a thrombus in his femoral artery. Which of the following clinical consequences is most directly associated with thrombosis at this site?

explanation.summary: Femoral artery thrombosis leads to peripheral vascular disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that arterial thrombi begin at sites of turbulence or endothelial injury, particularly on atherosclerotic plaques, and that the most common sites are the coronary, cerebral, and femoral arteries, leading respectively to myocardial infarction, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stroke results from cerebral artery thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolytic uremic syndrome is a thrombotic microangiopathy caused by Shiga-like toxin, unrelated to femoral thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary embolism arises from venous thrombi that travel to the lungs, not from an arterial thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myocardial infarction results from coronary artery thrombosis.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a deep vein thrombosis of the right calf suddenly becomes short of breath. A fragment of the thrombus has detached and traveled with the blood. Following the normal course of venous blood, where is this embolus most likely to lodge?

explanation.summary: Venous emboli from leg DVTs travel through the right heart to the lungs, causing pulmonary embolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that venous emboli predominantly arise from deep venous thrombi in the legs and pass through the venous system into the right heart and eventually the lungs, producing pulmonary embolism. The figure shows such an embolus lodged at a pulmonary artery branchpoint.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cerebral arteries are a destination of arterial emboli from mural thrombi in the heart, not venous emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A venous embolus enters the right heart and pulmonary circulation; it does not reach the coronary arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The renal arteries are systemic arterial targets, reached only by arterial emboli.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arterial emboli, not venous ones, lodge in lower extremity arteries.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: At autopsy of an 80-year-old man who died of unrelated causes, the pathologist finds a small thromboembolus lodged in a peripheral branch of the pulmonary artery. The medical record documents no dyspnea, chest pain, or hemodynamic instability. Which of the following best explains the absence of symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most pulmonary emboli lodge in small arteries and are clinically silent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only emboli of fat or air produce respiratory symptoms

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary emboli rarely originate from the deep leg veins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lung's dual blood supply prevents any embolus from lodging

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thromboemboli dissolve completely before reaching the lung

explanation.summary: The majority of pulmonary emboli (60-80%) are clinically silent because they occlude small arteries.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that pulmonary embolism is the most common form of thromboembolic disease, occurring at an estimated 100-200 cases per 100,000 people in the US, and that most pulmonary emboli (60-80%) are clinically silent because they occur in the small arteries.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Thromboemboli that obstruct a large portion of the pulmonary circulation are very symptomatic and can cause sudden death.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Venous emboli predominantly arise from deep venous thrombi in the legs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The dual supply protects against infarction but does not prevent an embolus from lodging in a pulmonary artery branch.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dissolution is one possible fate of a thrombus, but this embolus was found intact in the lung.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man collapses and dies within minutes while walking to the bathroom one week after knee surgery. Autopsy reveals a large thromboembolus obstructing well over half of the pulmonary arterial circulation. Which of the following is the most likely immediate mechanism of death?

explanation.summary: A large clot obstructing 60% or more of the pulmonary circulation causes sudden death from acute right heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that although most pulmonary emboli are silent, when a large clot obstructs 60% or more of the pulmonary circulation it can cause sudden death due to acute right heart failure. The post-operative setting provides the stasis that generates the deep venous source.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DIC is a consumptive thrombohemorrhagic disorder secondary to sepsis, trauma, and other triggers, not the acute effect of a massive PE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat embolism follows long-bone fracture and produces pulmonary insufficiency with neurologic symptoms, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, not a single large thromboembolus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A red infarct of the lung develops over time with a smaller obstruction; it does not explain death within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The obstruction is in the pulmonary circulation, acutely loading the right heart rather than infarcting the left ventricle.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with an untreated calf vein thrombus undergoes serial ultrasound examinations. Over one week the thrombus lengthens and thickens as additional platelets and fibrin are deposited on it. Which fate of the thrombus is being observed?

explanation.summary: Propagation is the growth of a thrombus by acquisition of additional platelets and fibrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists propagation as one of the fates of a thrombus in a surviving patient: the thrombus can acquire additional platelets and fibrin and continue to grow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dissolution is breakdown of the thrombus by fibrinolysis, which would shrink rather than enlarge it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Embolization is detachment of a piece of the thrombus that travels to a distant site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Organization is ingrowth of fibroblasts that deposit collagen within the vessel, not the accumulation of more platelets and fibrin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recanalization is the development of new lumina through an established thrombus, restoring partial flow.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man receiving heparin after a hip replacement is diagnosed with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia on day 7 of therapy. Which of the following is the most likely major complication of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute renal failure from Shiga-like toxin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia from antibody-coated red cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mucocutaneous bleeding from the nose and gums

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venous thrombosis such as DVT or pulmonary embolism

explanation.summary: Despite the low platelet count, the major complication of HIT is thrombosis, most commonly venous.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes HIT as a serious, potentially life-threatening disorder in which antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex activate and aggregate platelets, lowering the count but forming clots. It states that the major complication of HIT is thrombosis, more commonly venous thrombi (DVT, PE).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Shiga-like toxin causes hemolytic uremic syndrome, which is unrelated to heparin exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The antibody in HIT targets the heparin-PF4 complex on platelets, not red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucocutaneous bleeding is characteristic of von Willebrand disease; HIT drives clotting, not bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bleeding into muscles and joints is the pattern of hemophilia A, an inherited bleeding disorder, not HIT.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: An embolus is a detached intravascular mass carried by the blood from its point of origin to a distant site. Which of the following is the most common material composing an embolus?

explanation.summary: A thrombus is by far the most common material that embolizes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an embolus as a detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gaseous mass carried from its point of origin to a distant site, and states that the most common material is a thrombus, with fat, bone marrow, air, amniotic fluid, and foreign bodies as the other types.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare complication of labor and the postpartum period.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat embolism occurs after long-bone fractures or, rarely, soft-tissue trauma and burns; it is a less common embolic material.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foreign body embolism, such as a bullet entering a vessel, is an unusual event.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Air embolism requires communication between the vasculature and outside air and is uncommon compared with thromboembolism.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man sustains a penetrating stab wound to the chest wall. Shortly afterward he develops sudden circulatory collapse, and a frothy mass is found obstructing flow in the right side of the heart at emergency surgery. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A thrombus dislodged from the femoral vein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fat globules released from injured soft tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gas bubbles that entered the circulation and coalesced

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet aggregates from a heparin-PF4 antibody

explanation.summary: Air embolism occurs when a communication with outside air, such as a chest wall injury, lets gas bubbles enter and coalesce into frothy obstructing masses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes air embolism as gas bubbles within the circulation that can coalesce to form frothy masses that obstruct vascular flow. It occurs when there is communication between the vasculature and outside air, with examples including air introduced during endovascular and interventional procedures or chest wall injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A thromboembolus is a solid clot, not a frothy mass, and there is no leg thrombus described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat embolism produces microscopic fat globules, chiefly after long-bone fractures, not a frothy gaseous mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DIC produces microthrombi in small vessels throughout the body, not a single obstructing frothy mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIT requires heparin exposure and causes venous thrombi, not a gaseous obstruction after chest trauma.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man with bilateral femur fractures develops fat embolism syndrome with pulmonary insufficiency, confusion, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. His family asks about the likelihood of death from this syndrome. Based on the described outcomes of symptomatic fat embolism, which of the following is the most accurate estimate of fatality?

explanation.summary: Fat embolism syndrome is fatal in 5-15% of cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that only a minority of patients with fat emboli become symptomatic (fat embolism syndrome), experiencing pulmonary insufficiency, neurologic symptoms, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, and that the syndrome is fatal in 5-15% of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the mortality the brick reports for fat embolism syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This figure is below the stated 5-15% range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This substantially overstates the fatality of fat embolism syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fatality rate this high is not what the brick reports for fat embolism syndrome.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is shot in the abdomen. Imaging shows no bullet at the entry site; instead, the bullet is found lodged in a vessel in the thigh, far from the wound, with no exit wound. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: A bullet that enters a vessel and travels downstream is the classic example of a foreign body embolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines foreign body embolism as occurring when foreign bodies get introduced into the bloodstream, giving the classic example of a bullet that gets into a blood vessel and travels downstream to a distant site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Air embolism involves gas bubbles that coalesce into frothy masses, not a solid object.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amniotic fluid embolism is an obstetric complication of labor and the postpartum period.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat embolism consists of microscopic fat globules after long-bone fractures or soft-tissue trauma, not a projectile.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A thromboembolus is a detached blood clot, not an introduced foreign object.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman develops sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, and shock during a difficult vaginal delivery, and amniotic fluid embolism is diagnosed. By which of the following routes did amniotic fluid most likely enter her circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absorption through the gastrointestinal mucosa into portal blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aspiration into the maternal airways and lungs during pushing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Diffusion across an intact placental barrier into maternal blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage through a chest wall communication with outside air

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism results from infusion of amniotic fluid or fetal tissue into the maternal circulation through a tear in the placental membranes or ruptured uterine veins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines amniotic fluid embolism as infusion of amniotic fluid or fetal tissue into the maternal circulation via a tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins. It is a rare but often fatal complication of labor and the immediate postpartum period, presenting with dyspnea, cyanosis, and shock followed by neurologic impairment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Absorption from the gastrointestinal mucosa is the route of Shiga-like toxin in hemolytic uremic syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The embolus enters the maternal bloodstream directly, not the airway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick describes entry through a tear or venous rupture, not diffusion across an intact placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Communication between the vasculature and outside air is the mechanism of air embolism.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to define an infarct. Which of the following is the most accurate definition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gaseous mass carried to a distant site

choices.label: B
choices.text: A solid mass of clotted blood that partially or completely obstructs a vessel lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: An area of ischemic necrosis from occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversible hypoxic injury to a tissue whose arterial and venous supply remains intact

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncontrolled systemic activation of coagulation forming microthrombi throughout the body

explanation.summary: An infarct is an area of ischemic necrosis caused by occlusion of either the arterial supply or the venous drainage of a tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an infarct as an area of ischemic necrosis caused by occlusion of either the arterial supply or the venous drainage of a tissue, and notes that the vast majority of infarctions arise from arterial thrombosis or arterial embolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the definition of an embolus, not an infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the definition of a thrombus; the thrombus is a cause, not the infarct itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An infarct is necrosis, which is irreversible; reversible hypoxic injury without vascular occlusion is not an infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes disseminated intravascular coagulation.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: At autopsy, a 79-year-old man is found to have complete occlusion of the right coronary artery by an atherosclerotic plaque that had narrowed slowly over many years, yet the myocardium it supplies shows no infarct. Which of the following best explains the absence of infarction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardiac muscle is highly resistant to sustained hypoxic injury

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recanalization restored flow through new channels in the plaque

choices.label: C
choices.text: The heart has a dual arterial blood supply like the liver

choices.label: D
choices.text: The slow occlusion allowed collateral circulation to develop

choices.label: E
choices.text: The thrombus dissolved by fibrinolysis before causing damage

explanation.summary: Slowly developing occlusions are less likely to cause infarction because there is time for collateral circulation to develop.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists rate of occlusion as a factor influencing tissue sensitivity to infarction, explaining that slowly-developing occlusions are less likely to cause infarction because there is time to develop collateral circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heart muscle is relatively vulnerable, starting to die after only 20-30 minutes of ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recanalization involves new lumina through an organized thrombus; the artery here is completely occluded by plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The heart has a single, end-arterial circulation, which is why it develops white infarcts when acutely occluded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vessel is described as completely occluded at autopsy, so dissolution did not occur.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: Two patients each develop a thromboembolus of similar size in a comparable branch of the same artery. The first is a healthy 35-year-old marathon runner; the second is a 78-year-old with chronic heart failure and anemia. The second patient develops a much larger infarct. Which factor best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anatomy of the vascular supply to the tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rate of development of the occlusion

explanation.summary: Patients with a healthier cardiovascular system and blood supply tolerate thrombosis better.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists four factors that influence tissue sensitivity to hypoxia and infarction: anatomy of the vascular supply, rate of occlusion, tissue vulnerability to hypoxia, and cardiovascular status. It states that patients with a healthier cardiovascular system and blood supply typically better tolerate thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both emboli occur in a comparable branch of the same artery, so vascular anatomy is the same.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both events are acute embolic occlusions, so the rate of occlusion does not differ.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The emboli are described as similar in size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The same tissue is affected in both patients, so intrinsic vulnerability to hypoxia is equal.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man has an acute thrombotic occlusion of a coronary artery. Approximately how long after the onset of ischemia does the heart muscle begin to die?

explanation.summary: Heart muscle starts to die after only 20-30 minutes of ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under tissue vulnerability to hypoxia, the brick states that brain tissue undergoes irreversible damage after only a few minutes of hypoxia and, similarly, heart muscle starts to die after only 20-30 minutes of ischemia, whereas skeletal muscle may survive a few hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Even the brain, the most vulnerable tissue, requires a few minutes; cardiac muscle is not damaged within a minute.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A few hours is the approximate survival window the brick gives for skeletal muscle, not heart muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is far longer than the 20-30 minute threshold the brick gives for cardiac muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiac muscle death begins long before 24 hours of ischemia.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has an embolic occlusion of a branch of the superior mesenteric artery. At surgery the affected segment of small intestine is dark red and hemorrhagic rather than pale. Which of the following best explains the red color of this infarct?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deposition of microthrombi throughout the mucosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inflow of blood from an unobstructed parallel supply

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rapid organization of the infarct by fibroblasts

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the occluded artery with hemorrhage

explanation.summary: Red infarcts occur in dual-circulation tissues because blood from the unobstructed parallel supply flows into the necrotic zone.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that red infarcts occur in tissues with dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine) in which blood can flow from the unobstructed parallel supply into a necrotic zone. The names of red and white infarcts refer to the color seen macroscopically in the tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absence of a parallel supply produces a pale white infarct, as in the heart, spleen, and kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Widespread microthrombi are the hallmark of DIC, not the explanation for a red infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organization is a later fate of a thrombus and does not account for the hemorrhagic appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The red color comes from blood entering necrotic tissue through a parallel supply, not from rupture of the occluded vessel.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman is admitted three days after delivery with fever and persistent vaginal bleeding; ultrasound shows retained products of conception. She then begins oozing blood from venipuncture sites and develops thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Which of the following best describes her retained products of conception in relation to her new bleeding disorder?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recognized obstetric trigger of DIC

choices.label: D
choices.text: A trigger for antibodies against platelet factor 4

explanation.summary: Obstetric complications, including retained products of conception, are listed causes of DIC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table of causes of DIC lists infection, obstetric complications (amniotic fluid embolism, retained products of conception), major trauma or surgery, and acute hemolytic transfusion reactions. DIC occurs as a secondary complication of such disorders and presents with oozing from puncture sites and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inherited hypercoagulability refers to genetic disorders such as Factor V Leiden, not a postpartum complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Shiga-like toxin comes from E. coli O157:H7 gastroenteritis and causes hemolytic uremic syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex arise from heparin exposure, causing HIT.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retained products of conception are specifically named in the brick's table as an obstetric cause of DIC.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with extensive crush injuries after a building collapse develops disseminated intravascular coagulation. Which of the following pairs best describes the two major mechanisms that trigger DIC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Formation of heparin-PF4 antibody and antibody-mediated platelet aggregation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inherited Factor V Leiden mutation and the prothrombin G20210A gene mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary excess fibrinolysis and an inherited deficiency of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of tissue factor into the circulation and widespread endothelial injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venous stasis and turbulent arterial flow over plaques

explanation.summary: DIC is triggered by release of tissue factor or other procoagulants into the circulation and by widespread injury of endothelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that two major mechanisms trigger DIC: release of tissue factor or other procoagulants into the circulation, and widespread injury of endothelial cells. Major trauma is one of the listed causes. The resulting uncontrolled coagulation forms microvascular thrombi while using up platelets and clotting factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody against the heparin-PF4 complex is the mechanism of HIT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These are inherited hypercoagulable states that predispose to venous thrombosis, not the triggers of DIC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinolysis in DIC is a secondary consequence of consumption, and von Willebrand factor deficiency is a separate bleeding disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stasis and turbulence are abnormal blood flow patterns from Virchow's triad, not the mechanism of DIC.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A hematologist is evaluating three patients: one with DIC secondary to sepsis, one with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and one with hemolytic uremic syndrome. Which of the following features is shared by all three thrombotic microangiopathies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An elevated platelet count with large platelet-rich thrombi in the major arteries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody-mediated platelet activation directed at a drug-protein complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delayed bleeding into muscles and joints with a normal platelet count

choices.label: D
choices.text: Frothy gaseous masses obstructing the pulmonary arterial vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and microvascular thrombi

explanation.summary: DIC, TTP, and HUS are all thrombotic microangiopathies characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and microvascular thrombi.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that DIC is on the differential with other thrombotic microangiopathies like TTP and HUS, and that these disorders are characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and deposition of microvascular thrombi.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thrombotic microangiopathies cause thrombocytopenia and small-vessel thrombi, not thrombocytosis with large arterial clots.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Drug-protein complex antibodies describe HIT, which is not one of the three disorders listed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bleeding into muscles and joints is the pattern of hemophilia A, and these disorders lower the platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frothy gaseous masses are the finding in air embolism.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A 50-year-old long-haul truck driver is diagnosed with a deep venous thrombosis of the leg attributed to prolonged stasis during his trips. He is started on an anticoagulant. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional counseling to reduce his risk of recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoid all physical activity until the clot has dissolved

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stop driving permanently to avoid any further stasis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Take regular breaks during trips to walk and exercise the legs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Undergo testing to unmask a Factor V Leiden mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wear sequential compression devices while driving

explanation.summary: Patients at risk of stasis from long trips should take regular breaks to walk or perform lower extremity exercises.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case connection explains that the truck driver's clot developed from prolonged stasis during long road trips. In addition to anticoagulant medication, he is counseled on the importance of taking regular breaks to stretch his legs and get the blood moving. The clinical correlation encourages regular breaks to walk or do lower extremity exercises for bed rest, long flights, and long road trips.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Avoiding activity would worsen stasis; the advice is to keep the legs moving.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick's counseling is to take regular breaks during trips, not to give up driving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The clot is attributed to stasis; nothing suggests an inherited hypercoagulable state to be unmasked.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequential compression devices are described for post-operative patients who cannot ambulate, not for drivers who can take walking breaks.

questions.topicName: Thrombosis and its Consequences

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient being treated for dehydration has an intravenous line delivering 5% dextrose in water (D5W). A nurse draws a blood sample from the arm containing the running IV without first turning it off. The chemistry laboratory reports a markedly and falsely elevated glucose level. This error occurred during which of the following phases of laboratory testing?

explanation.summary: Errors introduced before the specimen reaches the laboratory belong to the pre-analytic phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pre-analytic phase spans from ordering the test to the specimen being received into the laboratory. Contamination of a blood draw by running IV dextrose fluid happens at collection, before the specimen ever reaches the lab, and most laboratory errors occur during this phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The analytic phase is the time actually spent performing the test on the specimen in the laboratory, which was not the source of this error.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 'Interpretive phase' is not a defined phase in the pre-/analytic/post-analytic model.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The post-analytic phase is the time from reporting the result to the clinician reviewing it and making decisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 'Quality-control phase' is not one of the three phases of laboratory testing described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A technologist loads a properly collected serum tube onto an automated chemistry analyzer, which is now measuring the patient's electrolytes. This step of the total testing process best represents which of the following phases?

explanation.summary: The analytic phase is the time spent actually performing the test in the laboratory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once a valid specimen is in the laboratory and the instrument is running the assay to generate a measurement, the process is in the analytic phase, defined as the time spent performing the test.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 'Collection phase' is not one of the three named phases; collection falls within the pre-analytic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The post-analytic phase begins only after the result is reported to the clinician.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pre-analytic phase already ended when the specimen was received into the laboratory.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 'Reporting phase' is not a named phase; reporting begins the post-analytic phase.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A surgical patient is scheduled to receive packed red blood cells. A blood sample is drawn so the correct product can be prepared. To which section of the clinical laboratory is this specimen primarily sent?

explanation.summary: Blood typing and preparation of blood products for transfusion are performed by the transfusion medicine (blood bank) laboratory.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blood bank / transfusion medicine laboratory is concerned with blood transfusion, cellular therapies, and apheresis. It performs ABO and Rh typing and antibody screening so blood products such as red cells, platelets, and plasma can be transfused safely.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical chemistry measures analytes such as electrolytes and glucose, not blood-product compatibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematology performs the CBC and coagulation testing but does not prepare transfusion products.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microbiology diagnoses infections and does not manage transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinalysis evaluates urine and accepts only urine specimens.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A recent medical school graduate undergoing residency orientation reveals a past infection with chicken pox (varicella-zoster virus). To confirm immunity, a blood sample is drawn to detect antibodies against the virus. This test is performed by which section of the clinical laboratory?

explanation.summary: Detecting antibodies to confirm immunity or past infection is a function of the immunology and serology laboratory.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immunology and serology laboratory identifies antibodies that can confirm current or past infection or establish immunity. Testing serum for antibodies against the varicella-zoster virus falls squarely within this section's role.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The blood bank types blood and prepares products for transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical chemistry measures analytes such as electrolytes and glucose, not immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematology counts blood cells and evaluates clotting, not viral antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinalysis evaluates urine samples, not serum antibodies.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: Blood is collected into a tube that contains an anticoagulant and is then centrifuged (spun down) to separate the cells. The fluid layer remaining above the packed red and white blood cells is used for analysis. This fluid is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Plasma is the fluid left above the cells when anticoagulated blood is centrifuged.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plasma analysis uses blood collected in a tube with an anticoagulant; once the specimen is centrifuged, the plasma is the fluid left over after the red and white blood cells are separated to the bottom.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cerebrospinal fluid is collected from the spinal canal by lumbar puncture, not from a blood tube.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryoprecipitate is a transfusion product, not the supernatant of a spun blood tube.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum is obtained from blood collected WITHOUT an anticoagulant that is allowed to clot.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole blood is analyzed directly and has not had its cells separated out.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A blood specimen is drawn into a tube that contains NO anticoagulant and is allowed to clot. The straw-colored fluid that separates from the clot is then used for antibody testing. Which of the following specimens is being described?

explanation.summary: Serum is the fluid that separates from blood after it clots, without any anticoagulant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum analysis uses blood collected in a tube without an anticoagulant; serum is the fluid that separates from the blood when it clots. Serology (antibody testing) is performed on this clot-derived fluid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bone marrow aspirate is taken from inside a bone, not from a clotted blood tube.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The buffy coat is the white-cell/platelet layer of centrifuged blood, not the clot supernatant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma requires an anticoagulant in the tube and is obtained by centrifuging unclotted blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole blood contains all cellular elements and is not separated from a clot.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A trauma patient is actively bleeding, and the team requests components of blood — red cells, platelets, plasma, and cryoprecipitate — to be issued urgently. Which section of the clinical laboratory is responsible for preparing and issuing these products?

explanation.summary: Issuing blood components for transfusion is the role of the transfusion medicine (blood bank) laboratory.
explanation.whyCorrect: A key aspect of the transfusion medicine laboratory is transfusing components of blood to a bleeding patient, such as giving red cells, platelets, plasma, and cryoprecipitate. This section also handles blood typing, antibody screening, and apheresis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical chemistry measures analytes like electrolytes and glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematology performs the CBC and coagulation studies but does not issue blood products.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunology and serology detect antibodies and determine transplant compatibility, not transfusion issuance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microbiology cultures specimens to diagnose infection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: During an annual physical, a healthy 45-year-old man has blood drawn for a routine test that measures cholesterol and triglyceride levels to assess his risk of developing atherosclerosis. This test is run by which section of the clinical laboratory?

explanation.summary: Lipid testing to gauge atherosclerosis risk is a clinical chemistry test.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical chemistry laboratory uses biochemical and molecular techniques and runs tests including lipid panels. A routine lipid test is ordered to assess a patient's risk of developing atherosclerosis, a stated clinical correlation for this section.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The blood bank types blood and prepares transfusion products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematology performs blood cell counts and coagulation testing, not lipid measurement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microbiology cultures specimens to diagnose infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinalysis evaluates urine, not serum lipids.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A physician orders a routine test that reports the numbers of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets along with a differential, and it reveals an unexpected anemia. Which section of the clinical laboratory performed this test?

explanation.summary: The complete blood count (CBC) with differential is a hematology test.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hematology laboratory performs routine hematologic testing such as the complete blood count with differential. A CBC is routinely ordered on annual physical exams and may reveal an abnormality such as anemia that needs further evaluation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The blood bank types blood and prepares transfusion products.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical chemistry measures analytes such as electrolytes and glucose, not blood cell counts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunology and serology detect antibodies and immune abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microbiology cultures specimens to diagnose infection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) test is performed on Staphylococcus aureus isolated from a wound. Antibiotic-impregnated disks are placed on a lawn of the growing organism. After incubation, there is a clear zone of inhibited growth around most disks, but NO zone around the ampicillin (AM) disk. What does the absence of a zone around the ampicillin disk indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ampicillin disk was placed at the wrong concentration

choices.label: B
choices.text: The culture is contaminated with a second organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organism cannot grow on this medium

choices.label: D
choices.text: The organism is highly susceptible to ampicillin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism is resistant to ampicillin

explanation.summary: No zone of inhibition around an antibiotic disk means the organism is resistant to that drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: In disk diffusion testing, a significant circle of inhibited growth around a disk indicates the antibiotic works against the organism. When there is no zone, such as around the ampicillin (AM) disk, it indicates the organism is resistant to that medication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The absence of a zone reflects the organism's resistance, not a disk concentration error.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Confluent growth up to the disk indicates resistance, not contamination by another organism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The organism clearly grew, since it formed a lawn and showed zones around other disks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Susceptibility is shown by a LARGE zone of inhibition, the opposite of what is described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hospital's microbiology laboratory compiles the antimicrobial susceptibility results from all cultures performed over the past year into a single summary report. A clinician consults this report when a patient presents with a serious infection before culture results are available. This report is best used for which of the following purposes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirming a single patient's blood type before transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Counting red and white blood cells in a specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Detecting antibodies that confirm immunity to a virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Guiding the choice of initial empiric antibiotic therapy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measuring a patient's serum electrolyte concentrations

explanation.summary: An antibiogram summarizes local susceptibility data to guide empiric antibiotic selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: An antibiogram is a compilation of antimicrobial susceptibility test results from cultures performed during a given time period in a particular hospital or reference lab. Hospitals use it to help clinicians pick the initial therapy and to understand local resistance patterns and trends.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood typing before transfusion is a blood bank function unrelated to an antibiogram.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Counting blood cells is the role of the hematology CBC, not the antibiogram.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody testing for immunity is performed by immunology and serology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Electrolyte measurement is a clinical chemistry test, not a susceptibility summary.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A patient presents with fever and dysuria, and a urinary tract infection is suspected. A urine sample is sent to the laboratory specifically to grow and identify the causative organism and to determine which antibiotic will be effective against it. To which section of the clinical laboratory should this sample be directed for that purpose?

explanation.summary: Growing an organism from urine and testing its antibiotic susceptibility is a microbiology function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The microbiology laboratory assists with diagnosis, treatment, and control of infectious disease, including urine culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. It identifies the organism causing the infection and determines which antibiotic will work against it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical chemistry measures analytes such as electrolytes and glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematology counts blood cells and assesses clotting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunology and serology detect antibodies rather than culturing organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinalysis can screen the urine for signs of infection but does not culture and identify the organism or its susceptibilities.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a serum potassium measured on an automated analyzer. The laboratory reports a critically high value in the electronic record. The admitting physician reviews the result that evening and decides to start treatment to lower the potassium. The physician's review of the reported value and the treatment decision that follows belong to which phase of the total testing process?

explanation.summary: The post-analytic phase runs from reporting the result to the clinician reviewing it and making clinical decisions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The post-analytic phase is defined as the time from reporting the results to the clinician reviewing and making clinical decisions based on the results. Once the potassium value is reported, everything the physician does with it, including reviewing it and deciding to treat, falls in this phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The analytic phase is the time spent performing the test in the laboratory, which ended when the analyzer produced the value.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 'Collection phase' is not one of the three named phases; specimen collection is part of the pre-analytic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pre-analytic phase spans ordering the test through receipt of the specimen in the laboratory, well before any result exists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 'Verification phase' is not one of the three named phases of the total testing process.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is told to arrive at the clinic fasting for a morning glucose measurement. She eats a full breakfast on the way in and does not mention it. Her specimen is correctly labeled, drawn from the arm opposite any IV, transported promptly, and run without instrument error, yet the glucose result is misleadingly high. This source of error is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A post-analytic error caused by delayed reporting of the final result

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pre-analytic error caused by mislabeling of the collected specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pre-analytic error caused by physiologic changes in the patient

choices.label: D
choices.text: An analytic error caused by improper calibration of the analyzer

choices.label: E
choices.text: An analytic error caused by malfunction of the testing instrument

explanation.summary: Physiologic changes in the patient, such as effects of diet, medications, or stress, are a pre-analytic source of laboratory error.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most sources of laboratory error occur during the pre-analytic phase, before the specimen reaches the laboratory. Besides collection problems, these include physiologic changes in the patient, specifically the effects of diet, medications, and stress on laboratory testing. A recent meal altering a fasting glucose is exactly this kind of error.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The result was not delayed or misreported; the problem existed before the specimen was drawn.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mislabeling is a pre-analytic collection error, but the specimen here was correctly labeled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calibration is part of performing the test (analytic phase) and is not implicated when the instrument ran correctly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stem states the test ran without instrument error, so the analytic phase was not the source.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hospital quality committee is mapping the total testing process to determine exactly where the pre-analytic phase ends and the analytic phase begins. Which of the following events marks that boundary?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The clinician makes a decision based on the result

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phlebotomist draws the specimen from the patient

choices.label: C
choices.text: The physician selects and orders the test

choices.label: D
choices.text: The result is reported to the clinician

choices.label: E
choices.text: The specimen is received into the laboratory

explanation.summary: The pre-analytic phase ends when the specimen is received into the laboratory, at which point the analytic phase begins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pre-analytic phase is the time from the physician selecting and ordering a test to the specimen being received into the laboratory. The analytic phase is the time spent performing the test in the laboratory, so receipt of the specimen into the lab is the hand-off point between the two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical decision-making based on the result is the end of the post-analytic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Collection of the specimen occurs within the pre-analytic phase; the specimen has not yet reached the laboratory.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Selecting and ordering the test is the START of the pre-analytic phase, not its end.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reporting the result marks the start of the post-analytic phase, after the analytic phase is complete.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hospital administrator asks a pathologist why the laboratory deserves so much investment in quality oversight. The pathologist cites the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate of how heavily clinicians depend on laboratory results. Roughly what proportion of healthcare decisions depend on laboratory test results?

explanation.summary: Roughly 70% of healthcare decisions depend on laboratory test results.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinicians heavily rely on laboratory tests to make critical decisions about patient care; according to the CDC, roughly 70% of healthcare decisions depend on laboratory test results. Because of this central role, pathologists and laboratory scientists oversee lab medicine testing to ensure high-quality results.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 10% greatly understates the stated dependence of clinical decisions on laboratory data.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 30% is well below the roughly 70% figure cited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 50% is below the roughly 70% figure cited.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 95% overstates the figure; the cited estimate is roughly 70%.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is told that a particular branch of pathology focuses on examining blood and other body samples for functional abnormalities and is concerned with disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. By which of the following alternative names is this branch also known?

explanation.summary: Clinical pathology is also known as laboratory medicine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clinical pathology, also known as laboratory medicine, is the section of pathology that focuses on the examination of blood and other body samples for functional abnormalities. It is concerned with disease diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, and its subdisciplines are based on the type of analysis performed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytopathology is not the name used for the branch that examines blood and body fluid samples in the laboratory sections described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forensic pathology is not the alternative name given for the branch that examines blood and body samples for functional abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular oncology is not an alternative name for clinical pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surgical pathology is not the alternative name for the branch described; it is not one of the clinical pathology subdisciplines listed.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with dysuria is handed a specimen cup and instructed to first cleanse the outer genital area and then urinate into the cup. Which method of urine collection is being used?

explanation.summary: A clean catch specimen is one in which the outer genital area is cleaned before the patient urinates into a cup.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urine can be collected as a clean catch specimen, a sterile collection, or a random urine. In the clean catch method, the outer genital area is cleaned before the patient urinates into a cup, which is exactly the instruction given here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fingerstick is a method of collecting blood, not urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A random urine is collected by the patient urinating into a cup WITHOUT previous cleaning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sterile collection is usually performed via catheter, not by the patient voiding into a cup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A suction catheter is a method for collecting sputum, not urine.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman with dementia cannot follow instructions for voiding into a cup, and the team wants a urine specimen obtained under sterile conditions. Which of the following is the usual method for obtaining a sterile urine collection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspirating fluid with a needle under bronchoscopic guidance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleansing the outer genital area and then having the patient void

choices.label: C
choices.text: Collecting the urine via a catheter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drawing the specimen with a needle from a forearm vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Having the patient void into a clean container without cleansing

explanation.summary: Sterile urine collection is usually performed via catheter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the urine collection methods, sterile collection is described as usually being performed via catheter, in contrast to the clean catch and random specimens that rely on the patient voiding into a cup.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoscopy is used to collect sputum from the airway, not urine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleansing the outer genital area before voiding describes a clean catch specimen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Venipuncture from a forearm vein is the method for collecting blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voiding into a cup without previous cleaning describes a random urine specimen, not a sterile collection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 70-year-old intubated man in the intensive care unit has a suspected pneumonia, and the team needs a specimen of phlegm from his lower airway for testing. Because he cannot cough a sample into a container, which of the following is an appropriate alternative method of collecting this specimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clean catch collection into a sterile cup

choices.label: B
choices.text: Joint aspiration of the synovial space

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lumbar puncture of the subarachnoid space

explanation.summary: Sputum can be coughed into a clean container or collected with a suction catheter or bronchoscope.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sputum (phlegm) is normally coughed into a clean container. When the patient cannot produce a sample this way, sputum can instead be collected with a suction catheter or a bronchoscope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clean catch is a urine collection method.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Joint aspiration collects joint fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lumbar puncture collects spinal fluid, not sputum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paracentesis collects abdominal fluid, not a respiratory specimen.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has a distended abdomen with fluid accumulation. His physician wants to send a sample of this abdominal fluid to the clinical laboratory. Which procedure is used to obtain this specimen?

explanation.summary: Abdominal fluid is collected by paracentesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the other body fluids sent to the clinical laboratory, abdominal fluid is obtained via paracentesis. Each body fluid has its own collection procedure: spinal fluid via lumbar puncture, pleural fluid via thoracentesis, joint fluid via joint aspiration, and bone marrow via bone marrow aspiration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow aspiration obtains bone marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lumbar puncture obtains spinal fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thoracentesis obtains pleural fluid from the chest, not abdominal fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venipuncture obtains blood from a vein.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with shortness of breath undergoes a thoracentesis, and the fluid obtained is sent to the clinical laboratory. Which type of specimen has been collected?

explanation.summary: Thoracentesis is the procedure used to collect pleural fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pleural fluid is one of the other body fluids sent to the clinical laboratory, and it is collected via thoracentesis. Body fluids such as this may be analyzed by several laboratory sections, including clinical chemistry, hematology, immunology and serology, and microbiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abdominal fluid is collected via paracentesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow is collected via bone marrow aspiration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Joint fluid is collected via joint aspiration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spinal fluid is collected via lumbar puncture, not thoracentesis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Clinical Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A phlebotomist prepares to collect a blood specimen from a 40-year-old man for routine testing. Which of the following describes the standard method of collecting blood, as listed for this specimen type?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aspiration with a needle from a joint space under sterile prep

choices.label: B
choices.text: Collection by the patient into a clean, dry container at home

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sterile collection through an indwelling bladder catheter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suction through a bronchoscope placed in the lower airway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venipuncture with a needle from a vein, often in the forearm

explanation.summary: Blood is collected by venipuncture (a needle drawing from a vein, often the forearm) or by fingerstick.
explanation.whyCorrect: The methods of collection listed for blood are venipuncture, in which blood is drawn with a needle from a vein, often in the forearm, and fingerstick. Venipuncture is the standard approach for routine blood testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Needle aspiration of a joint space obtains joint fluid, not blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Collection by the patient into a clean container describes stool collection.
